papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in Breast Cancer Diagnosis, Treatment, and Perioperative Management: A Systematic Review of Current Applications and Future Perspectives.
papers.authors: Mostafa AF, Mady R, Abu Halimah JH, Hassan N, Elshebiny AA, Abdelazeem MAA, Salem LN, Abdrabo AA, Ibrahem M, Elzeiny A, Abdelaziz SMME, Hakami AH, Sayegh AA, Hegazy HA, Ahmed IS.
papers.abstract: Background Breast cancer is the most frequently diagnosed malignancy in women globally, accounting for approximately 2.30 million new cases and 666,103 deaths in 2022. Artificial intelligence technologies including machine learning, deep learning, radiomics, and natural language processing have been widely applied across the breast cancer care continuum. However, no systematic review restricted to primary studies with patient-level or image-level data has synthesized evidence spanning all clinical domains simultaneously. Objectives To evaluate the performance, methodological quality, and clinical relevance of artificial intelligence primary studies across screening and diagnostic imaging, digital pathology, radiomics, perioperative management, prognostic prediction, and natural language processing in breast cancer. Methods PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched from January 2015 to May 2026. Eligibility was restricted to original primary research reporting patient-level or image-level data; secondary syntheses were explicitly excluded. Risk of bias was assessed using QUADAS-2 and PROBAST. Reporting followed PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Results Of 5,275 identified records, 17 primary studies met eligibility criteria. In screening mammography (seven studies; n = 7,540 to 144,231 examinations), deep learning achieved area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) values of 0.876 to 0.939; a randomised trial in 80,033 women demonstrated non-inferiority to double reading with a 44.3% reduction in radiologist workload. In digital pathology (five studies; 270 to 44,732 whole-slide images), deep learning achieved AUC 0.985 to 0.994, exceeding unassisted pathologist performance in lymph node metastasis detection. Magnetic resonance imaging radiomics predicted pathological complete response in HER2-positive breast cancer with AUC 0.80. No breast cancer-specific perioperative primary study met the eligibility criteria. Deep survival networks achieved concordance index 0.626 versus 0.612 for Cox regression in breast cancer cohorts. Natural language processing identified metastatic recurrence in breast cancer clinical records with sensitivity 83% and specificity 73%. Risk of bias was low to moderate for imaging and pathology studies and high for small sample radiomics studies. Density-stratified performance was reported by only two imaging studies, and receptor status prediction from haematoxylin and eosin staining had not been validated as a safe alternative to immunohistochemistry. Conclusions Artificial intelligence demonstrated clinically meaningful performance across the five domains with eligible primary studies. Breast cancer-specific perioperative and intensive care primary studies were absent, representing the largest evidence gap. External validation, demographic diversity, and prospective clinical integration evidence remained the most consistently identified limitations. Prediction of molecular receptor status without immunohistochemistry requires rigorous prospective safety validation before it can complement standard testing.
keywords: Artificial Intelligence; Machine Learning; Deep Learning; Breast Cancer; Mammography; Digital Pathology; Radiomics; Perioperative; Natural Language Processing; Systematic Review

papers.title: Evaluation of surrogate biomarkers of memory and cognition in aging adults with vitamin B12 deficiency: A cross-sectional study.
papers.authors: Mehraj S, Sudha K, Neelam MP, Sowndarya K, Dushyanth B.
papers.abstract: Background Vitamin B12 (Vit B12) is a cofactor in one-carbon metabolism, methylation reactions, myelin synthesis, and neuronal function. Its deficiency can lead to neurodegeneration and cognitive decline. This study aims to evaluate cognitive and memory-related biomarkers in otherwise healthy aging adults with vitamin B12 deficiency and to explore whether it is an under recognized contributor to dementia. Methods Serum levels of Aβ42, acetylcholinesterase (AChE), brain derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), GSH, and calcium were estimated in ninety healthy individuals, aged between 45 to 65 years. They were divided into 3 groups of 30 participants each, as vit B12 sufficient (>300 pg/ml), insufficient (201-300 pg/ml) and deficient (≤200pg/ml) groups. Serum BDNF and Aβ42 were estimated by sandwich ELISA. Calcium, GSH and AChE were measured spectrophotometrically. Results Aβ42 levels showed a significant increase in both insufficient and deficient groups relative to the sufficient group (p<0.001) There was an apparent decrease in BDNF levels and a significant decline in AChE levels in the deficient group compared to the sufficient group (p=0.029). There was a more pronounced decrease in GSH in the deficient group (p<0.001) compared to the sufficient group. Notably, serum calcium levels demonstrated a significant increase in the insufficient group followed by normalization in the deficient group. Conclusion Overall, the findings indicate that Vit B12 deficiency is associated with significant alterations in cognitive biomarkers and oxidative stress causing neuronal loss, which may contribute to memory deficits and cognitive decline. Therefore, vitamin B12 deficiency may be a significant, modifiable risk factor for dementia.

papers.title: Neurodevelopmental Outcomes of Very Preterm Infants Who Underwent Neonatal Gastrointestinal Surgery: A Single-Center Retrospective Cohort Study.
papers.authors: Kim JH, Shim S, Lin CY, Jeong Y, Lee S, Baek SH, Han J, Eun H, Park MS, Ho IG, Shin JE.
papers.abstract: Purpose Advances in neonatal care have improved the survival of very preterm infants, but neurodevelopment remains a concern. This study aimed to investigate whether neonatal gastrointestinal (GI) surgery independently contributes to adverse neurodevelopmental outcomes in such infants, distinct from the underlying illness severity. Materials and methods In this retrospective cohort study (2011-2023) of infants born at <32 weeks' gestation, propensity score matching (1:2) yielded 32 surgical and 66 non-surgical infants. Neurodevelopment was assessed using Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development (BSID) II or III at 6-12 and 18-24 months' corrected age. Brain magnetic resonance images (MRIs) at term-equivalent age (TEA) were analyzed for gross structural abnormalities and white matter injury (WMI). Results The surgery group demonstrated a higher rate of gross structural abnormality (31.3% vs. 9.1%, p =0.005) and a numerically higher proportion of moderate WMI (18.7% vs. 6.1%, p =0.079) on TEA-MRI. Neurodevelopmental assessments revealed that the surgery group had lower BSID scores and a higher prevalence of severe impairment (scores <70) in both cognitive and motor domains at all follow-up points (all p <0.05). Multivariable logistic regression identified neonatal GI surgery as being independently associated with severe cognitive delay [adjusted odds ratio (aOR): 11.16, 95% confidence interval (CI): 1.81-68.68] and severe motor delay (aOR: 10.72, 95% CI: 2.13-53.99) at 18-24 months. Conclusion Very preterm infants requiring neonatal GI surgery represent a high-risk population for adverse neurodevelopmental outcomes, even after accounting for prematurity and major comorbidities. Long-term neurodevelopmental surveillance and early intervention are warranted in this vulnerable group.

papers.title: Effects of Alendronate and Alfacalcidol on Preventing Bone Loss in Chemotherapy-treated Soft-tissue Sarcoma.
papers.authors: Nakanishi M, Tsuchie H, Nagasawa H, Hongo M, Kasukawa Y, Nozaka K, Kawaragi T, Watanabe M, Asaka Y, Morishita YO, Miyakoshi N.
papers.abstract: Background/aim Cancer treatment-induced bone loss (CTIBL) increases fracture risk and impairs quality of life, but little is known about CTIBL in soft-tissue sarcoma. This study aimed to investigate whether alendronate and alfacalcidol prevent doxorubicin-induced bone loss in a mouse model of soft-tissue sarcoma. Materials and methods Sarcoma S-180II cells were transplanted subcutaneously into 10-week-old female BALB/c mice using an air-pouch model. After tumor engraftment, mice received weekly intraperitoneal doxorubicin and were allocated to one of four groups: vehicle control, alendronate, alfacalcidol, and alendronate plus alfacalcidol. Alendronate was administered subcutaneously twice weekly, and alfacalcidol was administered orally three times weekly. Mice were euthanized 2 or 4 weeks after tumor transplantation. Body weight, tumor weight and volume, femoral microstructure by micro-computed tomography, histomorphometric indices by tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase (TRAP) staining and osteocalcin immunostaining, and receptor activator of nuclear factor-κB ligand (RANKL) and runt-related transcription factor 2 (RUNX2) expression were evaluated. Results Body weight and tumor parameters did not differ among groups. At 2 weeks, combination therapy had significantly increased trabecular bone volume fraction, thickness, and number compared with the vehicle control. At 4 weeks, alendronate alone and combination therapy had preserved trabecular bone volume and number and reduced trabecular separation; combination therapy resulted in higher bone-volume fraction and trabecular number than alendronate alone. Cortical bone area and thickness were also greater in all drug-treated groups than in the control at 4 weeks. TRAP staining showed significant suppression of osteoclast-related indices in the alendronate- and combination-treated groups, whereas no significant differences were observed in osteocalcin, RANKL, or RUNX2 expression. Conclusion Alendronate may prevent doxorubicin-associated bone loss in soft-tissue sarcoma, primarily by directly suppressing residual osteoclast activity in vivo .

papers.title: Cranial and Spinal Epithelioid Hemangioma: Systematic Review and Illustrative Calvarial Case.
papers.authors: Scalia G, Ferini G, Galvano G, Trombatore P, Giurato E, Graziano F, Nicoletti GF.
papers.abstract: Background/aim Cranial and neuraxial epithelioid hemangioma (EH) is exceptionally rare and anatomically heterogeneous. We systematically reviewed reported cerebral, cranial osseous, primary non-osseous spinal epidural, and vertebral-origin EH with clinically relevant neuraxial extension and present an illustrative hypervascular calvarial case. Materials and methods Electronic searches of MEDLINE via PubMed were supplemented by Google Scholar, Crossref, Semantic Scholar, publisher archives, conference/supplement searches, and backward and forward citation tracking through 19 August 2026. Histologically confirmed EH involving brain parenchyma, cranial bone with relevant intracranial or craniovertebral extension, primary non-osseous spinal epidural space, or vertebral bone with secondary intraspinal/foraminal extension was eligible. Results Twenty-two reports were included: 14 (63.6%) vertebral-origin and eight (36.4%) cerebral, combined calvarial-cerebral, cranial osseous, or primary non-osseous spinal epidural. Surgery was reported in 19/22 publications (86.4%), radiotherapy in 10/22 (45.5%), and preoperative embolization in 3/22 (13.6%). Recurrence, progression, or new post-treatment disease was explicitly described in three reports, but heterogeneous follow-up precluded pooled recurrence estimates. The illustrative 32-year-old man had a histomorphologically diagnosed hypervascular parasagittal calvarial EH compressing a patent superior sagittal sinus and underwent Onyx embolization followed by excision and cranioplasty. Conclusion Cranial and neuraxial EH is rare, with published evidence dominated by vertebral disease. Management should be individualized according to anatomical compartment, neural compression, structural instability, and vascularity. Histological distinction from epithelioid hemangioendothelioma and angiosarcoma is essential, while the available evidence is insufficient to establish comparative efficacy of radiotherapy or embolization.

papers.title: Capturing the Attentional Trade-off between Speech Planning and Comprehension.
papers.authors: Hustá C, Meyer A.
papers.abstract: In conversation, future speakers often plan speech simultaneously with comprehension, which means that they must divide attentional resources between these processes. In this EEG study, we used responses to linguistic attention probes (i.e., syllable "BA" presented during spoken sentences) to track temporal variations in attention to comprehension. Participants were asked to listen to prerecorded sentences with expected or unexpected sentence-final words. Each sentence was presented twice, once with and once without the attention probe starting 100 msec after the target word onset. Participants saw a picture 50 msec before the target word. Depending on the test block (picture naming or button press), participants either named the picture or pressed the space bar, both after an 850-msec delay. The probes elicited a negative potential approximately 100 msec after probe onset (i.e., an attention probe effect) in all probe conditions. Unexpectedly, neither word expectancy nor speech planning influenced the timing or strength of the attention probe effect. This indicates that expectancy of words in Dutch does not affect the allocation of attention toward these words 100 msec after their onset (i.e., the time of the probe presentation). Interestingly, engaging in speech planning does not seem to divert attentional resources away from comprehension at the moment of probe presentation. These findings imply that listeners are able to effectively distribute their attentional resources between comprehension and speech planning and carry out these processes at the same time. Considering these unexpected findings, using attention probes might not be the best approach to capture variations in temporal attention in dual-task paradigms.

papers.title: Distinct Patterns of Syntactic Errors Doubly Dissociate in Chronic Poststroke Aphasia.
papers.authors: Yeaton JD, Fahey D, Gomez M, Stark BC, Fridriksson J, den Ouden DB, Hickok G, Matchin W.
papers.abstract: The lesion correlates of syntactic deficits in aphasia remain poorly understood. Previous studies have suggested that distinct error types in expressive syntax may be associated with damage to different brain regions, but the specific lesion correlates of these errors have not been fully delineated. To address this gap, we analyzed spontaneous speech samples from individuals with chronic aphasia, categorizing errors into hierarchical (paragrammatic-like) and linearization (agrammatic-like) errors. Lesion-symptom mapping was conducted to identify brain regions associated with these error types. Lesion clusters in the medial superior temporal sulcus and inferior parietal lobe were associated with hierarchical errors, whereas frontal lesions, including those in the inferior and middle frontal lobe, were associated with linearization errors. These results provide support for a two-stage model of syntactic encoding, with distinct neural correlates for hierarchical and linearization processes. Our findings suggest that distinct brain regions contribute to different stages of syntactic encoding. Hierarchical processing seems to be supported by posterior temporal-parietal regions, whereas linearization seems to be supported by frontal regions. These results suggest that the diagnosis and treatment of aphasia could take into account the existence of distinct syntactic production deficits resulting from different patterns of brain damage.

papers.title: Theta and High-alpha Phase-locking Dynamics Unveil Face Perception in Ambiguous Stimuli.
papers.authors: Liu N, Weidner R, Chen Q, Fink GR, Daun S.
papers.abstract: Previous studies emphasize phase synchronization as a fundamental mechanism for integrating local features into coherent percepts. We employed a novel paradigm and dynamic graph analysis based on EEG to track neural dynamics associated with perceiving a face (or not) while keeping the stimuli identical. Thirty participants underwent a pretest to establish perceptual thresholds for detecting faces within images overlaid with visual noise. These thresholds were then applied in an EEG experiment with the same task, focusing on images with 50% and 75% detection probabilities. In the high-alpha band, we observed increased coupling (100-275 msec after stimulus onset) between the left and right occipitotemporal electrodes when an ambiguous stimulus was perceived as a face, indicating conscious face perception. The failure to perceive a face resulted in enhanced theta band phase synchronization between bilateral occipitotemporal electrodes and increased high-alpha-band coupling between the left frontal and right occipitotemporal electrodes, which showed face-selective responses. These synchronizations are likely to reflect the continuous gathering of individual bits of facial information rather than signaling the presence or absence of a face percept. Additionally, we identified frontal-occipitotemporal theta-band couplings related to the stimulus's informational content, irrespective of whether the inherent face was perceived. Our findings reveal distinct temporal dynamics in phase synchronization at specific frequencies, indicating a specialized system for face perception during integrated information processing across the frontal and visual cortex, resolving ambiguities.

papers.title: Memory Traces Reflect How They Were Last Accessed.
papers.authors: Qi X, Coutanche MN.
papers.abstract: Episodic memories are known to change with each act of retrieval. We hypothesize that accessing semantic knowledge in different ways during episodic retrieval-from unique perceptual features to taxonomic and thematic context-shapes how those memories are subsequently represented during recognition. In this fMRI study, human participants learned novel word-image pairs and underwent re-exposure that required accessing semantic knowledge at one of three different levels: item, category, or theme. Participants then completed a recognition task. Although behavioral memory performance was matched across conditions, neural activity during recognition varied based on prior semantic access history. Recognition patterns could be classified according to prior semantic access in early visual cortex, ventral temporal cortex, and the hippocampus for remembered concepts. A whole-brain searchlight analysis revealed bilateral clusters along the ventral visual stream where semantic access history was decodable. To further characterize how prior semantic access history shaped neural representations during recognition, we tested whether memories accessed at the same semantic level were expressed more similarly or distinctly in the brain. Category-level access increased similarity among items in early visual cortex, whereas item-level access led to more differentiated representations in the visual word form area. Together, these findings show that how we access semantic knowledge during episodic retrieval leaves measurable traces in subsequent neural representations, revealing how semantic-episodic interactions shape memory representations.

papers.title: Intracranial Evidence for the Cerebellum's Role in Semantic Processing.
papers.authors: Floden DP, Gopalakrishnan R, Srivastava A, Hogue O, Biars J, Schroedel M, Baker KB, Machado AG.
papers.abstract: Language impairments in patients with cerebellar damage or dysfunction strongly implicate the cerebellum in language processing but the nature, timing, and specificity of its contributions are unclear. A clinical trial of cerebellar stimulation for motor recovery after middle cerebral artery stroke provided a rare opportunity to record invasive, intracranial local field potential activity from the cerebellar dentate nucleus of eight patients during language processing. Patients performed semantic priming tasks that either discouraged or encouraged semantic predictions. We found evidence for communication between the dentate nucleus and frontal scalp EEG sites in the alpha band when semantic predictions were violated. This did not occur when semantic predictions were fulfilled or when prediction violations were nonlinguistic in nature. This language-specific activity occurred in the N400 window where semantic processing of a visually presented word takes place. These data point to a linguistic feedback function that could help to account for the language deficits observed in diseases and disorders involving the cerebellum.

papers.title: Neural Distinctions between Social and Nonsocial Reward Anticipation: An Examination of Activation Magnitude, Representational Patterns, Individual Differences, and Functional Connectivity.
papers.authors: Jiang Y, Ziyao Z, Khader A, Church J, Lewis-Peacock J, Beer J.
papers.abstract: Prevailing theories emphasize a "common neural currency" for social and nonsocial rewards, particularly during reward anticipation. However, direct comparisons of social and nonsocial reward anticipation remain limited, and clinical observations suggest that social reward processing can be selectively disrupted. The present fMRI study directly compared social and nonsocial reward anticipation to test differences in activation magnitude, functional connectivity, multivariate activity patterns, and modulation by individual differences in social reward motivation. Consistent with a "common neural currency" perspective, reward anticipation (collapsed across domains) was associated with increased activation in ventral striatum (VS), anterior insula (AI), dorsal ACC (DACC), and SMA. Furthermore, social reward anticipation did not significantly shape functional connectivity among ventral striatum, AI, DACC, and SMA. However, local activation patterns in AI and SMA reliably discriminated the anticipation of social versus monetary reward. Additional decoding emerged in TPJ, STS, and OFC-regions previously inconsistently linked to social reward anticipation or more commonly associated with later stages of reward processing. Moreover, individual differences in Need to Belong predicted greater ACC (including ventromedial PFC) engagement during social reward anticipation. These findings support the perspective that social and nonsocial reward anticipation share some neural circuitry but are dissociable when local activation patterns and social motivational priorities are considered. The current study recasts our understanding of ways in which social reward anticipation may be distinct and raises an expanded role for brain regions typically associated with reward and/or social processing.

papers.title: Transformer Mechanisms Mimic Frontostriatal Gating Operations When Trained on Human Working Memory Tasks.
papers.authors: Soni A, Traylor A, Merullo J, Frank MJ, Pavlick E.
papers.abstract: Working memory (WM) is thought to rely on sophisticated frontostriatal mechanisms for selective gating, supporting updating and readout of information to and from distinct memory "addresses" (neural populations). According to computational models, capacity limitations in WM arise due to challenges in "role addressability": learning to correctly bind items in memory to their respective roles and assigning credit to the corresponding gating operations. However, these conclusions are based on particular assumptions about biological neural networks, and it is unclear whether the principles generalize to other architectures. To address this question, we examine whether similar gating mechanisms emerge in Transformer neural network architectures, which have demonstrated success on tasks requiring executive function-the ability to represent, coordinate, and manage multiple subtasks-yet lack intentionally built-in gating mechanisms. We analyze the mechanisms that emerge within Transformers trained on human WM tasks explicitly designed to place demands on gating. We find that the Transformer's attention mechanism develops role-addressable input and output gating, but only when trained on task distributions that benefit from frontostriatal-like gating mechanisms. Moreover, these gating strategies support enhanced generalization and variable binding and increase the models' effective capacity to store and access multiple items in memory, resembling the constraints found in frontostriatal models. These results suggest that gating mechanisms serve a fundamental computational role in managing role addressability and binding and highlight opportunities for future research on computational similarities between modern artificial intelligence architectures and models of the human brain.

papers.title: Slow Oscillations Modulate Overnight Brain Changes in Working Memory Function.
papers.authors: Zhang J, Chen PC, Mednick SC, Tambini A.
papers.abstract: Working memory (WM), the transient storage and manipulation of information, is a cognitive function that can improve with training. Accumulating evidence suggests that sleep, particularly slow oscillations (SOs) that occur during nonrapid eye movement sleep, supports this improvement. Yet, how sleep and SOs in particular relate to neural processes supporting WM remains poorly understood. In this study, we investigated how WM-related neural activity evolves across nocturnal sleep and how these changes relate to neural processing during SOs. Participants performed a WM task during fMRI before and after sleep, with simultaneous EEG-fMRI capturing neural activity during the first 2.5 hr of sleep. Our results showed significant overnight changes in WM-related activity, characterized by reduced recruitment of the dorsal precuneus during WM encoding/maintenance phases and frontal regions during the retrieval phase of WM. In addition, sleep increased item-specific reinstatement in a sensory processing region during WM. This pattern of results suggests a combined influence of sleep on enhancing sensory reinstatement while reducing potential top-down control (i.e., reduced parietal and frontal activity). Critically, SO-related activity was directly linked to overnight activity changes: Stronger SO activation in the premotor cortex and ventromedial pFC predicted greater overnight reductions in WM-related activity, and multivoxel analyses in the ventral attention network revealed a parallel relationship. These findings suggest that SOs play a critical role in WM function by facilitating the reorganization of WM-related processing.

papers.title: Exploring Neural Mechanisms Underlying Error-related Impairments in Active Working Memory Suggests an Adaptive Shielding of Contents during Cognitive Control.
papers.authors: Choo Y, Adam KCS, Wessel JR.
papers.abstract: Goal-directed behavior relies on cognitive flexibility-the ability to rapidly adapt ongoing thoughts and behaviors while preserving task-relevant information. The performance monitoring system optimizes such behavior by detecting and evaluating errors, whereas the working memory (WM) system maintains relevant information and protects it from interference. We previously showed that motor errors impaired active WM maintenance (Error-Related Impairment of Active working Memory [ERIAM]; [Wessel, J. R., Jiang, J., & Stolley, J. J. Action errors impair active working memory maintenance. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 151, 1325-1340, 2022]). Here, we investigated the source of ERIAM by tracking the contralateral delay activity (CDA), a neural marker of visual WM maintenance, throughout the error-making process. Forty-two participants maintained visual information in WM while performing a flanker task during the delay period. Consistent with prior results, a significant ERIAM effect occurred. We observed the canonical CDA before flanker task onset, and this CDA declined after the flanker task began. Following the flanker response, however, we observed a sustained contralateral positivity (CDAp). Critically, CDA amplitudes did not differ between motor correct and error trials before the flanker task, ruling out a general performance deficit. The CDA was also unaffected immediately after flanker onset, ruling out a perceptual interference explanation. Neural differences emerged only after the flanker response, supporting a genuinely error-related origin of the ERIAM effect. Importantly, CDAp was larger following correct responses than errors, and greater CDAp modulation predicted a smaller ERIAM effect. On the basis of prior work, we interpret CDAp as reflecting disengagement from WM storage, suggesting a possible adaptive shielding strategy. These findings provide clear evidence regarding the timing of the ERIAM effect and suggestive evidence regarding potential mechanisms underlying error-related interference in active WM maintenance. Future work will help determine the functional significance of CDAp and its relationship to WM storage and cognitive control.

papers.title: Visual Perspective Shapes Subjective Experience: Dissociable Parietal Contributions to the Constructive Nature of Memory.
papers.authors: St Jacques PL.
papers.abstract: Subjective features of memory are often treated as secondary to the objective content of remembered events. However, growing evidence suggests that these features actively shape how memories are constructed, experienced, and used. Rather than treating visual perspective as a peripheral correlate of subjectivity, this review positions it as a key mechanism that shapes the memory. Because perspective can be flexibly controlled and reliably measured, it offers a unique window into how retrieval goals interact with mental simulation to produce vivid and emotionally resonant recollections. Drawing on behavioral and neuroimaging research, this review shows that visual perspective determines the spatial framing of memory and the emotional and sensory qualities of recollection. Focusing on the posterior parietal cortex, it outlines distinct roles for the angular gyrus (AG) and the precuneus in supporting perspective-dependent retrieval. The AG contributes to the selection and maintenance of a retrieval perspective, integrating perceptual and conceptual features into a coherent scene. In contrast, the precuneus supports spatial transformation and modulates the vividness, emotional tone, and embodied character of recollection, particularly when individuals recall events from a nondominant or shifted perspective. Together, these findings position visual perspective as a central mechanism in the construction of subjectivity. Understanding how perspective shapes the process of remembering provides insight into how memory supports emotion regulation, mental simulation, and the continuity of the self across time.

papers.title: Advanced Diffusion MRI-based MR Cytometry for Quantitative Microstructural Assessment and Grading of Bladder Cancer.
papers.authors: Roshanshad A.

papers.title: Radiologic Evaluation of the Nasopharynx: A Comprehensive Review.
papers.authors: Coelho Neto CAF, Machado Reali R, Souza SA, Vaccaro Sumi D, Cintra MB, Gomes RLE, Soares CR, Gebrim EMS, Kennedy TA, Garcia MRT.
papers.journal: Radiographics : a review publication of the Radiological Society of North America, Inc
papers.abstract: The nasopharynx is a critical component of the upper aerodigestive tract and has essential roles in respiration, auditory tube function, and speech resonance. Accurate imaging evaluation of this region allows assessment of deeper structures that cannot be evaluated by clinical examination alone. A thorough understanding of nasopharyngeal anatomy, embryology, and the spectrum of benign and malignant diseases is vital for accurate diagnosis. Key imaging features may be identified across CT and MRI modalities. Although CT effectively delineates local bone and soft-tissue structures, MRI provides superior soft-tissue characterization and allows better assessment of soft-tissue lesions and tumor extension. Disorders affecting the nasopharynx and surrounding structures include eustachian tube dysfunction, cystic lesions, anatomic variations of the clivus, and inflammatory and infectious conditions, as well as neoplasms such as nasopharyngeal carcinoma and lymphoma. Recognizing imaging pearls and pitfalls is useful for accurate diagnosis and to distinguish benign from malignant entities. Optimal patient management-including accurate radiologic diagnosis, early detection of malignancies, differential diagnosis, assessment of disease extent, and posttreatment surveillance-can be achieved through comprehensive radiologic evaluation. © RSNA, 2026 Supplemental material is available for this article.

papers.title: Imaging Features of Adrenal Glands Infiltration by Multicentric Lymphoma in Dogs and Cats.
papers.authors: Negro L, Pey P, Specchi S, Penninck D, Diana A, Linta N, Nanni C, Baldinetti M, Morabito S.
papers.journal: Veterinary radiology & ultrasound : the official journal of the American College of Veterinary Radiology and the International Veterinary Radiology Association
papers.abstract: Few case reports describe the imaging features of lymphoma involving the adrenal glands (AGs) in dogs and cats. This retrospective, descriptive, and multicentric study aimed to describe the ultrasound (US), computed tomography (CT), and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) findings of confirmed lymphomatous AG infiltration in patients with multicentric lymphoma. The inclusion criteria required cytological or histological confirmation of AG lymphoma and at least one imaging study. Eleven patients were included. Abdominal US was available in 10/11 patients (90%), CT in 2/11 patients (18%), and MRI in 1/11 patient (9%). Six patients (6/11, 54%) (5 dogs and 1 cat) had a bilateral involvement of the AGs, whereas the rest (5/11 patients, 54%) (3 dogs and 2 cats) had a unilateral involvement. On US, the findings included unilateral or bilateral enlargement with a preserved shape, hypoechoic and heterogeneous parenchyma, ill-defined or well-defined margins of the AGs, increased echogenicity of the surrounding retroperitoneal fat, and retroperitoneal effusion. On CT, one patient (1/11, 9%) with bilateral involvement showed enlargement of the AGs with multiple hypoattenuating and hypoenhancing nodules, whereas another patient (1/11, 9%) with unilateral involvement showed a hypoattenuating, hypoenhancing nodule in a rounded, heterogeneously enhanced gland. MRI of one patient (1/11, 9%) revealed bilateral enlargement of the AGs with T2W iso/hyperintensity, T1W isointensity, STIR hyperintensity, and strong and heterogeneous enhancement. Detection of these imaging findings on US, CT, and MRI may support the suspicion of adrenal involvement in the case of multicentric lymphoma in both dogs and cats.

papers.title: Association Between Neuropsychological Test Performance and Neuroimaging Findings in Cognitive Impairment: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
papers.authors: Dorukoğlu MM, Evyapan D, Eraslan C.
papers.journal: Psychogeriatrics : the official journal of the Japanese Psychogeriatric Society
papers.abstract: Background Structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and [18F]fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG-PET) provide different information about cognitive impairment, but the additional contribution of FDG-PET beyond MRI across cognitive outcomes remains unclear. This study examined associations between neuropsychological performance and MRI/FDG-PET findings. Methods This retrospective cohort included 200 patients with mild cognitive impairment or dementia. Neuropsychological assessment covered global cognition and memory, executive, visuospatial and language domains. Structural MRI was evaluated using the Modified Visual Magnetic Resonance Rating Scale; FDG-PET data were available for 68 patients. MRI-only, FDG-PET-only and combined models were compared. Results Structural MRI abnormalities showed broad associations with global and domain-level cognitive performance. Sulcal and ventricular atrophy were associated with multiple cognitive domains, while regional FDG-PET findings aligned with corresponding domains. The additional contribution of FDG-PET beyond MRI appeared most evident for global cognition, more modest for executive performance and limited for several other outcomes. Conclusions Structural MRI showed broad multidomain associations, while regional FDG-PET findings corresponded to cognitive performance. The additional explanatory contribution of FDG-PET appeared to vary across cognitive outcomes, warranting cautious interpretation and further evaluation.

papers.title: Resting-State and Task-State Dual-Paradigm fNIRS Study Reveals Dynamic Alterations in Brain Network Activity in Alzheimer's Disease With Behavioural and Psychological Symptoms.
papers.authors: Li FB, Zeng Q, Liu SW, Zhu JW, Yang Y, Li CG, Liu CF, Hu H.
papers.journal: Psychogeriatrics : the official journal of the Japanese Psychogeriatric Society
papers.abstract: Background Alzheimer's disease (AD) frequently presents with behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD), severely impacting prognosis. The dynamic brain network mechanisms remain unclear, and traditional neuroimaging faces limitations. Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) offers a unique approach to explore these mechanisms under natural conditions. Objective To systematically compare brain region activation, signal complexity and network topology in AD patients with and without BPSD using resting-state and verbal fluency task (VFT) fNIRS paradigms. Methods This cross-sectional study enrolled 48 AD patients (24 with BPSD, 24 without) and 25 normal controls (NC). fNIRS recorded hemodynamic changes in the frontal, temporal, parietal and occipital lobes during rest and VFT. Analyses included activation, time-frequency characteristics, functional connectivity and network topology. Partial correlations assessed links between fNIRS metrics and neuropsychological scores. Results In resting state, AD-BPSD showed altered coefficient of variation in left premotor and somatosensory cortices, and elevated information entropy in left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (lDLPFC), versus NC and AD-non-BPSD. Functional connectivity abnormalities emerged between right frontal eye field-left somatosensory cortex, and right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (rDLPFC)-left superior temporal gyrus (lSTG) (p < 0.05). During VFT, AD-BPSD had significantly lower lDLPFC and left somatosensory activation versus NC (p < 0.05), but increased signal fluctuation and power in right primary motor cortex (rM1) (p < 0.05), alongside reduced whole-brain clustering coefficient (p = 0.023). Conclusions AD-BPSD was associated with altered brain functional patterns across resting and task states, involving sensorimotor and executive networks as well as altered interhemispheric coordination. These fNIRS-derived alterations provide exploratory evidence of altered brain functional patterns associated with BPSD and warrant further investigation in larger longitudinal studies.
keywords: Behavioural And Psychological Symptoms Of Dementia

papers.title: A Cortical Stress Signature of Fear-Induced Walking: Mobile Electroencephalography Theta Suppression in Older Women With Fear of Falling.
papers.authors: Bueno GAS, Gervásio FM, Martins AC, Menezes RL.
papers.journal: Psychogeriatrics : the official journal of the Japanese Psychogeriatric Society
papers.abstract: Background Fear of falling is one of the most common and disabling stress responses of later life, yet how it is expressed in the brain during real walking is poorly understood. We examined whether walking under a naturalistic psychological threat, a fear-of-falling stressor, changes cortical oscillatory activity in older women, using mobile electroencephalography. Methods In this within-subject study, 30 community-dwelling women aged 65 years or older underwent three-dimensional gait analysis with concurrent 14-channel electroencephalography (128 Hz) during habitual walking and after introduction of a fictional disturbing factor, a psychological, nonmotor agent that elicits fear of falling without any mechanical perturbation. Relative band power and the theta/beta ratio were compared with paired t tests and Cohen's dz., with sign-flip permutation, false-discovery-rate correction and bootstrap confidence intervals; signal validity was confirmed by the eyes-closed alpha increase, and head movement and gait speed served as controls. Results Walking under threat reduced relative theta power across frontal, temporal, occipital and sensorimotor regions (p = 0.004-0.014; dz. around -0.5; confidence intervals excluding zero), confirmed by permutation and by seven electrodes surviving correction, while the frontal and central theta/beta ratio fell. The theta change was not accounted for by head movement, and in a smaller subgroup showed no detectable association with the change in gait speed, while gait became more cautious. Conclusions A naturalistic fear stressor produces a measurable cortical signature during walking, positioning fear of falling as a neurobehavioural stress response with implications for the health and mobility of older women.

papers.title: Inferior Frontal Gyrus Alterations in Freezing of Gait in Parkinson's Disease Without Evidence for Overall Hemispheric Lateralization: A Systematic Review and Activation Likelihood Estimation Meta-Analysis.
papers.authors: Taniguchi S, Deckmyn H, Gilat M.
papers.abstract: Freezing of gait (FOG) is one of the most debilitating motor symptoms of Parkinson's disease (PD). Prior studies have suggested a potential right-hemispheric preference in the pathophysiology of FOG. Yet, there is limited evidence regarding which brain regions are most consistently associated with FOG and whether these alterations indeed show right-hemispheric lateralization. We aimed to identify brain regions associated with FOG based on multimodal neuroimaging findings and to examine their hemispheric lateralization. A systematic review across multiple neuroimaging modalities was performed, followed by an activation likelihood estimation (ALE) coordinate-based meta-analysis to assess convergent brain alterations in PD patients with FOG (freezers) versus those without FOG (nonfreezers). Hemispheric lateralization was assessed using the distribution of reported stereotactic coordinates. The systematic review included 108 articles, of which 33 were included in the primary ALE meta-analysis. We identified a significant convergent cluster in the right inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) pars opercularis/dorsolateral prefrontal cortex in PD freezers compared with nonfreezers. No evidence of overall hemispheric lateralization was observed based on the distribution of reported coordinates. Our findings identify the right IFG as a consistent neural correlate of FOG, potentially reflecting heightened frontal recruitment, with no clear evidence of hemispheric lateralization. The lack of further consistency in brain regions could reflect the known heterogeneity in the pathophysiology of FOG.

papers.title: Opioid Modulation of Major Neurotransmitter Systems: Acute, Chronic, and Withdrawal Effects.
papers.authors: Novakova D, Pritulova E, Novotny J.
papers.abstract: Opioids are widely used in clinical practice for the management of moderate-to-severe acute and chronic pain. However, their use is associated with the development of tolerance and physical dependence, often followed by a withdrawal syndrome upon discontinuation. The mechanisms underlying opioid dependence and withdrawal are highly complex and remain incompletely understood. These processes involve multiple regions of the central nervous system and are accompanied by widespread alterations in neuronal signaling pathways. Neurotransmitters, which are essential for communication between neurons, play a critical role in opioid addiction and withdrawal. In this review, we provide a comprehensive overview of the major neurotransmitter systems, their involvement, and the changes that occur during acute and chronic opioid exposure. Particular attention is also given to the consequences of opioid discontinuation. Overall, this review summarizes current knowledge of the molecular mechanisms underlying both the acute and long-term effects of opioids on key neurotransmitter systems in the brain.

papers.title: Investigation of the Prolonged Impact of Severe Socioeconomic Hardship and Mother's Perceived Social Support on Neurocognitive Development in Young Children in the Rural Ecuadorian Amazon.
papers.authors: Cook ML, Boyce LK, Bradshaw SD, Santos M, Ortiz E, Balseca G.
papers.abstract: Children living in conditions of severe socioeconomic (SES) hardship are at elevated risk for neurocognitive delays, yet most developmental neuroscience research has focused on children in high-income, Western populations, limiting our understanding of diverse developmental contexts. This study examined maternal perceived social support as a potential buffer against the stressors associated with SES hardship on child neurocognitive development in a longitudinal sample of Indigenous families in the rural Ecuadorian Amazon. Twenty-eight children (M age = 28.02 months at T1; 57.6 months at T2) participated in the study completing an assessment of early cognitive ability at T1 and an inhibition task while functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) measured cortical activation at T2. A three-level linear mixed model revealed a significant interaction between early cognitive ability and maternal perceived social support on functional activation. Specifically, children of mothers with high social support showed no association between early cognitive ability and cortical activation, while those with low support exhibited atypical patterns (hyper- or hypoactivation), suggesting that increased maternal perceived social support may help buffer the risk exposure of chronic stressors associated with SES hardship. These findings underscore the importance of culturally embedded social resources in promoting resilience among children facing cumulative risk. Supporting maternal social networks may be a promising pathway for improving child neurodevelopment in underrepresented, low-resource communities and contributes to more inclusive global models of brain development.

papers.title: Perceived Neighborhood Disadvantage Predicts Similarity in Amygdala Representations of Negative and Neutral Images in Early Adolescents.
papers.authors: Bonar AS, Dai J, Feldman MJ, Capella J, Prinstein MJ, Telzer EH, Lindquist KA.
papers.abstract: Neighborhood disadvantage encompasses multiple co-occurring adversities, including threat and deprivation, yet its underlying neural mechanisms remain unclear. Applying a dimensional framework to neighborhood contexts may help clarify how distinct features of disadvantage influence brain development. Here, we used representational similarity analysis to investigate associations between adolescents' neural representations of affective valence and neighborhood disadvantage, as measured by caregiver self-report and the Area Deprivation Index (ADI). One hundred and twenty-one adolescents aged 11 to 14 (Mage = 12.81 years old, 52.07% female, 28.93% White non-Hispanic) completed an emotional reactivity fMRI task. Caregiver-reported neighborhood disadvantage was associated with greater representational similarity in right amygdala between negative and neutral images, while no such effect emerged for the ADI. Follow-up analyses examined whether specific dimensions of disadvantage drove these effects. Although our measure did not map cleanly onto threat and deprivation dimensions, factor analyses revealed distinctions between social (e.g., crime, loitering) and physical (e.g., abandoned buildings, walkability) disadvantage-related items; our preliminary findings suggest that the effects of reported overall neighborhood disadvantage may be driven by characteristics of the social environment. No associations between caregiver-reported neighborhood disadvantage or ADI were observed for positive/neutral similarity. These findings provide preliminary evidence that neighborhood disadvantage may impact the amygdala's differentiation of negative and neutral stimuli during early adolescence, supporting the view that neighborhoods are a critical ecological context for development.

papers.title: Early Emergence of Cultural Differences in Audiovisual Speech Perception.
papers.authors: Yan L, Hu S, Ding Y, Jin M, Krasotkina A, Ren L, Liu S, Xiao NG.
papers.abstract: Integrating auditory and visual cues is a hallmark of human speech perception, yet adults from East Asian backgrounds show less reliance on visual speech than their Western counterparts. The origins of this cultural difference, however, remain unknown. To investigate whether this divergence is established early in infancy, we examined audiovisual integration in 6- to 12-month-old White Canadian (n = 111) and Chinese (n = 115) infants using a novel paradigm measuring their perception of the McGurk effect. Across four experiments, we found a clear developmental divergence: Canadian infants showed a stable McGurk effect from 6 months onward, whereas Chinese infants showed a more protracted developmental trajectory, a cultural pattern that was further highlighted when their integration was challenged by other-race faces. These findings provide the first direct evidence that cultural differences in multisensory speech perception are established within the first year of life, suggesting that the brain's strategy for binding sight and sound is shaped by early experience, with broad implications for theories of language acquisition and developmental science.

papers.title: Nucleus Accumbens and Ventral Tegmental Area Functional Connectivity as a Marker of Reward Sensitivity in Infancy.
papers.authors: Hare MM, Niu Y, Zeanah CH, Humphreys KL.
papers.abstract: Early functional connectivity within the brain's reward circuitry may provide insight into the developmental origins of individual differences in pleasure and motivation. This study examined resting-state functional connectivity between two key reward-related regions, the nucleus accumbens (NAc) and ventral tegmental area (VTA), in 94 one-month-old infants (58% male; M = 4.84 weeks, SD = 0.86) and its association with later reward-related temperament. Infants completed a resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging scan during natural sleep with a mean of 11.09 (SD = 2.78) min of retained low-motion data. Caregivers reported their infants' temperament at age six months, including high- and low-intensity pleasure as indicators of individual differences relevant to reward sensitivity. Positive resting-state functional connectivity between the NAc and VTA was present in early infancy (Cohen's d = 0.44, 95% CI [0.22, 0.65]), p < 0.001). Less positive NAc-VTA connectivity was associated with greater high-intensity pleasure at six months (β = -0.32, 95% CI [-0.54, -0.10], p = 0.004), indicating that infants with stronger connectivity between these regions exhibited less enjoyment of highly stimulating, energetic activities. NAc-VTA connectivity was not associated with low-intensity pleasure (β = -0.01, 95% CI [-0.24, 0.21], p = 0.908). These findings suggest that early variation in mesolimbic connectivity may serve as a marker of emerging individual differences in reward responsiveness, with implications for understanding affective development in infancy.

papers.title: Association of Polygenic Risk Score for Suicidal Behavior With Ventral Prefrontal Morphology in Bipolar Disorder.
papers.authors: Katz Shroitman N, Levey DF, Pittman B, Zheng S, Quatrano S, Sankar A, Colic L, Gelernter J, Willour VL, Blumberg HP.
papers.abstract: Background Bipolar disorder (BD) studies consistently implicate the ventral prefrontal cortex (VPFC) in association with suicidal behaviors. A suicidal behavior polygenic risk score (PRS) can now be computed to test whether elevated genetic risk for suicidal behavior is associated with variation in VPFC gray matter and/or suicidal behavior history. Methods We explored relationships among a PRS previously associated with suicidal behavior, VPFC morphology, and suicidal behavior in 376 individuals of European ancestry (mean age 30y; 57% female): 225 with BD (76 suicide attempters (SAs), 149 non-suicide attempters (NSAs)) and 151 healthy control individuals (HCs). We calculated PRS and performed magnetic resonance imaging to assess VPFC (inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) and orbitofrontal cortex) cortical thickness and surface area. Associations were examined among PRS, diagnosis, suicide attempt history, and brain measures. Results Among individuals with BD, those with higher PRS showed decreased right VPFC surface area, primarily due to IFG reductions (p < 0.01). A significant group (SA, NSA, HC)-by-PRS interaction was observed for right IFG cortical surface area (p < 0.05); NSAs with high vs. low PRS had significantly smaller right IFG surface area. The mean PRS was highest for SAs, then NSAs, and lowest for HCs; however, differences did not reach significance. Conclusions These findings suggest this suicide PRS may reflect genetic mechanisms influencing IFG differences in BD. Given the modest sample size, replication of these preliminary findings in large-scale diverse cohorts is required to determine whether including this PRS and/or the corresponding IFG values could improve multimodal BD suicidal behavior prediction algorithms.

papers.title: Serial Cross-Sectional Mapping of Bone Marrow Microenvironment Remodelling During Fracture Repair Using Multiparametric MRI and Histopathology.
papers.authors: Zhou R, Li G, Zhou Y, Yao C, Deng L, Zeng X.
papers.abstract: Restoring bone marrow microenvironment (BMM) homeostasis is critical for fracture healing, yet non-invasively tracking physiological events like apoptosis, angiogenesis and matrix remodelling remains challenging. This study evaluated multiparametric 7.0T MRI (T2 mapping and proton density-weighted imaging [PDWI]) for in vivo tracking of BMM spatiotemporal remodelling during natural and pharmacologically accelerated bone repair. Utilizing a rat tibial drill-hole injury model (N = 36), we compared a natural healing control with a Huoxue Qiangji Decoction (HQD) intervention group. Serial high-resolution sagittal MRIs were acquired at days 7, 14 and 21, with signal intensity ratios (SIR) normalized to ipsilateral intact marrow using ITK-SNAP. Distance correlation (dCor) analysis explored non-linear dependencies between MRI metrics and histological features (c-cas3, Masson's trichrome and day-14 CD31/Ki67 expression). Results showed distinct MRI signal trajectories, with earlier homeostatic stabilization in the accelerated healing group. Spatiotemporal mapping revealed closely mirrored non-linear dependencies between MRI and histology. Specifically, T2 mapping SIR mirrored early-stage apoptosis (dCor = 0.527) and mid-term cellular proliferation (Ki67, dCor = 0.732). Concurrently, PDWI reflected dynamic trends of mid-term angiogenesis (CD31, dCor = 0.637) and late-stage collagen deposition (dCor = 0.480). In conclusion, normalized multiparametric MRI provides complementary macroscopic insights into BMM histological progression, highlighting its potential as an objective, non-invasive translational tool for monitoring musculoskeletal healing.

papers.title: Neurophysiological and Behavioural Effects of Combined Cannabis Concentrates and Alcohol Among People Who Regularly Use Alcohol and Cannabis.
papers.authors: Hetelekides EM, Davies PL, Prince MA, Gavin WJ, Karoly HC.
papers.abstract: Increasingly potent concentrated cannabis products containing high levels of Δ9 -tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) are being consumed with alcohol. This combination is known to acutely impair cognitive and psychomotor abilities, although few studies have evaluated alcohol and cannabis co-use using neural measures. This naturalistic feasibility study explored the acute effects of co-intoxication on behavioural performance and brain activity, measured via electroencephalography (EEG), during a performance monitoring task administered three times over a 4.5-h period. Participants (N = 17, 65% male) were heavy drinking community members (age M = 31.7 years; SD = 10.27) who regularly use cannabis. EEG was recorded while participants completed a speeded visual-flanker task at baseline (sober) before consuming a standardized dose of alcohol and a cannabis concentrate product, followed by EEG recordings 1-h (intoxicated) and 4-h post co-consumption (recovery). Recordings were processed to obtain six event-related potential components: the stimulus-locked N1, P2, N2 and P3 and response-locked error-related negativity (ERN) and error positivity (Pe). Repeated measures ANOVAs revealed that behavioural measures at the intoxicated timepoint showed an increase in errors (p < 0.005; η2 p = 0.35) and significant decrease in response time (RT) (p < 0.001; η2 p = 0.50) compared to sober and recovery periods. Measures of brain activity also demonstrated significant change across time with largest amplitudes when sober, smaller amplitudes when intoxicated, then an increase in amplitude to near sober levels at recovery for stimulus-locked (P2, N2 and P3) and response-locked components (ERN and Pe). Thus, compared to sober and recovery periods, the behaviour at the intoxicated timepoint revealed significantly greater impulsivity (RT) leading to significantly higher error rates, while measures of cognitive processing (i.e., decision-making, error detection, performance monitoring/adaptation) showed significantly diminished levels of brain activity. Performance and neurophysiology measures remained diminished at recovery compared to baseline. Understanding neurocognitive functioning during co-intoxication may provide insights into specific cognitive processes that may impact function in everyday activities such as driving. Trial Registration: NCT06259916.

papers.title: In Vivo Partial Cell Reprogramming With Yamanaka Factors Reduced Ischemic Brain Damage in Aging Mice.
papers.authors: Mallavibarrena PR, Martín-López G, Rodríguez-Morales J, Ávila J, Hernández F, Pérez-Álvarez MJ.
papers.abstract: Aging is associated with functional decline and reduced regenerative capacity in the brain, is also the strongest risk factor for ischemic stroke, which remains a leading cause of mortality and long-term disability worldwide, and is associated with impaired functional recovery. Here, we investigated whether short-term partial cellular reprogramming through cyclic expression of Yamanaka factors (OSKM) in a Tet-ON mouse model under Rosa-26 promoter has any impact on ischemic damage in aged mice. To assess ischemic resilience, mice underwent permanent middle cerebral artery occlusion (pMCAo). Forty-eight hours after ischemia, OSKM-induced mice displayed significantly smaller damaged area compared with wild-type controls, accompanied by improved neurological scores and enhanced performance in the tightrope test, suggesting preserved sensorimotor abilities. Notably, myelin integrity was preserved in OSKM-treated mice, as shown by Black-Gold staining and stable MAG and MBP expression, whereas wild-type mice exhibited pronounced demyelination. Given the role of oligodendrocytes in myelin maintenance, we quantified the abundance of their different populations. OSKM induction significantly increased total oligodendrocytes (Olig2+ ) and oligodendrocyte precursor cells (PDGFRα+ ) following ischemia, suggesting an enhanced reparative response. Moreover, partial reprogramming preserved neuronal density in the ischemic cortex and prevented the marked astrocytic activation observed in wild-type mice, while microglial responses remained comparable across genotypes. These findings demonstrate that cyclic partial reprogramming in aged mice reduces ischemic damage, highlighting OSKM induction as a promising strategy for enhancing brain resilience during cerebrovascular accidents.

papers.title: Lexico-Semantic and Morphosyntactic Skills in Individuals With Parkinson's Disease: A Scoping Review.
papers.authors: Escalada-Cebadero L, Moya-Galé G.
papers.journal: International journal of language & communication disorders
papers.abstract: Purpose This scoping review examines lexico-semantic and morphosyntactic skills in English-speaking individuals with Parkinson's disease (PD) using behavioral and neuroimaging data to inform clinical assessment and intervention. Method Following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, observational case-control studies published between 2004 and 2024 were retrieved from PubMed, PsycINFO, Web of Science, Scopus and ERIC. Thirty-nine studies met inclusion criteria. Methodological quality was evaluated using the Joanna Briggs Institute Checklist for Case-Control Studies. Results Lexico-semantic impairments in PD are characterized by deficits in semantic fluency, action-verb retrieval, and figurative-language processing, particularly under higher cognitive load. Individuals with PD show reduced efficiency in lexical access, difficulty shifting between semantic categories, and weaker inhibition of competing meanings. Morphosyntactic studies similarly report slower processing and lower accuracy for syntactically complex sentences. Conclusion Linguistic impairments in PD are best understood as a dynamic interaction between linguistic demands and domain-general cognitive resources, emerging most clearly under conditions of increased cognitive load. This pattern positions language as a sensitive indicator of broader cognitive vulnerability within the communication profile of PD, with direct implications for assessment and clinical practice. What this paper adds What is already known on the subject Language impairments are a well-recognized non-motor feature of PD and can significantly affect communication and quality of life. Previous studies have reported lexico-semantic and morphosyntactic difficulties in PD, but findings are scattered across heterogeneous tasks and study designs, with no synthesis examining these domains together. What this study adds to the existing knowledge This scoping review synthesizes evidence from behavioral and neuroimaging studies and shows that language difficulties in PD are most consistently observed under conditions of increased cognitive or processing demand, particularly in high-load contexts. Lexico-semantic impairments emerge reliably in such high-load contexts, while morphosyntactic difficulties appear to reflect vulnerability to processing demands rather than a generalized grammatical deficit. The review also demonstrates that methodological variability, such as cognitive screening practices, influences how language abilities are characterized across studies. What are the potential or clinical implications of this work? Language impairments affecting lexico-semantic and morphosyntactic processing constitute a meaningful component of the communication profile in PD and should be considered alongside speech and voice symptoms in clinical assessment. Incorporating cognitive-linguistic evaluation may support a more comprehensive understanding of communication difficulties in individuals with PD.

papers.title: Beyond Counting Words: Verbal Fluency Components and Executive Functions in Traumatic Brain Injury.
papers.authors: Villalobos D, Del Río D, Guzmán I, Bize A.
papers.journal: International journal of language & communication disorders
papers.abstract: Background Verbal fluency (VF) tasks are consistently included in neuropsychological assessment protocols because they provide a rapid and sensitive measure of lexical retrieval and executive functioning across a wide range of neurological conditions. In addition to considering the number of words produced by the individual, examining other variables can provide highly valuable information about their cognitive performance. Aims This study examines the clinical utility of looking into specific components of VF tasks by comparing the performance of patients with traumatic brain injury (TBI) to that of healthy controls. Method and procedures Twenty-seven individuals with TBI and 29 matched controls completed a neuropsychological assessment including phonological and semantic VF tasks, along with measures of processing speed, working memory (WM) and executive functioning. Group differences were analyzed across all variables, and within-group correlations were explored between VF components (total correct responses, perseverations, mean cluster size, and number of switches) and cognitive processes. Outcomes and results Significant group differences emerged for all cognitive measures and VF components, except for mean cluster size. In the TBI group, total correct responses on both VF tasks were associated with processing speed and WM measures. Additionally, the number of switches in phonological VF correlated with cognitive flexibility measures, while mean cluster size in semantic VF was related to a measure of WM. In contrast, within the control group, total correct responses and switching in phonological VF, as well as mean cluster size in semantic VF, were associated with WM performance. Conclusions and implications These findings highlight the sensitivity of VF tasks in detecting cognitive dysfunction following TBI. Importantly, the analysis of qualitative components (such as clustering and switching) provides a more detailed understanding of the executive mechanisms underlying VF performance. Thus, beyond simple word counts, these measures enhance the diagnostic and clinical value of VF tasks as tools for assessing cognitive functioning in both research and applied settings. What this paper adds What is already known on this subject Verbal fluency (VF) tasks, in both their phonological and semantic variations, are simple neuropsychological assessment tools that are sensitive to the cognitive performance of healthy individuals as well as patients with neurological conditions. Previous studies have demonstrated the relationship between this task and cognitive processes related to language, processing speed, and components of executive functions; nevertheless, the evidence remains inconclusive. What this paper adds to the existing knowledge Patients with traumatic brain injury (TBI) and health controls showed distinct patterns of performance across cognitive measures including VF components. In controls, VF indices were mainly associated with working memory (WM), whereas in TBI, total correct responses correlated with WM and processing speed; additionally, switching in phonological VF was linked to cognitive flexibility, and clustering in semantic VF to WM. What are the potential or actual clinical implications for this work? VF tasks should be regarded as complex cognitive measures. Beyond word counts, analyzing qualitative components provides valuable insights into executive processes, thereby enhancing their clinical applicability.

papers.title: SPD Matrix Learning for Neuroimaging Analysis: Perspectives, Methods, and Challenges.
papers.authors: Ju C, Kobler R, Collas A, Kawanabe M, Guan C, Thirion B.
papers.journal: IEEE transactions on pattern analysis and machine intelligence
papers.abstract: Neuroimaging provides essential tools for characterizing brain activity and inter-regional connectivity through modalities that capture complementary aspects of brain organization. At the same time, extracting meaningful neural signatures remains challenging because each modality introduces its own sources of variability, including measurement noise, spatial and temporal distortions, heterogeneous acquisition protocols, and limited sample sizes. A unifying perspective arises when these data are represented by symmetric positive definite (SPD) matrices, such as covariance, connectivity, diffusion, or deformation tensors, which encode second-order statistical relationships or local anatomical structure depending on the modality. Equipping the SPD space with Riemannian geometry yields a non-Euclidean framework for principled statistical analysis and machine learning on these representations. This review organizes learning methodologies on SPD manifolds under a unified framework termed SPD matrix learning. From this perspective, SPD modeling provides a common language across neuroimaging modalities and links modern learning pipelines to decades of geometric statistics. We show that (i) learning on the SPD manifold is mathematically well grounded and preserves key structural constraints such as symmetry and positive definiteness; (ii) SPD matrix learning encompasses a broad class of geometric statistical tools that have long been used in neuroimaging; and (iii) it is increasingly compatible with modern AI paradigms, thereby enabling new classes of neuroimaging problems involving manifold-valued data. Taken together, SPD matrix learning offers a unified and forward-looking framework for neuroimaging analysis.

papers.title: Signal Enhancement of Gadoquatrane for Standard Clinical Pulse Sequences: A Phantom Study in Human Plasma.
papers.authors: Jost G, Lohrke J, Pietsch H.
papers.abstract: Objectives The purpose of this phantom study in human plasma was to characterize the signal enhancement properties of gadoquatrane under clinically relevant, highly standardized conditions in comparison to gadobutrol. Gadoquatrane is a novel high-relaxivity, extracellular macrocyclic gadolinium-based contrast agent (GBCA) currently in clinical development at a dose of 0.01 mmol/kg body weight (corresponding to 0.04 mmol Gd/kg). Materials and methods Three GBCA-dilution series in human plasma were prepared: 2 series with equimolar Gd concentrations (0-10 mmol Gd/mL) for gadoquatrane (0.4 mol Gd/L) and gadobutrol (1.0 mol Gd/L), and 1 series with 60% lower Gd concentrations for gadoquatrane (12 samples/series). For each series, signal intensity versus Gd concentration profiles were obtained using standard T1-weighted MRI pulse sequences at 1.5 T. In addition, the impact of sequence parameters was investigated (repetition and echo time for spin-echo sequences; flip angle for gradient-echo sequences). Results The signal enhancement achieved with the 2 GBCAs depended on the Gd concentration and the pulse sequence. For all sequences tested, almost superimposable signal intensity profiles were found for gadobutrol and gadoquatrane, with 60% lower Gd concentrations for gadoquatrane. Sequence parameter variations affected both GBCAs in the same way. The optimal flip angles were equal for gadobutrol and gadoquatrane (60% reduced). Conclusions The signal intensity profiles obtained in human plasma using standard clinical pulse sequences were almost superimposable for gadobutrol and gadoquatrane at 60% lower Gd concentrations. For clinical use, this means that the same pulse sequence parameters can be used for both GBCAs and that, essentially, the same signal enhancement can be expected from gadoquatrane at a dose of 0.04 mmol Gd/kg body weight as from gadobutrol at a dose of 0.1 mmol Gd/kg.

papers.title: Optimizing Brachial Plexus Diffusion Tensor Imaging: The Impact of Deep Learning Reconstruction and Simultaneous Multislice Acceleration on Single-shot Echo-planar Imaging.
papers.authors: Shim E, Ham S, Kim BH, Kang WY, Kang CH, Ahn KS, Lee KC, Choi IY, Kim I, Choi H.
papers.abstract: Objectives This study aimed (1) to quantify the differential impact of deep learning (DL) reconstruction on brachial plexus (BP) diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) image quality and quantitative metrics compared with conventional single-shot echo-planar imaging (EPI), (2) to clarify the clinical utility and limitations of integrating simultaneous multislice (SMS) acceleration with DL DTI in the challenging BP anatomy, and (3) to determine the optimal, time-efficient DTI protocol for robust BP tractography. Materials and methods Twenty-seven healthy volunteers were prospectively enrolled (stage 1: n = 14; stage 2: n = 13). All DTI acquisitions used a single-shot EPI sequence. In the first stage, DTI with DL reconstruction was compared with a conventional non-DL DTI. In the second stage, the integration of SMS acceleration into DL DTI protocols was assessed across 5 protocol sets. Fiber tract number, tract length, tract-based DTI metrics, signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR), image consistency, and interreader agreement were assessed in the BP postganglionic nerve roots and spinal cord. Results In the first stage, DL DTI demonstrated significantly higher tractography success rates, fiber numbers, and fiber lengths in the BP ( P < 0.05). DL substantially improved interreader agreement and image consistency, with the Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) increasing from 0.537 to 0.740 ( P = 0.006). DL reconstruction resulted in changes in anatomy-specific fractional anisotropy, with a significant decrease in BP fractional anisotropy but an increase in spinal cord fractional anisotropy. In the second stage, SMS-integrated protocols produced significantly lower tractography success and degraded image quality compared with non-SMS DL protocols ( P < 0.05). SMS integration resulted in lower SNR and CNR ( P < 0.05), and reduced image consistency (DSC decreased from 0.727 to 0.486, P = 0.015). The DL12-2 protocol (12 diffusion directions and two b800 acquisitions) was identified as the optimal time-efficient solution. Conclusions DL reconstruction significantly improves the feasibility and reliability of BP DTI and affects quantitative metrics in an anatomy-specific manner. In contrast, the integration of SMS acceleration with single-shot EPI remains technically challenging in the high-susceptibility BP region. Our findings underscore that anatomy-specific optimization is essential for successful clinical integration of DL-enhanced DTI.

papers.title: Gadolinium Presence in the Brain After Gadolinium-based Contrast Agents: Evidence from Animal Behavioral Studies.
papers.authors: Akai H, Okimoto N, Kato S, Furuta T, Abe O.
papers.abstract: Since the discovery of gadolinium (Gd) in the brain following the administration of gadolinium-based contrast agents (GBCAs), considerable progress has been made in understanding their pharmacokinetics and neurotoxicology. This review summarizes animal studies assessing the presence of Gd after GBCA administration, with a specific focus on functional and behavioral outcomes, rather than providing a comprehensive overview of all aspects of Gd presence in the brain. These findings indicate that Gd accumulation in the brain depends on the chemical structure of GBCAs, with linear agents exhibiting greater retention and slower clearance than macrocyclic agents. Gd distribution is nonhomogeneous, primarily localized in deep gray matter structures, and is influenced by cerebrospinal fluid-mediated transport and perivascular deposition. Although motor and cognitive functions are generally unaffected under normal conditions, prolonged exposure to linear GBCAs or preexisting conditions such as inflammation or metabolic disorders may increase neurotoxic risks, resulting in motor and cognitive deficits. Pain and sensory hypersensitivity are frequently and reproducibly observed, particularly when linear agents are used. We will also discuss the potential mechanisms of neurotoxicity caused by free Gd 3+ ion. However, these mechanistic findings are limited because the studies cannot be extrapolated to clinical practice. Future studies should investigate the potential associations between GBCA exposure and neurodegenerative diseases. These insights are essential for enhancing GBCA safety and informing clinical guidelines.

papers.title: UCHL1 as a Biomarker of Brain Injury in Neonates and Infants Undergoing Cardiac Surgery: An Exploratory Study.
papers.authors: Swangwong S, Alhamdan F, Nishiori H, Maisat W, Odegard KC, Soriano S, Koutsogiannaki S, Ishibashi N, Yuki K.
papers.journal: FASEB journal : official publication of the Federation of American Societies for Experimental Biology
papers.abstract: As survival rates following pediatric cardiac surgery have improved, neurodevelopmental impairment has emerged as a significant long-term comorbidity. Neonates and infants are particularly vulnerable and are at the highest risk for neurodevelopmental impairment. Imaging study has identified new white matter injury in up to 20%-50% of this cohort postoperatively. Currently there is no clinical modality to accurately detect neurological events in real time during cardiac surgery. Brain imaging remains the gold standard for identifying cerebral injury, but it is only feasible postoperatively. In this study we intended to determine a plasma marker suitable to detect intraoperative brain injury by examining infant piglets undergoing cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) and neonates/infants undergoing cardiac surgery on CPB. We compared two different CPB strategies; full-flow bypass alone and bypass involving circulatory arrest (CA) in infant piglets where CA was associated with post CPB neurodevelopmental impairment in our previous study. We found that ubiquitin C-terminal hydrolase L1 (UCHL1), a protein abundantly expressed in the neuronal body, was elevated in the blood after CA in infant piglets. CA group showed more proinflammatory profiles than full-flow bypass group. Histological analysis of piglet brain demonstrated that neurons underwent more apoptosis after CA, along with lower UCHL1 expression. Plasma proteomics analysis in infant piglets suggested the disruption of blood brain barrier (BBB) after CA compared to full-flow bypass. We hypothesized that UCHL1 could serve as a promising neurological injury marker in patients, too. We compared neonates and infants who underwent full-flow bypass alone and bypass involving CA/regional perfusion (RP) groups. Neonates and infants subjected to CA/RP had higher odds of having neurodevelopmental impairment compared to full-flow bypass group. CA/RP group showed more proinflammatory profiles than full-flow bypass group. Plasma proteomics analysis in neonates and infants also demonstrated similar findings in CA/RP arm compared to full-flow arm as we observed in piglets. UCHL1 level at the rewarming during CPB showed highest area under the curve (AUC) value of 0.7022 (95% CI 0.5692-0.8287). Overall, this study suggested UCHL1 to be a promising biomarker of brain injury associated with neurodevelopmental impairment following pediatric cardiac surgery involving CPB.

papers.title: Primary intracranial sarcoma, DICER1-mutant: 5 cases highlighting variable clinical and molecular features.
papers.authors: Gestrich CK, Patel S, Shroff SM, Goodman A, Mohammedjoead S, Marshall MS, Kulich S, Skaugen JM.
papers.journal: Journal of neuropathology and experimental neurology
papers.abstract: Primary intracranial sarcoma, DICER1-mutant, a novel, rare entity in the 2021 WHO classification of central nervous system tumors, is characterized by spindled to pleomorphic cells with eosinophilic cytoplasmic globules, immunophenotypic evidence of myogenic differentiation and DICER1 mutations. These tumors mainly occur in children and have a distinct methylation profile.
