We report 5 additional cases of primary intracranial sarcoma, DICER1-mutant (age range 6 to 40 years) identified by methylation profiling and/or sequencing, including 1 in an unusual infratentorial location, 1 in an adult patient and 1 in the setting of a germline DICER1 mutation. All tumors were surgically resected and demonstrated spindle cells with fascicular growth and variable pleomorphism; 3 showed variably prominent eosinophilic cytoplasmic globules and at least focal myogenic differentiation by immunohistochemistry. All cases had a hotspot DICER1 mutation; 2 had concurrent DICER1 loss; and 1 had a known germline truncating DICER1 mutation. Three cases also demonstrated a KRAS mutation, 1 of which had a TP53 mutation. Two patients were alive with no evidence of disease after 26.7 and 39.3 months; 1 patient died of disease after 20.1 months. We demonstrate the utility of methylation profiling in combination with next generation sequencing testing in the diagnosis of this rare entity.

papers.title: Old organoids mimic brain maturation.
papers.authors: Whalley K.

papers.title: Diagnostic and sex effects on frontostriatal brain wiring structural organization in early psychosis affective subjects compared to healthy controls.
papers.authors: Levitt JJ, Zhang F, Vangel M, Nestor PG, Rathi Y, Cetin-Karayumak S, Kubicki M, Pasternak O, Coleman MJ, Lewandowski KE, Holt DJ, Keshavan M, Bouix S, Öngür D, Breier A, Shenton ME, O'Donnell LJ.
papers.abstract: Background Brain connectivity abnormalities may underlie affective psychosis which may be influenced by sex. Using diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (dMRI) tractography, we assessed frontostriatal brain wiring connectivity patterns in 46 early psychosis affective and 56 healthy control young adult, male and female participants. Methods We collected harmonized whole brain tractography dMRI data from three sites and applied our novel fiber clustering methodology to identify 17 white matter fiber clusters connecting the frontal cortex and caudate per hemisphere in each group. By comparing cortical and caudate inter-cluster endpoint distances between groups, we assessed their patterns of frontostriatal connectivity. Results 1) In both males and females in early affective psychosis and healthy controls, bilaterally, the frontal cortex to caudate wiring pattern deviated from a topographic organization. 2) in a right hemisphere frontal pole fiber cluster, independent of sex, we found a significant interaction effect of diagnosis on the connectivity pattern between frontal cortex and caudate, (p = 0.013); 3) in a left hemisphere inferior frontal gyrus, pars triangularis, fiber cluster, we found sex influenced the significant interaction effect of diagnosis on the connectivity pattern between frontal cortex and caudate, (p = 0.0085), with the effect much greater in females (p < 0.00001) than in males (p = 0.97); and, 4) post-hoc tests showed a significant effect of diagnosis on the pattern of frontal cortex to caudate connectivity in specific subregions (ps ≤0.04). Conclusions Importantly, while the frontostriatal wiring pattern in both early affective psychosis and healthy controls deviated from a topographic organization, we found in a right hemisphere fiber cluster, independent of sex, that a significant interaction effect of diagnosis was observed on the frontal cortex to caudate connectivity pattern, whereas, in a left hemisphere fiber cluster, the effect of diagnosis on connectivity pattern was influenced by sex, showing the importance of the role of sex in brain wiring patterns in early affective psychosis.

papers.title: Age-related changes in memory for gist and details: New perspectives on the representational quality of episodic memory.
papers.authors: Greene NR, Castel A, Naveh-Benjamin M.
papers.abstract: Substantial heterogeneity in adult age-related declines in episodic memory within and across tasks and individuals has prompted extensive theoretical debate about the source of these variations. Today, many theories assume that age-related changes in the representational fidelity of memory and the degree to which a test demands the retrieval of specific details of past experiences underlie much of this variability. This special issue of Psychology and Aging presents 19 contributions from researchers from around the world that together aim to enrich our understanding of the representational basis of age-related memory change. These contributions explore several interrelated themes related to measuring, predicting, and, at times, counteracting age-related declines in memory specificity while extending representational accounts to new tasks, more naturalistic contexts, and populations spanning the adult lifespan as well as individuals with neurocognitive impairment. The breadth of coverage spans multiple research domains with rich histories in the field of cognitive aging, including recognition memory, autobiographical memory, event memory, decision making, comprehension, and computational modeling. Collectively, the diversity of questions posed by the articles and the varied methods they advance to addressing them highlight the value of integrating findings across different research traditions to develop a more unified framework for studying age-related changes in memory specificity. papers.title: Icariin against neuroinflammation: emerging evidence for gut-brain axis modulation involving short-chain fatty acids, vagal signaling, and extracellular vesicles.
papers.authors: Wu C, Guo L, Sun X, Zhu J, Zhao Z, Qi S, Li Y, Li H, Zhao R, Xiu Z, Zhu G, Li Y.
papers.abstract: Neuroinflammation is a central pathological process in a wide range of central nervous system disorders, yet therapeutic strategies directed solely at single inflammatory targets have shown limited efficacy. Gut-brain axis dysfunction may contribute to neuroinflammatory progression through interconnected metabolic, immune, neural, and vesicle-associated routes. Icariin, a major flavonoid glycoside from Epimedii Folium, has attracted attention because of its anti-inflammatory, neuroprotective, and microbiota-modulating properties. In this review, we summarize current evidence for the anti-neuroinflammatory effects of icariin and explicitly stratify the evidence into three levels: direct icariin-related findings, icariin-related findings without causal gut-brain validation, and mechanisms inferred from broader gut-brain axis biology. Available studies provide relatively stronger support for intestinal barrier protection, microbiota remodeling, peripheral cytokine suppression, and central inflammatory pathway regulation. In contrast, short-chain fatty acid (SCFA)-associated signaling, vagal neuroimmune communication, and extracellular vesicle (EV)-mediated cargo transfer remain plausible but incompletely validated candidate routes. We further compare icariin with its major microbial metabolites, especially icariside II and icaritin, because oral icariin may act partly through metabolite-mediated exposure rather than through robust brain penetration of the parent compound. Major limitations include insufficient causal perturbation, incomplete organ-specific pharmacokinetic data, inter-individual microbiota variability, and uncertain therapeutic time windows. Overall, icariin emerges as a promising multi-target natural product for anti-neuroinflammatory research, but the causal hierarchy and translational relevance of proposed gut-brain pathways require direct validation.

papers.title: Reframing traumatic brain injury and spinal cord injury as chronic multisystem disorders: toward integrated, long-term care.
papers.authors: Marini S, Schneider ALC, Alshaya A, Bragge P, Corrigan JD, Dams-O'Connor K, Giacino JT, Halabi C, Hendrick K, Hutchinson PJA, Khan T, Khattak AF, Kirshblum S, Lala T, Løvstad M, Manley GT, Mediratta S, Nagayama M, Newcombe VFJ, Pugh MJ, Rosseau G, Tenovuo O, Venturini S, Wilson F, Wilson L, Menon DK, Hammond FM, Zafonte R, Izzy S, Global Coalition for TBI as a Notifiable and Chronic Condition.
papers.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) and spinal cord injury (SCI) affect more than 220 million people worldwide and are associated with cardiometabolic, endocrine, neurological, and psychiatric sequelae for years to decades after an acute injury. However, most health systems still treat neurotrauma (TBI and SCI, collectively) as a time-limited event, leaving long-term surveillance of these patients fragmented or absent, which leads to preventable mortality and avoidable readmissions. TBI and SCI in adults should be reclassified as acute-onset multisystem chronic-risk conditions. Existing cardiovascular, endocrine, and psychiatric services do not capture neurotrauma-specific risks, including trauma-induced hypopituitarism, autonomic dysregulation, accelerated ageing, and cognitive-behavioural impairment, so neurotrauma care is best framed as a missing node in chronic neurological care. We propose a risk-stratified pathway of care navigation, multisystem screening, and telehealth; convergence with adjacent stroke, cardiometabolic, memory, psychiatric, pain, and epilepsy services; and the financing, workforce, and registry reforms needed to deliver measurable reductions in 5-year mortality, avoidable rehospitalisation, and long-term disability.

papers.title: PET for Evaluation of Neurologic Diseases: Part one: Neurodegenerative Diseases.
papers.authors: Veziroglu E, Nikpanah M, Farhadi F, Kalbi D, Hensley C, McConathy J.
papers.abstract: This review of PET for evaluation of neurological diseases is divided into two parts; part one examines the clinical use of positron emission tomography (PET) in neurodegenerative diseases. FDG-PET can identify characteristic patterns of cerebral metabolism and help distinguish among neurodegenerative disorders. Amyloid and tau PET have expanding diagnostic and theranostic roles in Alzheimer's disease, including assessment of disease-specific pathology and treatment eligibility. FDOPA-PET evaluates presynaptic dopamine synthesis and supports assessment of Parkinson's disease and other parkinsonian syndromes. Combined with structural imaging and clinical evaluation, PET can improve diagnostic confidence, refine prognosis, and inform treatment decisions.

papers.title: Diagnostic Imaging Analysis of Humerus Bone Structure in Long-Legged Buzzard (Buteo rufinus): Radiology and CT-Scan Insights.
papers.authors: Alinejad N, Esmailinejad MR, Shafiei H, Jahedi M.
papers.abstract: Background Advanced imaging techniques, particularly computed tomography (CT), are revolutionising veterinary diagnostics by providing detailed structural insights essential for accurate diagnosis and treatment planning. Objectives This study aimed to compare the efficacy of CT imaging and digital radiography in the diagnosis and treatment of raptors, with the goal of identifying the more precise and efficient imaging technique for clinical management. By evaluating these methods, the research seeks to optimise diagnostic accuracy and treatment planning, ultimately improving rehabilitation outcomes for birds of prey requiring high-precision care. Methods This study evaluated the humerus bone structure of 10 adult Long-legged Buzzard (Buteo rufinus) individuals using digital radiology and CT imaging. Birds were sedated to minimise stress, and both left and right humerus structures were examined. Humerus indices, including cranio-caudal diameter, medullary cavity diameter, cortical thickness and bone density, were measured to compare the effectiveness of the two modalities. Results Results of this study revealed significant differences in humerus indices between radiology and CT techniques (P < 0.05), with CT providing more accurate and detailed measurements. CT excelled in visualising internal structures, such as the cortex and medullary cavity, offering superior diagnostic clarity. No significant differences were observed between left and right humerus indices (P > 0.05), indicating consistent bilateral symmetry. Conclusions The study concludes that CT imaging is superior to digital radiology for assessing humerus bone structure in the long-legged buzzard, providing precise information crucial for managing humeral injuries. These findings underscore the clinical utility of CT in avian veterinary medicine, particularly for raptors and recommend This technique helps surgeons prepare the necessary equipment more accurately and use more precise methods, ultimately increasing the success rate of surgeries.

papers.title: An Integrative Approach for Subtyping Mental Disorders Using Multimodal Data.
papers.authors: Zhao Y, Wang Y, Liu Y.
papers.abstract: Understanding the biological and behavioral heterogeneity underlying psychiatric disorders is critical for advancing precision diagnosis, treatment, and prevention. This paper addresses the scientific question of how multimodal data, which spans clinical, cognitive, and neuroimaging measures, can be integrated to identify biologically meaningful subtypes of mental disorders. We introduce Mixed INtegrative Data Subtyping (MINDS), a Bayesian hierarchical model designed to jointly analyze mixed-type data for simultaneous dimension reduction and clustering. Using data from the adolescent brain cognitive development (ABCD) Study, MINDS integrates clinical symptoms, cognitive performance, and brain structure measures to subtype attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). Our method leverages Pólya-Gamma augmentation for computational efficiency and robust inference. Simulations demonstrate improved stability and accuracy compared to existing clustering approaches. Application to the ABCD data reveals clinically interpretable subtypes of ADHD and OCD with distinct cognitive and neurodevelopmental profiles. These findings show how integrative multimodal modeling can enhance the reproducibility and clinical relevance of psychiatric subtyping, funding data-driven policies for early identification and targeted interventions in mental health.

papers.title: Volumetric and Intrastructural Characterization of the Substantia Nigra Using Optimized Synthetic MR Images Derived From Quantitative T1 Maps at 3 T.
papers.authors: von Erdmannsdorff L, Kovacheva L, C Thomas D, Hattingen E, Deichmann R, Arendt CT.
papers.abstract: Accurate imaging of the substantia nigra (SN) is critical for diagnosing and monitoring neurodegenerative conditions like Parkinson's disease. However, conventional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) struggles to precisely visualize this small structure within the deep brain due to poor intrinsic tissue contrast. Although quantitative MRI (qMRI) captures objective tissue properties with diagnostic value to assess neurodegenerative conditions of the SN, additionally acquiring multiple MRI contrasts inherently requires impractically long scan times. To overcome this, qMRI-derived synthetic MRI uses mathematical signal models to retrospectively generate various synthetic contrast weightings from a single map of quantitative T1-relaxation times (qT1). This study investigated which mathematical transformations of qT1 maps, including an approximation for pseudo-proton spin density (pPSD), are best suited to derive optimized synthetic MRI contrasts for accurate SN analysis. By evaluating six dedicated qT1-derived contrast weightings in healthy subjects, this work demonstrates that a nonlinear, signal-increased pPSD-based synthetic MRI contrast (si4 _PSD) yields a favorable balance by significantly enhancing optical contrast while maintaining a sufficient signal-to-noise ratio and preserving contrast-to-noise ratio. The si4 _PSD images enabled highly consistent, automated atlas-based segmentation of the SN that significantly outperformed traditional manual delineation, overcoming rater variability and bias from age-dependent contrast changes. Automated segmentation revealed significant sex- and hemisphere-dependent differences in SN volume, whereas qT1 data simultaneously uncovered distinct subregional and asymmetric intrastructural aging patterns. These findings highlight that macrostructural volume and intrastructural tissue properties must be assessed as independent variables. In conclusion, this qT1-based, automated framework offers a highly consistent, scalable approach to SN mapping without extending patient scan times. By clearly separating physiological intrastructural changes affecting MRI contrasts from mistakenly perceived general atrophy, this methodology provides a powerful foundation for developing more precise and objective imaging biomarkers for SN-related neurodegenerative diseases in both research and clinical settings.

papers.title: Fat-Water Swap Artifact Correction in MRI-Based Fat Quantification Using Physics-Informed Deep Learning With Branch Constrained Optimization.
papers.authors: Ganeshkumar M, Kandasamy D, Shalimar, Anshal S, Dasgupta R, Sharma R, Mehndiratta A.
papers.abstract: Commonly occurring fat-water swap artifacts in multi-echo MRI hinder accurate estimation of the clinical biomarker, proton density fat fraction (PDFF). This study evaluates a novel physics-informed deep learning (PI-DL) model to correct these swap artifacts. The proposed PI-DL model, the "Swap-Net," utilizes a branch-constrained optimization method to explore different bifurcate regions in the residual function optimized, thereby increasing the probability of reaching global minima, as the swap artifacts are caused by the optimization routine settling into a local minimum. Performance evaluation was conducted using multi-echo MRI of 37 (n = 37) subjects, and this included a cohort of 23 (n = 23) high-resolution MRIs. The proprietary mDixon Quant sequence, with optimized parameter settings for accurate liver fat quantification, served as the clinical standard for benchmarking performance. The results of the quantitative evaluations revealed that the average liver PDFF% from the proposed Swap-Net demonstrated excellent agreement with the clinical standard mDixon Quant (correlation coefficient R of 0.98 in the high-resolution cohort). The qualitative evaluations also showed that the fat-water maps from the Swap-Net contained no swap artifacts. In contrast, other state-of-the-art methods exhibited swap artifacts, particularly in high-resolution MRI. The proposed Swap-Net corrected swap artifacts in MRI-based fat quantification, particularly in high-resolution MRI, enabling high-resolution fat-water imaging.

papers.title: Investigating Postmortem Blood Clots as Endogenous Contrast for Mesoscopic Cerebrovascular Mapping at 7 T.
papers.authors: Li C, Leitner D, Pang H, Li A, Bruno M, Faustin A, Devinsky O, Wisniewski T, Wadghiri YZ, Zhang J, Ge Y.
papers.abstract: Vascular mapping of fixed postmortem human brain tissue remains biologically complex and technically challenging because postmortem changes, including clot contraction and fragmentation, vascular collapse, and fixation-induced alterations, substantially affect vascular MRI contrast. Furthermore, the mechanisms governing vascular contrast in postmortem MRI remain incompletely understood. In this study, we aim to determine the feasibility and reliability of using blood clot formation as a susceptibility contrast source to improve vascular visibility and enable quantitative assessment on ex vivo MRI. Postmortem brain hemispheres and tissue blocks were imaged to assess vascular conspicuity in the cortex, hippocampus, and white matter. Coagulated blood signal was clearly observed within the postmortem brain surface vasculature, with intact clots in small vessels and partial or discontinuous clotting in larger vessels. High-resolution gradient echo (GRE) imaging of tissue blocks enabled detailed reconstruction of local vascular networks, including intrahippocampal vasculature, for vessel density quantification. Quantitative analysis demonstrated markedly shorter T2* values for blood clots (6.6 ± 2.0 ms) compared with gray matter (34.8 ± 8.9 ms) and white matter (19.1 ± 3.6 ms) at 7 T, resulting in appropriate vascular contrast and conspicuity. Histological hematoxylin-eosin and Luxol Fast Blue staining confirmed intravascular clot formation and localization. These findings demonstrate that blood clots can act as an intrinsic contrast for mesoscopic vascular MRI in the postmortem human brain, enabling detailed assessment of microvascular changes and their pathological correlates relevant to vascular contributions to cognitive impairment and dementia.

papers.title: High-Resolution IVIM MRI Characterizes Diffusion-Perfusion Properties of the Parasagittal Dura.
papers.authors: Liu YJ, Liao CH, Peng SL, Lin SC, Lin CC, Lin CW, Hsieh CH, Chen CW, Chang HC.
papers.abstract: The objectives of this study were to characterize the diffusion-perfusion properties of the parasagittal dura (PSD) using high-resolution intravoxel incoherent motion (IVIM) MRI and to explore whether PSD-specific IVIM metrics reflect distinct fluid-transport-related signal behavior compared with CSF and brain parenchyma. Ten healthy volunteers underwent 3 T MRI, including high-resolution 3D T2-FLAIR for anatomical localization and multi-b-value diffusion-weighted imaging using MUSE and FOCUS IVIM sequences. Apparent diffusion coefficients (ADCs) and IVIM parameters-true diffusion coefficient (D), pseudo-diffusion coefficient (D*), and perfusion fraction (f)-were quantified in the PSD, CSF, gray matter (GM), and white matter (WM). A pseudo-diffusion residual analysis was performed to estimate the perfusion-related b-value transition. Tissue-specific differences were assessed using nonparametric statistics. The PSD showed diffusion-perfusion characteristics distinct from those of both CSF and brain parenchyma. ADC values decreased with increasing b values and were intermediate between those of CSF and GM/WM. IVIM analysis demonstrated higher perfusion fractions and pseudo-diffusion coefficients in the PSD than in GM and WM, indicating substantial microcirculatory or fluid-transport contributions. The perfusion-related b-value transition thresholds in the PSD were higher than those in CSF but lower than those in GM and WM, supporting its intermediate perfusion behavior. MUSE and FOCUS acquisitions produced comparable quantitative metrics, with MUSE demonstrating reduced geometric distortion and FOCUS providing higher signal-to-noise ratios. In conclusion, the PSD exhibits a distinct diffusion-perfusion profile consistent with its role as a transitional interface among CSF pathways, dural lymphatics, and venous outflow. PSD-specific IVIM metrics may provide a rapid, noncontrast approach for characterizing dural fluid-transport-related signal behavior at the interface between CSF spaces, meningeal lymphatics, and venous outflow.

papers.title: Cerebellar Glutamate Chemical Exchange Saturation Transfer Alterations Correlated With Cognitive Impairment in Parkinson's Disease.
papers.authors: Ma X, Li X, He X, Liu Y, Xie M, Lin Z, Shang D, Chen H, Chen M, Li C, Su W.
papers.abstract: The role of cerebellar glutamatergic dysfunction in cognitive impairment of Parkinson's disease (PD) remains poorly understood. Glutamate chemical exchange saturation transfer (GluCEST) imaging enables noninvasive assessment of regional glutamate levels. To investigate the associations between cerebellar GluCEST-derived alterations and cognitive impairment as well as other clinical characteristics in patients with PD, 64 PD patients underwent 3 T MRI including GluCEST sequence and clinical assessments. Patients were divided into PD with preserved cognition (PD-CN, MoCA > 22, n = 23) and PD with impaired cognition (PD-CI, MoCA ≤ 22, n = 41) subgroups. GluCEST-derived parameters including MTRasym , CESTRnr , and MTRRex were obtained from the bilateral cerebellar cortex and white matter. Between-group differences in the GluCEST-derived parameters were assessed using ANOVA, adjusting for age and sex. Pearson or Spearman correlation analyses were used to examine associations between GluCEST-derived parameters and cognitive performance. Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction was applied for multiple comparisons. Compared with the PD-CN group, the PD-CI group showed lower MTRasym values in the bilateral cerebellar cortex (CC) and the right cerebellar white matter (CWM) (p < 0.05) and a lower CESTRnr value in the right CWM (p = 0.016). Within the PD-CI group, MoCA total score was negatively correlated with MTRRex in the left CC (p = 0.013). Attention/working memory was negatively correlated with CESTRnr (p = 0.021) and MTRRex (p = 0.007) in the left CC. Orientation was negatively correlated with MTRRex in the left CWM, right CC, and right CWM (p < 0.05). In addition, negative correlation between disease duration and MTRRex in the right CWM remained significant after FDR correction (p = 0.020). Cerebellar GluCEST alterations are associated with cognitive impairment in PD. GluCEST may serve as a possible neuroimaging marker in PD.

papers.title: Low latency and generalizable dynamic MRI via L+S alternating gradient descent and minimization.
papers.authors: Babu S, Lingala SG, Vaswani N.
papers.abstract: Background Dynamic MRI reconstruction often requires accurate, fast, and low-latency algorithms that generalize across multiple applications, sampling schemes, and rates, without problem-specific parameter tuning. Existing methods either lack generalizability or require extensive parameter adjustment. Purpose To develop generalizable, low-latency MRI reconstruction algorithms based on low-rank (LR) and low-rank + sparse (L+S) models that are accurate, fast, and require minimal parameter tuning across diverse dynamic MRI settings. Methods We propose a novel Alternating Gradient Descent and Minimization (AltGDmin) approach for L+S matrix recovery from column-wise undersampled measurements, and extend it to a 3-level hierarchical L+S model for dynamic MRI. A few-shot (FS) learning modification (AGM-L+S-FS) is introduced to enable near low-latency reconstruction with per-frame processing time comparable to or faster than scan time. A simpler LR-only variant is also evaluated. Results The proposed algorithms were validated on 6 prospective and 12 retrospective dynamic MRI datasets, covering cardiac, speech, and abdominal applications, with Cartesian, pseudo-radial, radial, and spiral sampling schemes. Experiments demonstrate accurate reconstruction, generalizability across datasets and sampling rates, and low-latency performance. Detailed comparisons with state-of-the-art LR, L+S, low-latency, and unsupervised deep learning methods show superior or comparable performance. Conclusions Our AGM-L+S-FS approach provide generalizable, fast, and low-latency MRI reconstruction across multiple dynamic MRI applications and sampling schemes, without the need for problem-specific parameter tuning.

papers.title: Learning global and local representations for generalized category discovery in neurodegenerative diseases.
papers.authors: Shen Y, Yang X, Hu Y, Qiao K, Hai J, Chen J, Yan B.
papers.abstract: Background Artificial intelligence (AI) has achieved notable success in closed-set classification of neurodegenerative diseases, but its performance degrades significantly in more realistic open-set settings, such as discovering rare or novel disease subtypes from unlabeled data that are not seen during training. Purpose This study introduces, to our knowledge, the first framework for generalized category discovery (GCD) in neurodegenerative diseases using MRI. It aims to leverage labeled data from known categories to automatically identify novel categories within unlabeled datasets. Methods We propose a GCD framework integrating semi-supervised contrastive learning with global-local representation learning to jointly optimize feature learning. Globally, we enforce consistency between weakly augmented views of the same instance by aligning their similarity relationships with other embeddings in a support queue. Locally, we treat neighborhood embeddings from the support queue as positive pairs for cross-instance contrastive learning, enhancing fine-grained discrimination. This dual strategy results in a unified learning objective that is applicable to both labeled and unlabeled data, effectively narrowing the representation gap among semantically similar instances. Results We evaluate our method on a benchmark dataset comprising six neurodegenerative diseases, with over 1500 patient samples. Experimental results demonstrate that our framework consistently outperforms representative state-of-the-art methods. Specifically, our method achieves 66.02% Accuracy and 60.59% Normalized Mutual Information on all categories, and 54.53% Accuracy and 16.67% Normalized Mutual Information on novel categories, surpassing existing state-of-the-art methods. Conclusions Our framework underscores the model's robustness and its practical value in discovering new neurodegenerative disease conditions, highlighting its potential for advancing open-set diagnostic AI.

papers.title: Betaine Attenuates Cuprizone-Induced Cortical Demyelination: The Role of the WNT4/mTOR Signalling Pathway in Regulating Astrogliosis and Synaptic Integrity.
papers.authors: Said YM, Abd Elkader HAE, Bekheet GJ, Abdel Salam S, Essawy AE.
papers.journal: Journal of biochemical and molecular toxicology
papers.abstract: Cortical grey matter pathology manifests early demyelinating diseases and is a primary driver of permanent neurological impairment. Our study investigated the neuroprotective effects of betaine against cuprizone (CPZ)-induced damage to the cerebral cortex in rats, focusing on its ability to modulate the upstream WNT4/mTOR signalling pathway. Cortical tissues were collected for biochemical assessments of oxidative and inflammatory markers, real-time PCR analysis for WNT4, GFAP, and mTOR gene expressions, histopathological examination, and immunohistochemical analysis of vimentin, S100, and synaptophysin. Exposure to CPZ resulted in severe cortical damage with profound oxidative stress. This oxidative status triggered a pronounced neuroinflammatory response, leading to elevated levels of IL-17A, IL-1β, and TNF-α, which in turn caused chronic, hyper-reactive astrogliosis. This was confirmed by the upregulation of GFAP gene expression and enhanced immunohistochemical staining of vimentin and S100β, resulting in extensive loss of cortical synaptic integrity (depletion of synaptophysin). Importantly, treatment with betaine served as a molecular brake, significantly downregulating the aberrant gene expressions of WNT4 and mTOR. This targeted downregulation effectively reduced the overactive glial response, leading to a significant reduction in astrogliosis (GFAP, vimentin, and S100β), alleviated the pro-inflammatory cytokines, restored endogenous antioxidant functions, and ultimately preserved cortical synaptophysin expression and cellular structure. Overall, these results demonstrate that betaine exerts a neuroprotective effect against CPZ-induced cortical injury, which is strongly associated with the attenuation of WNT4/mTOR signalling pathway hyperactivation, suppression of astrogliosis, and preservation of synaptic density. The preservation of cortical grey matter integrity is directly associated with alleviating cognitive deficits and long-term physical disabilities in multiple sclerosis patients, emphasising the translational relevance of targetable neuroprotective therapies.

papers.title: Hippocampal Subfield Volumes and Spatial Memory Performance in Older Adults At-Risk for Type 2 Diabetes.
papers.authors: Al-Shaikh JH, Ghosh-Swaby OR, Khan AR, Thornton J, Bussey TJ, Saksida LM, Palmer D, Liu-Ambrose T, Nagamatsu LS.
papers.abstract: Older adults at risk for type 2 diabetes (T2D) are more likely to experience accelerated cognitive aging and neurodegeneration due to impaired metabolism in the hippocampus. However, the precise relationship between T2D risk factors, brain volumes (i.e., gray matter, white matter, hippocampus subfields), and hippocampus-dependent functions (i.e., spatial pattern separation, a component of spatial memory) remains unexplored. To investigate these relationships in this cross-sectional study, 60 older adults at risk for T2D (e.g., high BMI or elevated A1c levels) completed a touchscreen-based spatial pattern separation behavioral task-the Trial-Unique delayed Nonmatching-to-Location (TUNL) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). HippUnfold was utilized to segment the hippocampus from high-resolution, T1 -weighted images. We found positive correlations between A1c levels and volumes of the dentate gyrus (DG) and cornu ammonis (CA) 2, indicating that higher A1c was associated with larger volumes of hippocampal subregions. Additionally, TUNL accuracy was correlated with gray matter and distinct hippocampus subfield volumes (i.e., subiculum, CA1, and CA4), with larger volumes associated with better spatial memory performance. Understanding early structural changes in T2D risk allows us to further characterize changes in brain health associated with metabolic dysfunction.
keywords: Touchscreen Trial‐unique Delayed Non‐matching To Location

papers.title: Functional Network Organization Underlying Individual Differences in False Feedback Susceptibility: A Graph Theoretical Analysis.
papers.authors: Patchitt J, Karapanagiotidis T, Garfinkel SN, Miller M, Tsakiris M, Clark A, Critchley HD.
papers.abstract: Individual differences in susceptibility to somatosensory false physiological feedback reflect variations in interoceptive processing, yet the underlying neural network mechanisms remain unclear. We analyzed resting-state functional connectivity using graph theoretical approaches in 41 healthy adults who completed a somatosensory false feedback paradigm. Nine regions of interest were defined from previous activation analyses, and network topology metrics including local efficiency, clustering coefficient, centrality measures, and path length were calculated across multiple thresholds. Three distinct patterns of network organization predicted false feedback susceptibility. Individuals more susceptible to false feedback showed: (1) increased posterior insula eccentricity, indicating network peripheralization of this key interoceptive region; (2) consistent orbitofrontal cortex segregation across multiple metrics including increased path length and decreased centrality measures; and (3) cerebellar network reconfiguration with reduced local efficiency but increased betweenness centrality. Somatosensory false feedback susceptibility reflects specific alterations in functional network topology, particularly reduced integration of interoceptive regions (posterior insula) and emotional appraisal systems (orbitofrontal cortex). These findings support a network-based model where interoceptive processing depends on efficient integration between visceral sensation, emotional evaluation, and cognitive control systems. Understanding these network properties may inform interventions targeting interoceptive awareness and emotional regulation.

papers.title: IFN-γ-Responsive Microglia-Derived Extracellular Vesicles Impair White Matter Repair After Stroke Through a miR-9-5p/NEDD4-Dependent Mechanism.
papers.authors: Qian D, Xu T, Guo Y, Deng S, Geng Y, Li H, Gan L, Lian Q, Xu J, Yao H, Ye J, Myagmartsend E, Yang GY, Wang J, Tang Y, An Q.
papers.abstract: Promoting white matter repair is crucial for functional recovery after ischemic stroke. Our previous study has identified an IFN-γ-responsive microglia phenotype in the brain after stroke. However, its role in white matter repair remains poorly understood. Herein, we find that extracellular vesicles derived from IFN-γ-responsive microglia (IFN-γ EVs) are internalized by oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs), leading to impaired OPCs proliferation, survival, and differentiation and reduced white matter repair in a murine transient middle cerebral artery occlusion (tMCAO) model. Mechanistically, miR-9-5p enrichment in IFN-γ EVs suppresses NEDD4 expression, a key regulator of myelination, leading to reduced OPCs maturation and white matter repair. Genetic interventions including miR-9-5p knockdown in IFN-γ EVs or NEDD4 overexpression in OPCs restore remyelination and functional recovery. Our findings demonstrate that IFN-γ EVs act as negative regulators of OPCs differentiation and remyelination following ischemic stroke via miR-9-5p/NEDD4 pathway. Targeting this signaling axis may represent a novel therapeutic strategy to enhance remyelination and functional recovery after stroke.

papers.title: Pathogenic Variants in HEPACAM Alter Protein Localization and Interactome in Astrocytes of the Developing Mouse Cortex.
papers.authors: Lewis RW, Dogan BC, Stanek AL, Evans EB, Coble MG, Spence-Osorio HE, Farizatto KLG, Mordant AL, Mills CA, Herring LE, Baldwin KT.
papers.abstract: Megalencephalic leukoencephalopathy with subcortical cysts (MLC) is a rare leukodystrophy characterized by early-onset macrocephaly, white matter edema, seizures, and motor and cognitive decline. Approximately 25% of MLC patients carry HEPACAM pathogenic variants, many of which are dominant missense variants causing remitting MLC Type 2b. HEPACAM encodes hepatic and glial cell adhesion molecule (hepaCAM), also known as GlialCAM, an astrocyte-enriched transmembrane protein with important roles in astrocyte territory establishment, gap junction coupling, branching organization, synaptic function, and development of the gliovascular unit. The molecular mechanisms through which pathogenic variants in HEPACAM alter hepaCAM protein function in vivo and facilitate MLC pathogenesis during brain development remain largely unknown. Here, we used new viral tools and proximity-based proteomics to examine how three different dominant pathogenic variants alter hepaCAM subcellular localization and protein interactome in astrocytes of the developing mouse cortex. We found dramatic changes in hepaCAM distribution throughout the astrocyte, which were common to all mutants tested. We also observed significant changes in protein interactome between wild type and mutant hepaCAM, including decreased association with previously described hepaCAM-interacting proteins Connexin 43 and CLC-2. Moreover, we identified the epilepsy-associate potassium channel KCNQ2 as a novel hepaCAM interaction partner and found reduced association between KCNQ2 and pathogenic variants. Collectively, our data provide new insights into hepaCAM protein function in astrocytes during brain development, reveal altered protein dynamics of pathogenic variants, and provide a new resource to explore the molecular underpinnings of MLC pathogenesis.

papers.title: Mechanisms of Exercise Training in Ameliorating Cognitive Function in Patients With Depression: A Narrative Review of Molecular Targets and Clinical Prescriptions.
papers.authors: Guo Z, Dong L, Lin JJX, Duan Y, Liu W, Jiang W, Liu C, Jia S, Song Y, Ding F, Xie Z, Yin M, Zhu K, Ma X, Wang P, Wei C, Schuch FB, Wang X.
papers.abstract: Depression is frequently accompanied by core cognitive impairments, notably in executive function and memory. Although the ameliorative effects of exercise training have been widely corroborated, the evidence regarding its underlying mechanisms remains fragmented. To provide a comprehensive and integrated view, this review proposes a testable, cross-scale "peripheral-central-behavioral" hypothetical mechanistic model to explain the effects of exercise on cognition. The core theoretical contribution of this study lies in explicitly postulating a "molecule-structure-function" cross-level mediation hypothesis. The exercise-induced upregulation of peripheral neurotrophic factors must be mediated by a core "structural mediator", specifically the enhanced white matter integrity of key tracts, to ultimately drive the "electrophysiological output" of optimized cerebral information processing efficiency. Furthermore, this model proposes the temporal cascade effects of neuro-psychological interactive regulation, distinguishing between early subacute HPA axis normalization and mid-to-long-term reward system activation. Crucially, recognizing the profound translational gap between biological mechanisms and clinical application, this review emphasizes that optimal exercise prescriptions cannot be dictated solely by physiological targets. Addressing the heterogeneity of depressed individuals, we propose a precision intervention framework that meticulously balances neurobiological efficacy by tailoring specific modalities and optimal dose-response thresholds to distinct depression subtypes. Ultimately, this review provides a theoretical framework for future stratified randomized controlled trials (RCTs) based on longitudinal multimodal co-measurements, paving the way for clinically viable, predictable, and highly individualized exercise prescriptions.

papers.title: Structural Reorganization of Hypothalamic Subfields in Postherpetic Neuralgia: Volumetric and Morphometric Covariance Network Analyses.
papers.authors: Oh D, Lee DA, Lee HJ, Park KM.
papers.abstract: Background Postherpetic neuralgia (PHN) is a chronic neuropathic pain condition associated with central nervous system reorganization, but hypothalamic alterations remain poorly understood. We investigated hypothalamic subfield volumes and morphometric covariance network organization in patients with PHN. Methods This prospective cross-sectional study included 42 patients with PHN and 41 healthy controls whose hypothalamic subfield volumes were obtained from T1-weighted MRI using automated FreeSurfer segmentation. Bilateral mean raw subfield volumes were compared between groups using analysis of covariance, adjusting for age, sex and estimated total intracranial volume, with false discovery rate correction for multiple comparisons. Morphometric covariance networks were constructed from age- and sex-residualized subfield volumes and graph-theoretical measures were compared using permutation testing. Results After adjustment for estimated total intracranial volume, age and sex, the tubular superior subfield was nominally larger in PHN (adjusted difference, 4.95 mm3 ; 95% CI, 0.05-9.85; p = 0.048), but did not survive FDR correction. No other subfield or whole-hypothalamic volume differed significantly. PHN showed reduced local efficiency and clustering coefficient and increased characteristic path length, without a significant difference in global efficiency. No pain-side-dependent lateralization or significant associations between subfield volumes and pain measures or disease duration were observed. Conclusions PHN was associated with altered hypothalamic morphometric covariance organization, characterized by reduced local network segregation and increased characteristic path length, while regional volume differences were limited after intracranial volume correction. These findings suggest that PHN-related central reorganization may involve hypothalamic systems related to homeostatic regulation and stress adaptation. Significance statement This study demonstrates altered morphometric covariance organization of hypothalamic subfields in postherpetic neuralgia, despite limited evidence of regional volumetric differences after intracranial volume adjustment. These findings suggest that hypothalamic involvement in PHN may be better reflected by altered coordinated structural organization than by regional volume changes alone.

papers.title: Visuospatial and Verbal Abilities in Poor Readers: Cognitive Differences and Strategy Use.
papers.authors: Kheradmandsaadi Z, Im HY, Giaschi D.
papers.abstract: Developmental dyslexia is characterized by difficulties in reading and impairments in cognitive functions. It has also been linked to dysfunction of the brain regions involved in verbal and visuospatial processing. Although some research suggests individuals with dyslexia may rely on visuospatial strategies to compensate for their verbal difficulties, other studies have reported contradictory findings on visuospatial abilities. This study compared the cognitive performance of 11 poor readers and 15 typical readers across two verbal and four visuospatial tasks. Additionally, the strategies employed by each group to complete these cognitive tasks were explored. While poor readers showed worse performance across all verbal and visuospatial tasks than typical readers, there was no significant group difference in strategy use. Moreover, verbal cognitive inefficiencies were associated with reading difficulties. Poor readers' cognitive challenges, despite no difference in the strategies employed, highlight the importance of addressing both verbal and visuospatial difficulties in dyslexia.

papers.title: Event-Related Potential Components and the Lexical Decision Task in Greek-Speaking Children With and Without Reading Difficulties.
papers.authors: Fella A, Christoforou C, Papadopoulos TC.
papers.abstract: The present study examined neurocognitive differences in visual word processing between children with reading difficulties (RD) and chronological-age-matched controls (CA) using event-related potentials (ERPs) during a lexical decision task. Participants were Grade 3 and Grade 6 children (ages 7.6-12.1 years) who were required to discriminate real words from orthographically similar pseudowords. ERP analyses focused on the N200 and N400 components, which are thought to reflect early stages of visual word processing and later processes involved in lexical access and stimulus evaluation. The results showed that the Grade 3 RD group exhibited significantly higher Ν200 amplitudes than their CA controls, suggesting less efficient early processing of the presented stimuli. However, no differences in the N200 were observed between the Grade 6 groups. Children with RD in both grades exhibited reduced N400 amplitudes compared to their counterparts, suggesting differences in the neural processes supporting word recognition. These findings contribute to a clearer understanding of the temporal dynamics of written word processing in children with RD in transparent orthographies and highlight the value of ERP measures for examining neurocognitive mechanisms underlying reading development.

papers.title: Maternal Depression, Childhood Resting-State Brain Connectivity, and Adolescent Depression During the COVID-19 Outbreak.
papers.authors: Liu P, Vandermeer MRJ, Daoust AR, Green HE, Ali OM, Stanton K, Harkness KL, Barch DM, Joanisse MF, Hayden EP.
papers.abstract: Adolescents of mothers with a history of depression are at increased risk for developing depression themselves. These adolescents may have been especially vulnerable to depression under conditions of stress, such as the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic. To understand the complex processes involved in the transmission of maternal depression risk to adolescent offspring in the context of stress, we examined potential mediating and moderating factors that link maternal depression history and offspring depressive symptoms, including resting-state functional connectivity (rs-FC) and mothers' depressive symptoms, in 85 adolescents during the pandemic. Adolescents' prepandemic rs-FC between the posterior and anterior cingulate cortices (PCC-ACC) moderated the association between maternal depression history and adolescents' symptoms during the pandemic, such that maternal depression history predicted adolescents' symptoms only in youths with heightened PCC-ACC rs-FC. Mothers' depressive symptoms during the pandemic mediated and moderated the link between maternal depression history and adolescents' symptoms. Mothers with a history of depression had greater depressive symptoms early during the pandemic, which were further associated with offspring depressive symptoms. Additionally, maternal depression history predicted depressive symptoms in adolescents whose mothers had lower depressive symptoms during the pandemic. Findings speak to the mediating and moderating processes in the transmission of maternal depression risk to adolescent offspring in the context of the pandemic.

papers.title: Potential Locations for Noninvasive Brain Stimulation in Treating Poststroke Deficits: Exploration From Multimodal Neuroimaging.
papers.authors: Yuan S, Yang Y, Han Y, Gao Y, Chang J, Lin H, Yu J, Zhang B.
papers.abstract: Aims Noninvasive brain stimulation (NIBS) shows promise for poststroke deficits (PSDs), but efficacy may be limited by inconsistent stimulation sites. Methods By integrating neuroimaging meta-analysis, lesion-symptom mapping (LSM), and resting-state functional connectivity (FC) analysis, we employed three analytical pipelines to explore potential NIBS targets for alexia, aphasia, apraxia, ataxia, dysarthria, hemiplegia, paresthesia, and dysphagia. Pipeline 1 identified cortical regions directly associated with each PSD via coordinate-based meta-analysis using Neurosynth Compose. Pipeline 2 identified cortical regions exhibiting maximal functional connectivity with neurosynth-derived regions of interest (ROI). Pipeline 3 identified cortical regions functionally connected to ROIs from a prior large-scale LSM study. During Pipeline 2 and 3, ROIs were used for seed-to-voxel FC analysis using resting-state fMRI data from 100 healthy subjects. Identified cortical targets were mapped onto the scalp and referenced by the 10-20 system and continuous proportional coordinates. Results Potential cortical targets and scalp locations were identified for all eight PSDs. For instance, for hemiplegia, validated targets included primary motor and somatosensory cortices and supplementary motor area; novel targets included angular gyrus, superior frontal gyrus, inferior parietal lobule, medial prefrontal cortex, and precuneus. Conclusions This multimodal approach systematically identified precise NIBS targets, confirming established sites and revealing novel regions to broaden neuromodulation strategies for poststroke recovery.

papers.title: Quantification of the Impact of Slice Thickness on Volumetric Analysis of Brain Tumors.
papers.authors: Vogl D, Ruff C, Haas P, Gohla G, Gött H, Becker H, Tatagiba M, Hauser TK, Roder C.
papers.abstract: Background The partial volume effect influences the results of volumetrics performed on MRI sequences with different slice thicknesses. Although a standardized brain tumor imaging protocol with high-quality 1 mm slices is recommended, segmentation is still commonly performed on thicker slices, especially in retrospective studies. We aimed to quantify the impact of different slice thicknesses on volumetric measurements of brain tumors, using treatment-naive glioblastoma as a representative example. Methods Volumes were measured on T1-weighted contrast-enhanced (CE) sequences using semiautomatic segmentation across three predefined slice thicknesses: 1 mm ("thin"; reference measurement), 3 mm ("intermediate"), and 5 mm ("thick"). Data from 46 patients with the availability of all three slice thicknesses were statistically analyzed, including repeated-measures ANOVA with post hoc comparisons, Bland-Altman analysis, correlations, and linear regression. Results The tumor volumes measured increased with slice thickness, with mean values of 36.4 cm3 ("thin"), 38.6 cm3 ("intermediate"), and 41.0 cm3 ("thick"). Repeated measures ANOVA showed significant differences between groups (p < 0.01). The mean deviation of the tumor volumes on "thick" relative to "thin" slices was 16% (±10%). Bland-Altman analysis and linear regression confirmed systematically higher measured volumes on "thick" slices. Tumor size on "thin" slices correlated negatively with the percentage deviation on "thick" slices (r = -0.56; p < 0.01). Conclusion Volumetric measurements obtained from "thick" slices showed systematically higher tumor volumes and greater variability relative to the 1 mm reference. Volumetric data obtained from different slice thicknesses should not be combined, or concepts for adjustment should be considered to maintain methodological consistency and reliability in volumetric studies. We advocate the use of high-quality 3D 1 mm imaging for volumetric analysis whenever possible.

papers.title: Intrinsic Activity Reductions and Cerebello-Cortical Diaschisis-Like Mechanism in Friedreich Ataxia: An fALFF Resting-State fMRI Study.
papers.authors: Gilles N, Nicola T, Antonin R.
papers.abstract: Background Friedreich ataxia (FA) is characterized by progressive degeneration of the cerebellum and its output pathways, particularly the dentato-thalamo-cortical system, leading to motor impairment and the cerebellar cognitive affective syndrome (CCAS). Resting-state fMRI studies in FA have focused on alterations of long-range functional connectivity, but little is known about how intrinsic regional neural activity is affected within cerebello-cortical networks. Methods Twenty-eight adults with genetically confirmed FA and 28 age- and sex-matched healthy controls underwent resting-state functional MRI. Intrinsic brain activity was quantified using the fractional amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations (fALFF). Whole-brain comparisons were performed between controls and patients, and between patients with definite CCAS (FA-Cog) and cognitively preserved patients (FA-NoCog). Within the FA group, voxelwise regressions assessed associations between fALFF, motor severity (Scale for the Assessment and Rating of Ataxia [SARA]), and cognitive performance (Cerebellar Cognitive Affective Syndrome Scale [CCAS-S]), adjusting for age, sex, head motion, and cerebellar gray matter volume. Results Compared with controls, patients exhibited reduced fALFF in medial and lateral prefrontal regions. Higher SARA scores were associated with lower fALFF in occipital, sensorimotor, posterior cingulate, and cerebellar regions, whereas higher CCAS-S scores correlated with higher fALFF in bilateral prefrontal and cerebellar cognitive networks. Compared with FA-NoCog, FA-Cog patients showed lower fALFF in bilateral frontal and insular regions. Conclusions Resting-state fALFF reveals downstream dysfunction of distributed cerebello-cortical networks in FA. Associations with motor severity and cognition, together with additional fronto-insular dysfunction in patients with definite CCAS, support progressive cerebello-cortical disconnection consistent with a diaschisis-like mechanism.

papers.title: The Impact of Cladribine Tablets on Cognition Over One Year in Patients With Multiple Sclerosis: A Preliminary Study.
papers.authors: Callen AM, Glanz BI, Tauhid S, Healy BC, Jinich A, Khalil S, Houtchens MK, Mateen FJ, Napoli S, Rizvi S, Singhal T, Zurawski J, Bakshi R.
papers.abstract: Introduction Cognitive impairment is common in multiple sclerosis (MS), affecting >40% of patients. Cladribine tablets are a high-efficacy MS disease-modifying therapy to prevent relapses and limit disease progression. Our previous study showed cortical gray matter lesion stability over one year after the start of cladribine, though its effect on cognition is not well known. This study aimed to investigate the one-year impact of cladribine tablets on cognition in multiple sclerosis. Methods Fourteen MS subjects [age (mean ± SD) 50.2 ± 10.8, 7.14% men, 57.1% relapsing-remitting MS (n = 8), 42.9% secondary progressive (n = 6), expanded disability status scale 4.1 ± 2.1] were administered the Brief Repeatable Battery of Neuropsychological Tests (BRB-N) and the Stroop Color and Word Test (Stroop) at an average of 1.5 months from cladribine start. The BRB-N measures information processing speed (Symbol Digit Modalities Test, Paced Auditory Serial Addition Test [PASAT]), verbal memory (Selective Reminding Test [SRT]), visual-spatial memory (10/36 Spatial Recall Test), and verbal fluency (Word List Generation). Stroop assesses processing speed and executive function. When available, alternate versions of the individual cognitive tests were used at follow-up to reduce practice effects. Paired t-tests compared within-subject baseline and follow-up data. Results After one year, no worsening was noted on any cognitive test. Furthermore, both PASAT 3-second total correct and SRT total delayed recall trended toward improved scores on-study, with an average 3.4 (p = 0.07) and 1.1 (p = 0.05) point increase, respectively. Conclusion In this preliminary study, no clear decline in cognitive performance was detectable over one year in patients newly started on cladribine tablets.

papers.title: Technical development and implementation of 3D-QALAS on a 1.5T MR-Linac for the brain: A prospective R-IDEAL stage 0/1 technology development report.
papers.authors: McCullum L, Harrington A, West N, Nehring G, Fu Z, Subashi E, Taylor BA, Hwang KP, Fuller CD.
papers.journal: Journal of applied clinical medical physics
papers.abstract: Background Quantitative relaxometry of the brain on the integrated MRI / linear accelerator (MR-Linac) at high isotropic reconstructed resolution is currently limited due to prohibitively long scan times and limited field-of-views. Purpose The purpose of this study was to assess the technical feasibility of the 3D-QALAS technique on the 1.5T MR-Linac which can acquire whole-brain 1 mm isotropic quantitative T1, T2, and PD maps along with multiple synthetic images in a 7-minute acquisition time. Methods A 1 mm isotropic 3D-QALAS acquisition was scanned in both phantoms and five healthy volunteers on the 1.5T Elekta Unity MR-Linac device with scan times around seven minutes. A test-retest protocol across five independent sessions for the phantom was conducted. The Lin's Concordance Correlation Coefficient (LCCC), repeatability, and reproducibility between measured and reference quantitative T1, T2, and PD values were determined in the phantom. Distortion was also studied. Vendor-provided reconstruction through SyMRI was performed to extract synthetic images and brain volume metric assessments in the healthy volunteers. Results The slope and LCCC between the measured and phantom reference values was 1.02 (1.00), 1.09 (0.90), and 0.99 (1.00) for T1, T2, and PD, respectively. Median distortion across the phantom remained below 2 mm. The repeatability and reproducibility coefficient-of-variation (CoV) was under 8% for all measured values. The measured brain volumes in the healthy volunteer was within expected age-adjusted reference values. Conclusions The technical feasibility of using 3D-QALAS on the integrated 1.5T MR-Linac was confirmed. Applying this technique to the adaptive radiation therapy workflow of the brain will provide new opportunities to integrate quantitative imaging relaxometry biomarkers at 1 mm isotropic reconstructed resolution.

papers.title: Diagnostic image quality of shoulder magnetic resonance imaging at 0.55T in healthy subjects and patients with rotator cuff injury: Prospective comparison with 1.5T.
papers.authors: Liu J, Gao Y, Gao G, Li W, Wang X, Zhu J, Liu X, Wang X, Zhou K, Liu H, Qiu J.
papers.journal: Journal of applied clinical medical physics
papers.abstract: Background Lower‑field 0.55 T MRI scanners with large‑bore design could offer patients more comfortable feeling and flexible position. With the advances in deep‑learning reconstruction and hardware optimization, 0.55T have greatly improved their image quality and cost‑effectiveness for musculoskeletal applications. However, its feasibility for shoulder evaluation remains unstudied. Purpose To evaluate the image quality of shoulder using 0.55T MRI in volunteers and patients with rotator cuff injury with comparison of conventional 1.5T. Methods Fifty participants (25 volunteers, 25 patients) were prospectively enrolled. All participants underwent shoulder MRI both at open 0.55T with contour coils and deep learning (DL) and 1.5T MR without DL. The nonparametric method was utilized to compare image quality scores and quantitative metrics (signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and contrast-to-noise ratio (|CNR|)). Arthroscopy have been conducted in 16 patients. Kappa statistics was used to assess interobserver and interstudy agreement for lesion evaluation. Comfort feeling was also compared. Results The scan time was 11'25″ for 0.55T MRI and 11'42″ for 1.5T MRI. The interobserver analyses showed high consistency (κ = 0.771-1.000, P: 0.008 ∼ < 0.001) among 3 readers. The scores for coronal fat suppressed T2 weighted imaging (fsT2WI) and coronal T1 weighted imaging (T1WI) were significantly higher for 0.55T MRI. Most sequences at 0.55T demonstrated significantly higher SNRs (P:0.04 ∼ < 0.001). Additionally, |CNR| values for lesions were significantly higher in fs proton weighted imaging (PDWI) and fsT2WI at 0.55T. Perfect interstudy agreement between 0.55T and 1.5T was observed between 2 readers (Kappa = 1, P < 0.001) for lesion assessment. Agreement between MRI findings and arthroscopic results was perfect or good. The 0.55T system received higher scores in comfort ratings. Conclusion The 0.55T MRI with DL, showed comparable or better image quality in healthy subjects and patients with rotator cuff injury to 1.5T MRI without DL.

papers.title: Neurocognitive outcomes in preschool and early school aged children with myelomeningocele or myeloschisis: a comparison of fetal and postnatal surgical groups.
papers.authors: Bergmann J, Lenart A, Mehta SD, Mathew L, Salwi SR, Reynolds T, Schmidt K, Adzick NS, Heuer GG, Schreiber JE.
papers.journal: Child's nervous system : ChNS : official journal of the International Society for Pediatric Neurosurgery
papers.abstract: Research examining the longer-term neurocognitive outcomes of children who undergo fetal versus postnatal surgery for myelomeningocele (MMC) and myeloschisis (MS) is limited. To address this gap, the current study used the Wechsler Preschool and Primary Scale of Intelligence, Fourth Edition (WPPSI-IV) to compare cognitive outcomes of preschool and early school-age children who underwent fetal versus postnatal MMC/MS repair. We performed a retrospective study of children who underwent fetal or postnatal surgical closure of MMC/MS at an academic medical center in the mid-Atlantic region. To compare performance by surgical group, two-sample t-tests were calculated for each index score. Multiple regression was conducted for each index to compare outcomes by surgical group while controlling for predictors of cognitive functioning established in the broader spina bifida literature. Children who underwent postnatal surgery had significantly lower mean Full-Scale IQ (FSIQ), Fluid Reasoning Index (FRI), and Verbal Comprehension Index (VCI) scores compared to the fetal surgery group. FSIQ and FRI scores remained significantly lower among children with postnatal surgery in the adjusted analysis. On average, the postnatal surgery group had FSIQ scores that were 12 points lower than the fetal surgery group. Secondary findings included older gestational age at birth as a significant predictor of higher FSIQ, Processing Speed Index (PSI), and Working Memory Index (WMI) scores, and larger prenatal ventricle size as a predictor of lower PSI scores. Fetal surgery emerged as a significant predictor of overall intellectual functioning among preschool and early school-age children. Future research is necessary to determine whether similar findings persist with age, especially given the potential for children to "grow into" cognitive weakness over time.

papers.title: Distinct gradients of cortical architecture capture visual representations and behavior across the lifespan.
papers.authors: Chen X, Liu X, Hoyos PM, Daniel Hertz E, Yao JK, Zhen Z, Gomez J.
papers.abstract: The microstructure of cells within the human cerebral cortex varies across the cortical ribbon, where changes in cytoarchitecture and myeloarchitecture are thought to endow each region of the cortex with its unique function. While fine-scale relative to a cell, these changes at the population level impact architectural properties of the cortex measurable in vivo by noninvasive MRI, such as the thickness and myelin content of the cortex. This raises the question of whether or not we can use these in vivo architectural measures to understand cortical organization, function, and development more broadly. Using the human visual cortex as a test bed, we demonstrated two architectural gradients, one in which cytoarchitecture and myeloarchitecture converge and another in which they diverge. These two gradients underlie the structural and functional topography of the visual cortex, even predicting the presence of new visual representations. Moreover, the two gradients show distinct visual behavior relevance and lifespan trajectory. These findings provide a more general framework for understanding the human cortex, showing that architectural gradients are a measurable fingerprint of functional organization and ontogenetic routines in the human brain.

papers.title: Brain and kidney Extracellular Vesicle Morphology and Complementary Brain proteomics after Inflammatory Challenge
papers.authors: Brown K, Wang Y, Shan Z, Bi L.
papers.abstract: Shape, size variation, and protein composition describe different properties of tissue extracellular vesicle (EV) preparations. We compared brain and kidney EV shape and size using transmission electron microscopy (TEM). We also assessed repeated protein detection and reanalyzed a deposited brain proteomics cohort, with attribution to its original source. The study used intracerebroventricular lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and an intravenous miRNA-associated EV formulation. Each group contained three biological samples, as labelled in the source data. Source morphometry summaries included 385 brain and 101 kidney profiles. Kidney circularity was 0.9225, 0.8977, and 0.9288 in the control, LPS, and treatment groups, respectively. The corresponding values for diameter quartile dispersion, a measure of size variation, were 0.2603, 0.5334, and 0.6018. Thus, near-control outline shape coexisted with persistent size variation. None of the six primary morphology tests remained significant after Holm correction. Independent recalculation confirmed 1,527 eligible rat protein accessions across individual searches. The complete quantitative matrix contained 953 features. The main peptide filter combined unique and razor peptides. A stricter analysis retained 916 features. PTGFRN and LAMB2 remained the only significant treatment-versus-LPS findings. In the main analysis, PTGFRN increased 14.71-fold (q = 0.0365), and LAMB2 increased 6.23-fold (q = 0.00585). Their LPS levels were already close to control values. Exploratory normalization used the geometric mean of four measured EV-associated markers. The resulting treatment-versus-LPS increases were 16.43-fold and 6.96-fold, respectively. These ratios support selective changes in relative protein representation within the recovered mixture. They do not establish protein copies per EV. Analysis of the full protein profile and calibration of the complete selection process did not support an overall return to control. This study compares morphology and composition as separate outcomes. It identifies membrane and matrix associations as priorities for validation. Original TEM measurements were unavailable, sample matching remained unresolved, and kidney proteomics were absent. These limitations prevent causal conclusions and individual-sample comparisons between morphology and protein composition.

papers.title: NeuroPack: Advanced Learnable Packaging Toolkit Towards Ultra-High Compression Ratio for Volumetric Neuroimaging
papers.authors: Zhao R, Yang X, Wu J, Zheng Q, Zhang J, Guan J, Cai W, Du J, Bai L, Du X, Ouyang W, Lu G, Song C.
papers.abstract: High-throughput 3D microscopic imaging generates brain-volume datasets at terabyte to petabyte scale, posing significant storage challenges for large-scale neuroimaging data. In this study, we introduce NeuroPack, a hyperprior-driven 3D deep-learning-based packaging toolkit specifically designed for compressing 3D microscopic volumes at the mesoscale. NeuroPack encodes a compact hyperprior stream that conditions its entropy model on local voxel-wise variance, adaptively allocating bits to preserve mesoscale anatomical details for an optimal rate-distortion balance. To ensure reproducible deployment across heterogeneous microscopy datasets and computing environments, NeuroPack implements model integerization for the hyperprior side-information pathway, whose hyper-decoder predicts the Gaussian mean and scale parameters used by the arithmetic coder. By replacing platform-dependent floating-point hyper-decoding with deterministic fixed-point integer convolutions, NeuroPack produces bit-exact entropy models across CPUs, GPUs, local workstations, and cloud servers, thereby preventing decoding drift caused by floating-point rounding, fused-multiply-add ordering, or library-specific kernels. This integerized design preserves rate-distortion behavior while maintaining efficient encoding and decoding for large anisotropic 3D microscopy volumes. Our method enables high-fidelity microscopy reconstruction at 100- to 1000-fold compression across diverse modalities and species. Quantitatively, NeuroPack delivers the strongest overall rate-distortion performance in both BD-PSNR and BD-MSSSIM, with average relative gains of 73.4% and 50.8%, respectively, over the best competing codec. Importantly, NeuroPack preserves image fidelity required for downstream morphological reconstruction and analysis, as validated by simultaneous human annotation of original and decompressed confocal whole-brain zebrafish microscopy images. Together, NeuroPack provides a learning-based compression framework explicitly tailored for microscopy data, establishing a scalable storage solution for data-intensive neuroimaging and AI-empowered biological discovery.

papers.title: Item-specific clustering of high gamma-band activity on theta phase during speech categorization
papers.authors: Ten Oever S, Reithler J, Archila-Melendez ME, Gommer E, Rouhl R, Kranen-Mastenbroek V, Roberts MJ, Peters J.
papers.abstract: Theta-gamma phase-amplitude coupling (PAC) has been proposed as a mechanism for separating neural representations in time. Although item-specific PAC has been reported, its role in perception remains unclear. Notably, previous work has shown that theta phase can bias perception, raising the question whether such biases are linked to phase-specific gamma activity. Here, we investigated whether phase-dependent perceptual biases are accompanied by item-specific theta-gamma PAC. We presented ambiguous speech sounds that could be interpreted as either /da/ or /ga/ in patients with epilepsy implanted with intracranial electrocorticography. We found that pre-stimulus theta phase predicted both the neural and perceptual response, with /da/ and /ga/ tuned channels exhibiting gamma activity clustering at distinct theta phases. These findings suggest that neural and perceptual biases stem from phase-specific pre-activation of item-specific neural representations. They demonstrate the generalizability of the theta-gamma code, shaping behavior and enhancing representational capacity.

papers.title: Atlas-Based MRI Spatial Phenotyping in Pediatric Low-Grade Glioma
papers.authors: Vunnava B, Men L, Batal F, Chrysochoou D, Kraya A, Gandhi D, Storm PB, Madsen PJ, Resnick A, Vossough A, Nabavizadeh A, Fathi Kazerooni A.
papers.abstract: Pediatric low-grade gliomas (pLGGs) arise throughout the developing brain, and their anatomic distribution is related to age, molecular subtype, and extent of resection (EOR). In clinical studies, pLGG location is commonly represented by a single manually assigned anatomic category, which does not quantify the full spatial extent of tumors spanning multiple brain regions. We developed and evaluated a reproducible, publicly available pediatric atlas-based framework integrating voxel-wise probabilistic mapping with patient-level atlas-derived spatial features. In this retrospective study, preoperative MRI from 349 patients with pLGG was registered to the Haskins pediatric template using EasyReg. Probabilistic maps showed differences in tumor distribution by age, molecular subtype, and EOR, including greater optic pathway and suprasellar involvement at 0-2 years and greater cerebellar involvement in KIAA1549-BRAF fusion tumors. Atlas-derived spatial, tumor morphometric, and clinical features distinguished gross total resection/near total resection from subtotal resection or biopsy/no-surgery (Replication area under the curve, 0.864). Substituting 107 automatically computed regional overlap features for the manually assigned location variable in previously published clinico-imaging risk stratification models did not significantly alter discrimination (smallest P = 0.12). Together, these group- and patient-level analyses demonstrate the utility of the framework for quantitative spatial phenotyping in imaging and clinical studies of pLGG.

papers.title: Single-nucleus transcriptomics links telencephalic cell signatures to ocean acidification effects on social behaviour in a coral reef fish
papers.authors: Desantis D, Schunter C.
papers.abstract: Mutualistic interactions are fundamental to the health and stability of reef ecosystems. While elevated CO2 has been implicated in impairments in interaction behaviours, how this environmental change alters cellular states and intercellular communication in the brain remains unresolved. Here, by analysing the single-nucleus RNA profile of ~66,000 telencephalic nuclei from a keystone mutualist, the cleaner wrasse ( Labroides dimidiatus ), interacting under ambient or elevated CO2 conditions, we identify highly cell type specific neural responses to elevated CO2. We highlight a substantial depletion in Oligodendrocyte Precursor Cells (OPCs), notably linked to oligodendrocyte myelination and neural structure maintenance. Elevated CO2 also elicited targeted transcriptional shifts across discrete cell types, characterised by widespread glutamatergic signalling and altered co-expression networks associated with pH regulation, energetic metabolism, and circadian rhythm, thereby compromising the cleaner's physiologic equilibrium. Additionally, cell-cell communication was altered under elevated CO2, including remodelling in SEMA4 and PTPR signalling pathways within radial glial and OPCs, respectively, revealing network signalling rewiring in response to the changed environment. These findings uncover the high-resolution neural substrates vulnerable to ocean acidification, providing mechanistic insight into how climate-driven environmental changes alter brain function and destabilise complex mutualistic ecological interactions.

papers.title: Salience network expansion as a transdiagnostic neural marker for psychopathology risk in adolescence
papers.authors: Koirala S, Hermosillo R, Godfrey KJ, Anderson M, Lundquist J, Moser J, Feczko E, Miranda Dominguez O, Weldon KB, Linder I, Mahmoudi M, Uddin LQ, Nelson SM, Elison JT, Fair D, Tervo-Clemmens B.
papers.abstract: Increased cortical surface area of the brain's salience network (SAL) has been observed in depression and appears to emerge during early adolescence. However, similar expansion has also been reported in bipolar disorder (BD), obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD), and other atypicalities of salience network function have been broadly implicated across multiple psychiatric conditions. Whether increased SAL surface area is specific to depression or related more generally with psychopathology remains unclear. Using data collected as part of the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study (baseline: N = 7942; ages 9-10; Year 2: N = 5901; ages 11-12), we quantified individual SAL size and examined associations with dimensional symptoms from the Child Behavior Checklist. SAL surface area showed substantial inter-individual variability, with expansion occurring primarily through encroachment into the default mode (DMN), action-mode (AMN), and frontoparietal (FP) networks. Larger SAL size showed a modest positive association with depressive symptoms in the baseline sample, consistent with prior reports; however, this association did not replicate in the year 2 internal replication sample. Instead, associations with total problems were stronger and replicated across both timepoints, suggesting a subtle, dimensional relationship between SAL organization and general psychopathology burden. These findings suggest that individual differences in SAL organization may represent a broader transdiagnostic neural correlate of dimensional psychopathology rather than a disorder-specific neural signature.

papers.title: Few-shot regulatory sequence design with a genomic language model
papers.authors: Hie B, Hao YA, Liu M, Nori D, Brixi G, Lau T, Ramakrishnan CA, Chang D, Park R, Allen WE.
papers.abstract: A central challenge in generative biology is translating knowledge learned from natural sequences and experiments into designs with desired functions. In-context learning (ICL) is an emergent capability of large language models that allows them to adapt to new tasks from a few examples without additional training, enabling these models to become general-purpose learners. Here, we show that the genome language model, Evo 2, exhibits generative ICL in biological sequence design. Prompting with just tens of examples conditions Evo 2 to generate novel and diverse regulatory DNA sequences without any additional training. Mechanistic analysis suggests that genomic ICL may originate from induction, similar to phenomena observed in natural language. Reinforcement learning leveraging sequence-to-function models as experiment-derived rewards further strengthens ICL. We first validate this approach by generating enhancers that drive cell-type-specific gene expression in three human cell lines. Extending this approach in vivo, enhancers designed using human regulatory element data selectively label layer 5 extratelencephalic neurons in the mouse cortex with high specificity and stronger activity than existing enhancers. Our study provides evidence of emergent properties in genomic sequence models and introduces a promising approach for improving functional conditioning in generative biology.

papers.title: Algorithmic Geometry Shapes the Biological Meaning of Thalamocortical Structural Covariance
papers.authors: Liu Y, Sydnor VJ, Dai A, Ziolkowski J, Fu S, Devenyi GA, Satterthwaite T, Chakravarty M, Yee Y.
papers.abstract: Neuroimaging studies often derive and discuss structural covariance (SC) as a representation of underlying brain circuitry that reflects coordinated maturation, anatomical connectivity, transcriptional similarity, and shared genetic influences. These associations motivate its use to study brain organization across development, aging, and disease. However, the algorithms used to derive SC networks impose constraints that may shape their biological interpretation. To understand the impact of algorithm choice, we used the thalamocortical system as an example and compared five common representations of voxelwise SC, namely, principal component analysis (PCA), independent component analysis (ICA), non-negative matrix factorization (NMF), orthogonal projective NMF (OPNMF), and \textit{k}-means clustering, in 755 participants aged 8--22 years from the Philadelphia Neurodevelopmental Cohort (PNC).
