Unsupervised clustering based on these individualized networks revealed two neuroanatomical subtypes with distinct network configurations. Most subtype-differentiating edges showed higher values in one subtype, whereas a smaller set of edges, primarily involving the basal ganglia and cerebellum, showed higher values in the other. Integration with transcriptomic data from the Allen Human Brain Atlas identified genes spatially associated with subtype-related differences. These genes were enriched in processes including receptor tyrosine kinase signaling and glycerolipid metabolism, with preferential expression in the striatum and cerebellum. Together, these findings characterize interindividual variation in brain structural covariance in T2DM and identify candidate molecular processes associated with the observed subtype differences.

papers.title: A multimodal MRI study of DTI-ALPS and cerebral blood flow changes across the Alzheimer's disease continuum.
papers.authors: Gao Y, Xu M, Ou P, Yang H, Wang J, Liu W, Sun Y, Du W, Wang Y, Liu T, Xia H, Fu L, Shu N, Yuan Z, Ma G.
papers.abstract: Introduction Alzheimer's disease (AD) is characterized by cerebral blood flow (CBF) abnormalities and alterations in the neurofluid-related brain tissue environment, but their evolution along the AD continuum and links to cognitive decline and plasma biomarkers remain unclear. Using multimodal MRI, we quantified the diffusion tensor image analysis along the perivascular space (DTI-ALPS) index and CBF alterations and examined their associations with cognitive performance and plasma biomarkers across the AD continuum. Methods This study enrolled 78 healthy controls (HC), 53 subjective cognitive decline (SCD), 40 mild cognitive impairment (MCI), 110 AD. All subjects received MRI and neurocognitive assessments. The DTI-ALPS index was used as a diffusion-based marker of directional water diffusivity within periventricular white matter and the neurofluid-related tissue environment. CBF changes were calculated, and plasma biomarkers associated with neurodegeneration were measured. Partial correlation analysis explored relationships among ALPS index, CBF in cognition-related brain regions, cognitive scores, and plasma biomarkers. Statistical mediation analyses were performed to assess indirect effects involving the ALPS index and plasma biomarkers in the association between regional CBF and cognitive performance. Results ALPS index decreased stage-dependently along the AD continuum, significantly lower in MCI and AD versus HC and SCD. HC and SCD showed higher CBF than AD in right middle cingulate and left inferior parietal lobule. CBF in bilateral angular gyri and right superior frontal gyrus positively correlated with MoCA and RAVLT scores. Cognition-related CBF positively correlated with bilateral mean ALPS index, and negatively with NfL and p-tau217. Statistical mediation analyses identified significant indirect effects involving the bilateral mean ALPS index and plasma NfL in the association between regional CBF and cognitive performance. Discussion Cerebral hypoperfusion, altered DTI-ALPS measures, and axonal injury were closely associated across the AD continuum, suggesting interrelated neurovascular, neurofluid-related tissue, and neurodegenerative alterations associated with cognitive impairment.

papers.title: Impact of hearing loss on visual selective attention: Evidence from N2pc and resting-state networks.
papers.authors: Zeng T, Bu X, Zhu H, Liu Z, Xiao H, Li F, Zhang W, Yang F, Chen J, Ma H.
papers.abstract: Efficient visual attention is fundamental to environmental adaptation and social interaction. While previous studies have observed alterations in visual processing among deaf individuals, findings remain controversial regarding whether these changes stem from hearing loss (sensory compensation vs. cognitive deficit) or sign language experience. To address this issue, the present study provides task-related and resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) evidence to disentangle the specific drivers of visual selective attention plasticity. A visual search task was used to examine selective attention in 95 participants (34 prelingual deaf, 27 hearing signers, and 34 hearing nonsigners). Compared to both hearing groups, deaf individuals exhibited significantly lower hit rates and diminished N2-posterior contralateral (N2pc) amplitudes. Hearing signers and nonsigners showed comparable behavioral performance, N2pc amplitudes, and resting-state network topology, whereas the deaf group was further characterized by a degraded resting-state alpha network topology, evidenced by reduced clustering coefficients, global efficiency, and weakened frontal-occipital connectivity. N2pc amplitude correlated significantly with resting-state network properties and behavioral accuracy. These results suggest that deaf individuals may suffer from an imbalance in the regulation of visual selective attention, most clearly indexed by the evoked N2pc and by intrinsic alpha-network organization, and likely linked to increased resource competition following the loss of auditory monitoring. Our findings provide neurophysiological evidence that these attentional deficits are associated with hearing loss rather than with sign-language experience, offering a new perspective for understanding the boundaries of cross-modal plasticity in the human brain.

papers.title: An Adversarial Deep Learning Framework for Non-Rigid Brain MRI Registration in Brain Shift Compensation.
papers.authors: Muniya EJ, Kronreif G, Biguri A, Birkfellner W, Hatamikia S.
papers.journal: Journal of neuroradiology = Journal de neuroradiologie
papers.abstract: Accurate compensation for intra-operative brain shift remains a fundamental challenge in neurosurgical procedures, as misalignment between pre-operative and intra-operative images can lead to suboptimal surgical guidance. In this work, we propose a bidirectional, unsupervised 3D brain shift compensation framework for non-rigid MRI registration, designed to directly estimate dense deformation fields between pre-operative and intra-operative volumes. The proposed approach employs dual image-translation pathways coupled with a dedicated deformation field predictor, enabling robust alignment without requiring paired training data. A key component of the framework is the integration of bidirectional consistency constraints to enforce anatomical correspondence across domains, while deformation field estimation is explicitly optimized for registration accuracy. In addition, we incorporate a Haar wavelet-based perceptual similarity (HaarPSI) loss to improve the preservation of fine-scale anatomical structures during registration. The proposed method is evaluated against classical and state-of-the-art baselines, including Elastix, Voxelmorph, and several adversarial and GAN-based learning approaches adapted with comparable registration modules. Qualitative analyses of deformation fields and error maps further demonstrate improved alignment in regions most affected by brain shift. These results highlight the effectiveness of bidirectional deformation modeling combined with adversarial and perceptual constraints for accurate, physically plausible, and unsupervised 3D non-rigid registration in neurosurgical applications.

papers.title: Regular exercise augments gut-brain communication and visceral feedback control of appetite.
papers.authors: Borgmann D, Rausch DM, Lundh S, Hassan S, Tokgöz C, Glatzel A, Cabot L, Ten Voorde MC, Bæch-Laursen C, Sanchis Tortosa P, Brandt C, Backes H, Pers TH, Fenselau H.
papers.abstract: Objectives Regular exercise is widely accepted to support long-term body weight management; however, the neurobiological adaptations that contribute to the beneficial effects of habitual physical activity beyond increases in energy expenditure per se remain unclear. Here, we investigated whether regular exercise alters gut-brain communication and visceral feedback control of feeding. Methods Mice were subjected to regular voluntary wheel running. Energy expenditure and feeding were assessed under basal conditions and following an overnight fast. Nutrients were delivered directly into the stomach by intragastric infusion. Brain-wide responses to intragastric nutrient delivery were assessed using positron emission tomography (PET). Single-cell sequencing and histological analyses were used to determine nutrient-responsive neuronal populations in the caudal brainstem. Genetic associations with body weight were evaluated using GWAS data. Results Intragastric nutrient delivery suppressed feeding more strongly in exercising mice. Brain-wide PET revealed enhanced responses to intragastric nutrients in various brain regions. Single-cell sequencing identified several nutrient-responsive caudal brainstem populations, including a previously unrecognized population marked by expression of fibrinogen C domain containing 1 (FIBCD1). Regular exercise selectively enhanced the nutrient-evoked activation of FIBCD1 neurons. Histological analyses demonstrate that FIBCD1 neurons are also present in the human brainstem, and GWAS data suggest a potential relevance of this neuron population to body-weight regulation. Conclusions Regular exercise enhances behavioral and brain responses to intragastric nutrient delivery and sensitizes FIBCD1 neurons in the brainstem of mice. These findings reveal an exercise-associated adaptation of gut-brain communication that may contribute to improved matching of caloric intake to energy expenditure.

papers.title: GradLint: a fast, open-source Rust tool for b-vector flip detection, gradient-scheme QC, and auto-repair in diffusion MRI.
papers.authors: Tagliaferri M, Cattaneo L.
papers.abstract: Background Diffusion MRI (dMRI) infers white-matter tracts using stored gradient tables. If a table is flipped or permuted relative to the image coordinates during conversion or transfer, downstream tractography is silently corrupted. New method GradLint is a fast, open-source tool that detects gradient flips, audits acquisition schemes, and repairs corrupted tables. It evaluates all 48 signed-permutation candidate conventions from a single DTI fit using an analytic matrix transformation, ranking them with an anatomy-anchored, directional-stepping fiber-coherence index. Results On 1106 corrupted cases (HCP, single-site, and clinical datasets), GradLint ranked the correct convention first in every case and retained antipode-aware agreement with the field reference dwigradcheck. At the default 2% relative-margin threshold, --apply-repair yielded 1022 correct FLAG repairs; 84 L5 WARN cases required additional --force-repair authorization. Without authorization, corrections were withheld. It successfully resolved acquisition obliquity in voxel space. The frame-aware writer verified correctness on 190 subjects. With eight threads per tool, the median within-subject speed-up was 12.90-23.25× across the three timing groups; with automatic/default threading it was 5.27-8.91×. GradLint's eight-thread median check times were 2.85-14.07s. Comparison with existing methods Unlike tools that repeat expensive tracking or DTI fitting for every candidate, GradLint obtains all candidate eigenvector fields analytically from one fit. It integrates a scheme quality-control audit, outputs machine-readable provenance, returns exit codes for CI/CD integration, and generates optional DTI principal-direction glyph figures. Conclusions GradLint is a fast, open-source Rust tool that acts as a quality-control gate, guarding dMRI preprocessing pipelines against silent orientation errors.

papers.title: Chaihu-Shugan-San Attenuates Depression by Downregulating Liver LCN2 to Suppress LHb GluN2B-Associated Glutamatergic Signaling.
papers.authors: You X, Song C, Chen W, Zheng Y, Wang R, Liu W, Wei Y.
papers.abstract: Ethnopharmacological relevance The liver-brain axis has emerged as a critical pathway in depression pathogenesis, yet the molecular basis of this crosstalk remains largely unexplored. Chaihu-Shugan-San (CSS), a classic Traditional Chinese Medicine formula for "soothing the liver and relieving depression" has shown both hepatoprotective and antidepressant effects, but whether these actions are linked via the liver-brain axis and through what molecular mechanism remains unknown. Aim of the study This study aimed to determine whether Chaihu-Shugan-San (CSS) exerts antidepressant effects via the liver-brain axis and to elucidate the mediating role of liver lipocalin 2 (LCN2) and its receptor SLC22A17 in regulating lateral habenula (LHb) function. Materials and methods A chronic unpredictable mild stress (CUMS) mouse model was established. CSS (2, 4, 8 g/kg) or fluoxetine (10 mg/kg) was orally administered. Depressive-like behaviors were assessed by sucrose preference, open field, and forced swim tests. Hepatic injury was evaluated by serum ALT/AST and H&E staining. Liver transcriptomics and LHb single-cell RNA sequencing were performed to identify key molecules, followed by qRT-PCR, Western blot, ELISA, and immunofluorescence for validation. The causal role of LCN2 was tested via liver-specific AAV-mediated overexpression. Results CSS ameliorated CUMS-induced depressive-like behaviors and liver injury. Transcriptomics and PPI network analysis identified Lcn2 as a hub gene. CSS reversed CUMS-induced elevation of LCN2 in the liver, serum, and LHb, as well as the upregulation of its receptor SLC22A17 in the LHb. LHb single-cell sequencing revealed that CSS restored CUMS-induced changes in astrocyte subcluster ASC6, including downregulation of AQP4 and SLC38A1 and impaired intercellular communication. Consequently, CSS reduced the elevated expression of c-FOS and GluN2B and restored AQP4 and SLC38A1 in the LHb. Importantly, liver-specific Lcn2 overexpression recapitulated CUMS-like depressive phenotypes and LHb abnormalities, including elevated SLC22A17 and GluN2B, and largely abolished the antidepressant effects of CSS. Conclusion CSS ameliorates depressive-like behaviors in association with downregulation of hepatic LCN2 and its candidate receptor SLC22A17 in the LHb, restoring ASC6-mediated glutamate homeostasis, and suppressing GluN2B-related Glutamatergic Signaling. These findings are consistent with a model in which LHb function may be modulated via the liver-brain axis through hepatic LCN2 and its candidate receptor SLC22A17, although the direct source of LHb LCN2 remains to be determined, offering experimental support for the scientific basis of CSS in "soothing the liver and relieving depression."

papers.title: Disrupted gray matter morphological network topology associated with suicide attempts in adolescents with major depressive disorder and bipolar disorder.
papers.authors: Liu J, Zhang J, Tian J, Gao M, Huang M, Zhang Y, Zhou Y, Cheng Z, Lei D, Hu L.
papers.abstract: Background Suicide is a leading cause of death among adolescents with major depressive disorder (MDD) and bipolar disorder (BD), yet the suicide-related structural network alteration patterns remain poorly understood. The study investigates the structural network topological alterations and associations with suicide attempts in unmedicated adolescents with MDD and BD. Methods High-resolution T1-weighted MRI data was acquired from 41 healthy controls (HCs), 34 adolescents with BD, and 48 with MDD. Gray matter morphological similarity networks were constructed through the Jensen-Shannon Similarity Estimation. The global and nodal topology were characterized by graph theory. Additionally, a nested 5-fold cross-validation framework was used to classify suicide attempters (SA) and non-suicide attempters (nSA). Results Compared with HCs, both MDD and BD exhibited lower normalized characteristic path length (λ), whereas MDD showed higher normalized clustering than BD. In within-diagnosis comparisons, BD-SA showed higher λ than BD-nSA. Alterations in nodal topological properties were observed across multiple brain regions in both the MDD and BD. Additionally, in the SA, higher suicidal tendency-wp scores were associated with higher nodal degree and efficiency in the right middle frontal gyrus (orbital part) (p ≤ 0.001). The five fold-specific optimal models distinguished SA from nSA with 79.85% accuracy (AUROC = 0.801), with features from the right inferior frontal gyrus (orbital part), right supplementary motor area, and left Heschl's gyrus contributing most strongly. Conclusions Exploratory findings suggest regional morphological similarity network patterns are associated with suicide-attempt history in adolescents with MDD and BD. Moreover, network features showed preliminary value for classifying lifetime attempt history.

papers.title: Low-intensity pulsed ultrasound activates Piezo1 to restore brain lymphatic drainage and improve outcomes in traumatic brain injury mice.
papers.authors: Wang S, Wang B, Wang Y, Nie M, Yuan J, Wu C, Mi L, Chen B, Liu T, Jiang R.
papers.abstract: Background Meningeal lymphatic vessels (mLVs) are specialized lymphatic structures that drain cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and facilitate immune surveillance of the central nervous system. This drainage system is impaired after traumatic brain injury (TBI); mLVs undergo structural regression, and CSF outflow to peripheral lymphoid tissues is markedly slowed. The resulting accumulation of hyperphosphorylated tau, amyloid-β, and inflammatory mediators drives sustained neuroinflammation and cognitive decline. The neuroprotective effect of low-intensity pulsed ultrasound (LIPUS) in TBI mice has been previously demonstrated, however, its impact on brain lymphatic drainage is unclear. Methods Here, we employed a controlled cortical impact (CCI) mouse model of TBI combined with serial LIPUS stimulation to investigate its therapeutic potential for mLV function. Results LIPUS restored neurological function in TBI mice, improving motor coordination and spatial/recognition memory while attenuating tau pathology, Aβ burden, and astrocyte reactivity. Mechanistically, LIPUS activated Piezo1 on meningeal lymphatic endothelial cells (LECs), triggering a downstream signaling cascade that promoted LEC proliferation and migration in vitro and restored lymphatic coverage and drainage function in vivo. To identify the critical mediator of this process, we examined the pathway's downstream components and found that vascular endothelial growth factor C (VEGFC) served as the critical downstream effector: VEGFC overexpression rescued meningeal lymphatic restoration and CSF drainage. Conclusions These results establish LIPUS as a non-invasive therapeutic strategy that functionally restores brain lymphatic drainage after TBI, representing a promising preclinical therapeutic strategy for proteinopathy-associated neurological diseases that warrants further optimization for clinical translation.

papers.title: Graph Neural Network Reveals the Cortical Morphology of Local Brain Aging in Normal Cognition and Alzheimer's Disease.
papers.authors: Anderson SD, Jomsky J, Chaudhari NN, Chowdhury NF, Zheng XR, Irimia A, Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative.
papers.abstract: Estimating brain age (BA) from T1 -weighted magnetic resonance images (MRIs) provides a powerful framework for quantifying anatomical brain aging. Whereas global BA (GBA) summarizes overall brain health, local BA (LBA) provides cortically specific patterns of aging at the subject level. Although previous studies have examined anatomical contributors to GBA, to our knowledge, no framework has been established to estimate LBA using cortical morphology. To address this gap, we introduce a graph neural network (GNN) that uses morphometric features-cortical thickness, surface area, curvature, gray/white matter intensity ratio (GWR), sulcal depth-to estimate LBA across the cortical surface at high spatial resolution (mean inter-vertex distance = 1.37 mm). Trained on cortical surface meshes extracted from the MRIs of cognitively normal (CN) adults (N = 14,423), our model achieves better test-retest performance than the existing state-of-the-art, while identifying more biologically plausible patterns of aging in Alzheimer's disease (AD) on the ADNI dataset. Association cortices emerge as primary sites of morphometric aging in CNs, whereas mild cognitive impairment is characterized by widespread aging that is pronounced in the parahippocampal gyrus. AD subjects demonstrate significant aging across the entire cortex, particularly within medial temporal regions and associated cortical networks. Feature ablation highlights curvature and GWR as preferentially sensitive to AD pathology. Regional LBA gaps are significantly associated with neuropsychological measures of AD-related cognitive impairment, linking cortical aging patterns to clinical outcomes. These results demonstrate that GNN-based modeling of cortical morphometry enables biologically interpretable mapping of local brain aging with greater fidelity than prior work.

papers.title: Improving dysarthric speech classification with generative AI-based data augmentation.
papers.authors: Lillini D, Basili T, Migliorelli L, Aironi C, Gabrielli L, Squartini S.
papers.abstract: Dysarthria is a neurological speech disorder characterized by impaired motor control of speech production, resulting in reduced intelligibility. It commonly arises in the context of neurodegenerative conditions, including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and cerebral palsy. The development of deep learning systems for dysarthria assessment is hindered by the scarcity of annotated data, which restricts the ability of models to generalize to unseen speakers. This study proposes a cross-corpus diffusion-based data augmentation strategy for improving automatic speech intelligibility classification from dysarthric speech. A Grad-TTS model is trained on dysarthric speakers from the TORGO dataset and used to synthesize the vocabulary of UA-Speech, producing speaker-conditioned samples intended to transfer pathological acoustic traits across corpora. The proposed strategy is evaluated both independently and in combination with conventional signal-level augmentation using ResNet-50 and ResNet-152 classifiers in binary and four-class intelligibility classification tasks. The results indicate that cross-corpus synthetic augmentation improves average performance and that, in most settings, its integration with conventional augmentation yields further gains, suggesting that the two strategies introduce complementary forms of variability.

papers.title: Examining the Cognitive Profile of Small Vessel Disease across Stages of Severity - A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
papers.authors: Francis MJ, Rogers JM, Furey RT, Ottaway G, Pase MP, Stolwyk RJ.
papers.abstract: Cognitive impairment is a key consequence of small vessel disease (SVD), yet prior work has often dichotomised cognitive outcomes as either intact or impaired, obscuring domain- and severity-specific effects. We conducted three-level random-effects meta-analyses to examine cognitive performance across multiple cognitive domains and levels of SVD severity. A total of 24 studies met the inclusion criteria, of which 16 provided sufficient group summary data of White Matter Hyperintensity (WMH) pathology for quantitative synthesis. The remaining studies contributed to descriptive analyses, which synthesised broader SVD pathology types. Processing speed showed the earliest and strongest deficits, with small effects at low WMH burden and medium-to-large effects by high WHM burden, Fazekas 3 (Fazekas 3 pooled g = - 1.02, 95% CI [- 1.46, - 0.58]). Executive function deficits emerged at moderate-to-severe stages and were large by Fazekas 3 (Fazekas 3 g = - 1.11, 95% CI [- 1.53, - 0.69]); attention/working memory estimates trended in the expected direction but did not reach significant effects at any Fazekas level, reflecting the small number of contributing studies. In contrast to processing speed and executive function, verbal and visual memory showed small effects at low burden that reached large by Fazekas 3, while confrontation naming effects remained small-to-medium across severity levels and general intelligence did not differ significantly from controls at any level. Between- and within-study variance components indicated substantial residual heterogeneity across several cognitive domains. Together, the meta-analytic and descriptive findings provide converging evidence that reduced processing speed is an early marker of SVD-related cognitive change, with broader deficits emerging at greater severity. Collectively, these findings provide further insights into the cognitive profile of SVD and underscore the need for additional research, particularly across SVD pathologies beyond WMH.

papers.title: Effects of STN-DBS on voluntary facial mimicry in Parkinson's patients: a pilot study.
papers.authors: Scagliotti E, Pirola E, Remore LG, Ampollini A, Fornara GA, Ferrucci R, Mameli F, Zirone E, Cogiamanian F, Mailland E, Luiso F, Isaias IU, Locatelli M.
papers.journal: Neurological sciences : official journal of the Italian Neurological Society and of the Italian Society of Clinical Neurophysiology
papers.abstract: Purpose Parkinson disease (PD) causes hypomimia, an early manifestation driven by motor, limbic and basal ganglia dysfunction that impairs nonverbal communication. Traditional clinical rating scales used to assess facial expressivity are subjective, traditional clinical scales are subjective, whereas automated video analysis based on the Facial Action Coding System (FACS) provides an objective, fine-grained measurement of specific facial Action Units (AUs). Subthalamic Deep Brain Stimulation (STN-DBS), a widely adopted therapy for PD, modulates basal ganglia circuits, yet its precise effect on facial mimicry remains poorly characterized. This study evaluates how STN-DBS influences voluntary facial expressivity by comparing Stim-ON/Med-ON and Stim-OFF/Med-ON states. Methods 18 PD-patients with STN-DBS were evaluated in two experimental conditions (Stim-ON/Med-ON VS Stim-OFF/Med-ON). Video recordings captured participants reproducing seven voluntary facial expressions (six basic emotions plus neutral). Facial mimicry was quantified using OpenFace 2.0 to extracts AUs intensities according to the FACS system. Results MDS-UPDRS-III scores improved significantly in the DBS-ON state (p < 0.001), confirming the expected improvement in motor symptoms. Automated FACS analysis revealed emotion-specific differences in AUs, showing reduced mimicry in the Stim-OFF/Med-ON condition, for neutral (AU06, p = 0.042), happiness (AU06, p = 0.034), fear (AU25, p = 0.043), and anger (AU23, p = 0.036). For sadness, AU09 activation was higher in the OFF state (p = 0.021). No significant differences emerged for disgust or surprise. Conclusion STN-DBS appears to selectively modulate voluntary facial mimicry in PD, enhancing activation of emotion-relevant AUs, and reducing non-pertinent activations for sadness. These findings indicate that STN-DBS influences emotional motor output beyond classical motor control, potentially benefiting nonverbal social interaction.

papers.title: Changes in gait function associated with cerebral small vessel disease-related cognitive impairment during dual-task walking: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
papers.authors: Li T, Liu X, Meng T, Liu S, Ming D.
papers.abstract: Cerebral small vessel disease (CSVD) is a major contributor to vascular cognitive impairment. As gait abnormalities emerge early in the disease course and are closely related to cognitive decline, quantitative gait assessment offers a promising approach for the early detection of CSVD-related cognitive impairment (CSVD-CI). Dual-task (DT) gait assessment increases cognitive demands during walking and may reveal cognitive-motor deficits that are less apparent under single-task (ST) conditions. However, heterogeneity in gait metrics, imaging criteria, and cognitive paradigms has resulted in inconsistent findings, thereby impeding the identification of robust gait markers for CSVD-CI. A systematic search of PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and EBSCO identified nine studies reporting DT gait outcomes and eight reporting ST gait outcomes in patients with CSVD-CI, with four studies reporting outcomes under both conditions. Compared with ST conditions, DT gait assessment more effectively discriminated patients with CSVD-CI from cognitively unimpaired controls. Under DT conditions, CSVD-CI patients exhibited significantly slower gait speed (p = 0.014), greater stride time variability (p = 0.027), and higher dual-task costs (p < 0.001), suggesting a slower and less stable gait pattern. Subgroup and sensitivity analyses suggested that CSVD imaging characteristics may contribute to between-study heterogeneity, although these findings remain exploratory. These findings support further investigation of selected DT gait parameters as potential behavioral indicators of CSVD-CI. Further studies in CSVD populations defined using standardized diagnostic and inclusion criteria should evaluate the screening performance and longitudinal predictive value of DT gait parameters, as well as their associations with CI severity.

papers.title: Combined melatonin and edaravone therapy attenuates methylmercury-induced amyotrophic lateral sclerosis-like neurodegeneration through GLP-1 modulation and myelin preservation.
papers.authors: Raina GS, Mehan S, Das Gupta G.
papers.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a progressive and fatal neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the selective degeneration of upper and lower motor neurons, resulting in progressive muscle weakness, paralysis, and respiratory failure. Despite the availability of disease-modifying therapies, current treatment options provide only modest clinical benefits, highlighting the need for novel therapeutic strategies targeting multiple pathological mechanisms. Melatonin, a pleiotropic neuroprotective molecule with antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and anti-apoptotic properties, has emerged as a promising candidate; however, its influence on glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1)-associated neuroprotective signaling and related molecular events in ALS remains poorly understood. Therefore, the present study investigated the neuroprotective efficacy of melatonin in a methylmercury (MTMR)-induced rat model of ALS and explored its effects on GLP-1-associated molecular alterations, neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, apoptosis, neurotransmitter homeostasis, demyelination, and neuronal injury. Molecular docking analysis was performed to predict the interaction of melatonin with proteins implicated in ALS pathology. Adult Wistar rats were exposed to MTMR (5 mg/kg, p.o.) for 21 days to induce ALS-like neurodegeneration, followed by treatment with melatonin (5 or 10 mg/kg, i.p.), edaravone (3 mg/kg, i.p.), or their combination for an additional 21 days. Neurobehavioral performance, biochemical alterations, hematological parameters, molecular biomarkers, and histopathological changes were subsequently evaluated. MTMR administration produced profound motor deficits accompanied by reduced GLP-1 levels, neurotransmitter imbalance, increased neuroinflammatory and apoptotic markers, elevated neurofilament light chain (NEFL), skeletal muscle injury, methylmercury accumulation, and extensive myelin and neuronal damage. Melatonin treatment significantly attenuated these pathological alterations in a dose-dependent manner by increasing GLP-1 levels, improving antioxidant status, reducing inflammatory and apoptotic responses, restoring neurotransmitter balance, preserving myelin integrity, and improving neuronal morphology across multiple brain regions and the spinal cord. Molecular docking further predicted favorable interactions between melatonin and several proteins associated with ALS pathophysiology, supporting its potential as a multitarget therapeutic agent. In most outcome measures, combined treatment with melatonin and edaravone produced greater neuroprotective effects than either intervention alone. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that melatonin substantially attenuates methylmercury-induced ALS-like neuropathology through coordinated modulation of multiple pathological processes associated with neurodegeneration. Although the precise molecular mechanisms require further experimental validation, the observed restoration of GLP-1 levels together with improvements in oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, apoptosis, neurotransmitter homeostasis, and myelin integrity suggests that melatonin may represent a promising adjunctive therapeutic strategy for ALS.

papers.title: Reduced Sensory Attenuation Scales with Tic Severity in Tourette Syndrome.
papers.authors: Stanco G, Marotta A, Mariano M, Emadi Andani M, Fiorio M, Porta M, Zapparoli L.
papers.journal: Movement disorders : official journal of the Movement Disorder Society
papers.abstract: Background Patients with Tourette syndrome (TS) often describe tics as reactions to uncomfortable somatic sensations (premonitory urges), suggesting a breakdown in how the brain filters internally generated sensory information. This filtering capacity is indexed by sensory attenuation (SA), a mechanism relying on sensorimotor predictions to dampen the perceived intensity of self-produced inputs. However, objective behavioral evidence of such impairment in TS remains lacking. Objectives The aims were to determine whether patients with TS exhibit reduced SA and to evaluate whether the magnitude of this impairment correlates with the severity of the symptoms related to the syndrome. Methods Thirty adults with TS and 30 healthy controls performed a force-matching task. Participants reproduced a target force in a direct condition (directly with their finger) and in an indirect condition (controlling force via a button). TS patients underwent a comprehensive clinical assessment, including the Yale Global Tic Severity Scale (YGTSS). Results Compared with controls, patients with TS exhibited reduced SA, evidenced by lower force overestimation during direct force reproduction, whereas no group differences were observed in the indirect condition. This reduction was associated with greater tic severity and accounted for additional variance in YGTSS total tic scores beyond medication load, obsessive-compulsive symptoms, and premonitory urge severity. Conclusions These findings provide the first direct behavioral evidence of reduced SA in adults with TS. The observed association with tic severity suggests that SA may represent a clinically relevant behavioral marker of altered sensorimotor predictive processing in TS. © 2026 International Parkinson and Movement Disorder Society.

papers.title: Risk Stratification of Prostate Imaging Reporting and Data System (PI-RADS 3) Lesions in the Peripheral and Transition Zones Using Clinical and Quantitative MRI Markers.
papers.authors: Kaur T, Chahine R, Seiberlich N, Hussain H, Wells S, Gulani V, Jiang Y.
papers.journal: Journal of magnetic resonance imaging : JMRI
papers.abstract: Background Prostate Imaging Reporting and Data System (PI-RADS) 3 lesions often undergo biopsy despite a low positive predictive value (< 25%) for clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa), defined as International Society of Urological Pathology (ISUP) Grade Group ≥ 2. Purpose To determine whether mean apparent diffusion coefficient (mADC), alone or with prostate-specific antigen (PSA)-based metrics, improves zone-specific PI-RADS 3 classification for csPCa detection. Study type Retrospective, single-center. Population One hunderd and seventy-one males (71 ± 8 years) with 191 PI-RADS 3 lesions who underwent multiparametric MRI and targeted biopsy. Field strength/sequence 3 T, T2-weighted turbo spin-echo imaging, single-shot echo-planar diffusion-weighted imaging, and fat-suppressed dynamic contrast-enhanced T1-weighted gradient echo sequences. Assessment mADC, PSA, PSA density (PSAD), prostate volume, and body mass index were analyzed. Statistical tests Logistic regression and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses assessed associations with malignancy and diagnostic performance. Results mADC was significantly lower in cancers than non-cancers in 133 PZ lesions (885 ± 165 vs. 1068 ± 168 × 10-6 mm2 /s) and 58 TZ lesions (670 ± 127 vs. 832 ± 179 × 10-6 mm2 /s). In the PZ, mADC alone, and with PSAD showed no significantly different area under the curve (AUC, 0.79 vs. 0.80, p = 0.28). A combination of mADC and PSAD would result in hypothetical estimated lesion-level biopsy avoidance. In the TZ, combining mADC with PSAD yielded significantly higher AUC than mADC alone (0.88 vs. 0.77, difference: 0.109 [95% CI: 0.010-0.208]). This combination would result in hypothetical estimated lesion-level biopsy avoidance in 58 of 82 non-cancers (71%) while missing one csPCa in the PZ, and 27 of 35 noncancerous lesions while missing one csPCa in TZ. Data conclusion mADC combined with PSAD showed a significant increase in discrimination in the TZ, suggesting improved PI-RADS 3 stratification; independent validation is required before clinical implementation. Evidence level 3. Technical efficacy 2.

papers.title: Disrupted Top-Down Modulation as a Mechanism of Impaired Multisensory Processing in Autistic Children.
papers.authors: Vanneau T, Foxe JJ, Beker S, Molholm S.
papers.abstract: Atypical sensory processing is commonly observed in autism, particularly when integration across sensory modalities is required. The neural mechanisms underlying multisensory differences remain unclear. We recorded EEG while autistic children aged 8-13 (AU;n = 40), siblings of autistic children (SIB;n = 26), and non-autistic controls (NA;n = 36) performed a simple reaction-time task to auditory (A), visual (V), and audiovisual (AV) stimuli. Analyses targeted event-related potentials (ERPs), alpha-band event-related desynchronization (α-ERD), and long-range theta-band functional connectivity. Groups did not differ across unisensory measures, indicating comparable unisensory processing. By contrast, multisensory integration (MSI;AV-(A+V)) differed across groups: NA children showed significant ERP MSI over parieto-central sites that was absent in AU and SIB; and α-ERD MSI was significantly reduced in AU, with SIB showing an intermediate profile. Connectivity analyses revealed reduced AV fronto-parieto-occipital coupling in autistic children relative to non-autistic children, suggesting weaker large-scale coordination during multisensory processing. These results point to a multisensory-specific deficit spanning early sensory encoding, posterior α-ERD, and fronto-posterior coupling and support disrupted multisensory influences on sensory processing due to reduced multisensory attentional orienting. SIB profiles suggest inherited liability for these neural phenotypes. These results help explain well-documented behavioral MSI differences in autism by linking impaired early enhancement with attenuated top-down control of sensory cortex.

papers.title: The Unbroken Integrative Psycho-Trauma Care Model: Health System Implementation in Wartime Ukraine.
papers.authors: Berezyuk O, Rubinstein D, Duek O, Amen S, Samchuk O, Krynytska-Berezyuk U, Filts O, Svirchuk M, Herych H, Paolini L, Patsalides Hofmann B, Bluvshtein M, Umarbekov A, Philip NS, Harpaz-Rotem I.
papers.abstract: Importance The ongoing war in Ukraine has generated an unprecedented burden of psychological trauma, frequently compounded by posttraumatic stress disorder, traumatic brain injury, severe physical injury, and the psychiatric consequences of captivity among former prisoners of war. In large military conflicts, civilian hospital systems are essential for delivering trauma-informed mental health care at scale while managing patients with complex, overlapping medical and psychiatric conditions under active conflict, with limited implementation guidance. Observations This Special Communication describes the implementation and clinical workflow of the Unbroken Integrative Psycho-Trauma Care Model, a multidisciplinary health system approach embedded in the Lviv First Medical Union in Western Ukraine to organize trauma-informed mental health care within a wartime civilian hospital. From February 24, 2022, through December 31, 2025, the Lviv First Medical Union treated more than 15 000 individuals for war-related injuries and cared for more than 400 former prisoners of war. During this period, 7538 unique individuals received psychiatric care through the Unbroken Model, including 4165 who received trauma-focused psychotherapy. The model was implemented through proactive psychiatric rounds across medical and surgical departments, structured triage into 4 clinical pathways, stabilization-first care sequencing, and longitudinal case management integrated with neurological, surgical, and rehabilitation services. This organization of care enabled early identification of trauma-related distress, continuity between medical and psychiatric treatment, and adaptive delivery of trauma-focused psychotherapies within a high-volume conflict setting. Conclusions and relevance The Unbroken Model demonstrates how trauma-informed mental health care can be delivered at scale within a civilian hospital during active conflict. Its primary innovation lies in the organization of care delivery, integrating proactive outreach, triage-driven pathways, multidisciplinary coordination, and stabilization-first sequencing into a unified, scalable framework. This approach may be applicable to conflict-affected and postconflict health systems worldwide.

papers.title: Prefrontal Cortical Changes With Mindfulness-Oriented Recovery Enhancement in Opioid Use Disorder: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
papers.authors: Huang Y, Ceceli AO, Kronberg G, Drury KR, King SG, McClain NE, Wong YY, Boros M, Butelman ER, Gaudreault PO, Parvaz MA, Alia-Klein N, Garland EL, Goldstein RZ.
papers.abstract: Importance Despite decades of clinical implementation of medications for opioid use disorder (OUD), overdose mortality rates remain high, underscoring a critical need for interventions that target the brain mechanisms underlying addiction. Objective To assess the neural mechanisms of Mindfulness-Oriented Recovery Enhancement (MORE) and their associations with clinical outcomes, including craving and abstinence duration. Design, setting, and participants This randomized clinical trial was conducted from November 2020 to September 2024 among individuals with OUD recruited from an inpatient rehabilitation facility in New York and randomized to MORE or psychoeducational supportive therapy (PST). Data were analyzed from October 2024 to August 2026. Interventions Treatment with MORE (comprising training in mindfulness, drug cue reappraisal, and savoring positive experiences) or PST (active control condition) across 8 weekly 2-hour group sessions. Main outcomes and measures Outcomes included treatment-related changes in functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) blood oxygen level-dependent signal (primary), abstinence length (secondary), and cue-induced craving (secondary). Results Drug cue reactivity task analyses included 59 participants (MORE, n = 24; 5 women [20.8%]; mean [SD] age, 43.6 [11.3] years; PST, n = 35; 8 women [22.9%]; mean [SD] age, 42.8 [10.0] years). Movie-watching and follow-up analyses were conducted in subsets of 37 (MORE, n = 18; PST, n = 19) and 38 participants (MORE, n = 13; PST, n = 25), respectively. Compared with PST, MORE reduced drug-biased activity in the middle frontal gyrus and other brain areas, including the precuneus, during downregulation of responses to drug cues relative to upregulation of responses to natural reward cues (even when controlling for passive cue viewing; z > 3.1; P < .05). The shift from drug to natural reward responses in the lateral and ventromedial prefrontal cortex (PFC) was associated with lower cue-induced craving exclusively in the MORE group (z > 3.1; P < .05). Relative to PST, MORE also reduced medial PFC synchronization to naturalistic drug-related movie scenes (q = 0.019) and significantly extended abstinence duration at follow-up (approximately 4 months posttreatment; χ2 = 6.7; P = .04; Cohen w = 0.19). Conclusions and relevance This neuroimaging randomized clinical trial demonstrates that MORE may restructure function in PFC nodes of the reward, salience, and control networks, positioning it as a biologically grounded adjunct to pharmacotherapy for OUD. Trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04112186.

papers.title: Repeated VU0155069 Treatment Is Associated with Region- and Pathological Stage-Specific Dendritic Spine Remodeling in Female 3xTg-AD Mice
papers.authors: Mohanty S, Bosworth S, Ramaswamy K, Natarajan C, Krishnan B.
papers.abstract: Background Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is increasingly recognized as a disorder of synaptic integrity in which changes in dendritic spine abundance and morphology accompany progressive cognitive dysfunction. Phospholipase D1 (PLD1), a regulator of membrane trafficking and cytoskeletal signaling, is aberrantly elevated in AD-related pathological states (ADRD). Previous studies from our lab demonstrated that repeated VU0155069 treatment promotes functional resilience in female 3xTg-AD mice, including improvements in novel-object recognition, fear-conditioning performance, hippocampal LTP, later-stage LTP and LTD, selected neuropathological outcomes, and most importantly, CA1 spine integrity. Objective To determine how this previously demonstrated functional resilience is represented structurally across cortical, hippocampal, and amygdalar circuits at earlier and later stages of AD-like pathology. Methods Female 3xTg-AD mice received vehicle or VU0155069 at 1 mg/kg intraperitoneally every other day for one month beginning at 5 or 11 months of age, with Golgi-Cox analysis at 6 or 12 months, respectively. Age-matched vehicle-treated 3xTg-AD littermates served as the primary comparator for evaluating the structural response to pharmacological attenuation of disease-associated PLD1 signaling. Results Auditory and visual cortical fields showed selective changes in spine-subtype distribution and morphometry. Hippocampal cornu ammonis (CA)2, CA3, and dentate gyrus (DG) exhibited distinct patterns involving spine abundance, density, and geometry, whereas the central, lateral, and basolateral amygdalar nuclei showed nucleus- and stage-dependent remodeling. Across the multiregional dataset, recurring responses comprised spine-subtype redistribution, changes in spine abundance, and morphometric remodeling rather than uniform structural rescue. Conclusions VU0155069 engages circuit- and pathological stage-specific forms of dendritic spine remodeling across distributed recognition- and associative-memory networks. Graphical Abstract

papers.title: Neurotransmitter receptor architecture links local neurochemistry to semantic memory
papers.authors: Jung J, Gim J, Lambon Ralph M.
papers.abstract: A fundamental challenge in neuroscience is understanding how the molecular and neurochemical architecture of the human cortex gives rise to sophisticated higher cognitive functions. The anterior temporal lobe (ATL) is a key hub for semantic memory, and its underlying GABAergic and glutamatergic neurochemistry supports semantic memory performance. However, the molecular receptor architecture underlying these neurochemical-cognitive relationships remains unknown. Here, we combined imaging transcriptomics and in vivo magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) to investigate how neurotransmitter receptor organisation relates to local neurochemistry and semantic memory in the human ATL. We found that the ATL exhibited a distinct transcriptomically inferred receptor-subunit profile relative to control cortical regions (occipital cortex and vertex). Individual-specific spatial estimates of receptor-subunit gene expression were systematically associated with local GABA+ and Glx concentrations, revealing preferential coupling between GABAergic receptor genes and GABA+ and between glutamatergic receptor genes and Glx, alongside widespread cross-system associations between GABAergic receptor architecture and Glx. ATL GABA+ and Glx concentrations were positively associated with semantic memory performance, and GABAergic and glutamatergic receptor-subunit expression showed selective relationships with semantic memory accuracy. Crucially, mediation analyses revealed that GABA+ mediated associations between GABAergic receptor architecture and semantic performance, whereas Glx mediated both glutamatergic and widespread GABAergic receptor associations. Together, these findings reveal a coupled molecular-neurochemical architecture of the human ATL, linking neurotransmitter receptor organisation to regional neurochemical state and individual differences in semantic memory. Our findings provide a multiscale account of how cortical molecular organisation is associated with human higher cognitive function.

papers.title: Microstructure of white matter association tracts in the temporal lobe predicts the timing of electrophysiological activity and behaviour in picture naming
papers.authors: Chupina I, Roos NM, Sierpowska J, Oostenveld R, Tuladhar AM, Westner BU, Piai V.
papers.abstract: White matter (WM) microstructure has been mainly associated with accuracy of picture naming. However, little is known about how WM properties relate to the timing of picture naming and its underlying electrophysiological activity. Here, we linked diffusion-weighted, electrophysiological, and behavioural data, using time-based measures to conceptually connect WM deterioration to alterations in conduction speed and precision. Our sample included individuals of varying age, with or without stroke. We correlated fractional anisotropy (FA) of bilateral WM tracts traversing the temporal lobe with mean response times (RTs) and response time variability (coefficient of variation, CV) in picture naming, and with the onset latency of neuronal activity, represented by the electrophysiological P2 component time-locked to picture onset. We selected tracts showing associations with P2 latency and naming performance separately, on which we conducted path analyses examining the relationship between structure, neuronal activity and behaviour. Depending on the tract, higher FA was associated with faster and/or more consistent naming, suggesting that ventral tracts differentially contribute to naming speed and consistency. Importantly, path modelling for the right inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus (IFOF) revealed that FA predicted P2 latency, which in turn predicted RTs, possibly reflecting a structure-activity-behaviour relationship in lexical-semantic processing. P2 source reconstruction demonstrated anatomical proximity to posterior segments of the right IFOF, supporting these findings. Overall, this study provides a proof of concept for modelling structure-activity-behaviour relationships in language research, while highlighting the need for elaboration of such relations at a more mechanistic level.

papers.title: Older Adults Show Preserved Neural Signatures of Audiovisual Integration but Altered Links to Speech Comprehension
papers.authors: Reynolds C, Jensen O, Segaert K, Park H.
papers.abstract: Older adults often experience difficulty understanding speech in noisy environments despite relatively preserved hearing. Although visual speech cues can improve speech perception, it remains unclear whether the neural mechanisms supporting audiovisual integration are preserved in healthy ageing. We addressed this question using magnetoencephalography (MEG) combined with Rapid Invisible Frequency Tagging (RIFT) during challenging audiovisual speech task. Forty younger and forty older adults attended to one of two competing speech streams while the speaker’s lip movements were frequency tagged, with the visual modulation driven by either the attended or unattended speech envelope. Task-Relevant amplitude modulation of frequency tagging in visual speech improved speech comprehension in younger adults as previously reported for this cohort; this accuracy benefit was absent in older adults. Auditory and visual tagging responses were modulated by task relevance similarly across age groups, indicating largely preserved modality-specific sensory processing in older adults. Intermodulation responses, reflecting nonlinear interactions between auditory and visual speech signals, also remained sensitive to task relevance and did not differ in their condition-dependent modulation between age groups. Greater Task-Relevant versus Task-Irrelevant differences in intermodulation coherence were also associated with greater comprehension benefits in younger adults; no significant association was found in older adults, and this relationship differed significantly between age groups. These findings suggest that the absence of a comprehension benefit in older adults is linked to a change in the relationship between audiovisual intermodulation and behaviour, despite largely preserved task-sensitive brain responses.

papers.title: Stratified Palliobulbar and Midbrain Circuits Control the Timing and Acoustics of Learned Vocalizations
papers.authors: Zhao Z, Roberts TF.
papers.abstract: In mammals and birds, production of learned vocalizations depends on prominent projections from the pallium to the brainstem 1–8 . Although pallial and cortical coding mechanisms for speech and birdsong are becoming increasingly clear 9–19 , understanding how palliobulbar projections supervise brainstem circuits has remained challenging. Here we identify the functional organization of pallial and brainstem control of learned song in the zebra finch, a songbird in which genetic control of neuronal pathways is now feasible 18,20,21 . We find that palliobulbar projections to the medulla and midbrain periaqueductal gray (PAG) arise from largely non-overlapping neuronal populations. Genetic silencing of these pathways reveals that projections to the medulla control the learned acoustic content defining individual song syllables, while projections to the PAG control the respiratory timing needed to sequence syllables. Using large-scale neuronal recordings, we find that song and innate calls are uniquely encoded within the PAG. Dual recordings from the palliobulbar neurons and the PAG suggest hierarchical encoding of expiratory and inspiratory events along this pathway. Lastly, genetic silencing reveals that PAG projections to the medulla are needed for birds to generate learned song and innate calls. Thus, stratified palliobulbar pathways control respiratory-timing and acoustics for song. Yet, without the PAG, they are insufficient to produce any vocalizations.

papers.title: Cerebello-basal ganglia networks and behavior across adulthood and aging
papers.authors: Delaney CA, Herrejon IA, Magalhaes TN, Jackson TB, Hicks TH, Bernard JA.
papers.abstract: The cerebellum contributes to aging, cognition, and reward related processing, but has been understudied in these domains. The cerebello-basal ganglia (CB-BG) circuit may be key to better understanding how the brain ages, as it has been implicated in modulation of cognitive, motor, and reward-related functions. Prior work has implicated this circuit in aging in a small sample, though it is also of interest in age-related neurodegenerative disease, particularly Parkinson’s Disease. Here, we investigated the CB-BG network in a sample of 138 participants between the ages of 35 and 86. Participants completed motor and cognitive testing batteries followed by 26 minutes of resting state functional connectivity magnetic resonance imaging (fcMRI), replicating previously mapped cognitive and motor subcircuits. When examining connectivity by age group (early and late middle age and older adulthood), we found higher functional connectivity in early middle age compared to older adulthood, with no results related to late middle age. Analysis of connectivity related to Stroop task performance showed higher connectivity-behavior associations in early middle-aged adults compared to older adults. Regarding sex differences, we found lower functional connectivity in females compared to males. Analysis of steroid hormone levels revealed higher connectivity associated with progesterone in females relative to males. We have replicated CB-BG subcircuits and further elucidated connectivity patterns associated with age, sex, progesterone levels, and cognitive performance. This expanded investigation of CB-BG networks represents an essential step in increasing our knowledge of age-related cognitive and motor declines and may be particularly relevant for consideration in Parkinson’s Disease.

papers.title: Habitual sleep duration is associated with the cortical organisation of brain network controllability
papers.authors: Liu X, Lu R, Wang S, Yu Q, Zhang M, Cui R, Xiao J, Liu X, Fan T.
papers.abstract: Sleep is fundamental to adaptive brain function, yet how habitual sleep relates to the structural network properties that support flexible transitions between brain states remains poorly understood. Combining wrist-accelerometer sleep measures with diffusion MRI connectomes from 15,799 UK Biobank adults, we show that longer workday sleep is associated with higher modal controllability of somatomotor systems and lower controllability of visual cortex. This system-specific signature reproduced in a locked test set (n = 4,740) and was robust across extensive sensitivity analyses. Decomposition showed that it reflects a redistribution of structural connection weight, with greater absolute visual connectivity and a smaller somatomotor share of the whole-brain total. Weekend catch-up sleep showed no comparable association. The signature was distinct from brain-ageing patterns and, across 1,226 phenotypes, related mainly to physical activity and body composition rather than cognition. These findings link everyday sleep habits to the system-specific organisation of brain network controllability.

papers.title: Physiological Oscillations of Lateral Ventricular Volume Revealed by Fast fMRI: Effects of Aging and Vigilance
papers.authors: Wang L, Wright AM, Zhao Y, Tong Y, Allen JW, Wen Q.
papers.abstract: Background Cyclic ventricular deformation may contribute to CSF displacement. However, the physiological mechanisms underlying ventricular motion remain poorly understood. This study characterized physiological oscillations of lateral ventricular volume (LVV) and examined their associations with aging and vigilance. Methods We analyzed two fast resting-state fMRI scans from 99 adults aged 35–82 years. The first scan was acquired during eyes-open wakefulness, followed by 30 min of eyes-closed rest and a second scan during eyes-closed drowsiness. LVV was estimated for each image volume using automated ventricular segmentation, yielding time-resolved volume measurements. Temporal variability was quantified using the standard deviation and coefficient of variation, and spectral power was quantified for low-frequency, respiratory, and cardiac oscillations. Age-related associations were assessed using multiple linear regression adjusted for sex. Awake–drowsy differences were assessed using paired t-tests. False discovery rate correction was applied for multiple comparisons in all analyses. Results After quality-control exclusions, 97 participants were analyzed. LVV exhibited distinct low-frequency, respiratory, and cardiac oscillatory components. Respiratory and cardiac oscillations accounted for 37.7% and 38.4% of total physiological spectral power, respectively, compared with 23.9% for low-frequency oscillations. Mean lateral ventricular volume increased with age (FDR-adjusted p = 0.010), while respiratory and cardiac power also showed positive associations with age, although neither survived FDR correction (both FDR-adjusted p = 0.067). The transition to eyes-closed drowsiness was associated with greater LVV fluctuation magnitude, reflected by increases in standard deviation (FDR-adjusted p < 0.001) and coefficient of variation (FDR-adjusted p = 0.028) and accompanied by increased low-frequency (FDR-adjusted p < 0.001) and respiratory power (FDR-adjusted p = 0.015). Mean LVV and cardiac power did not change significantly between conditions. Conclusions LVV exhibits prominent respiratory and cardiac oscillations in addition to low-frequency fluctuations, suggesting that ventricular dynamics reflect multiple physiological influences rather than a single dominant physiological driver. Aging was primarily associated with ventricular enlargement, whereas reduced vigilance was accompanied by increased LVV fluctuation magnitude, primarily reflected in increased low-frequency and respiratory power, without a change in mean LVV. Time-resolved LVV provides a complementary approach for investigating the physiological regulation of ventricular dynamics in health and disease.

papers.title: Insula functional connectivity development follows a canonical antero-posterior axis of organization
papers.authors: Flook EA, Shafiei G, Cieslak M, Horien C, Luo AC, Meisler SL, Salo T, Sydnor VJ, Tong TT, Barch DM, Goldsmith J, Gur RE, Somerville LH, Uddin LQ, Alexander-Bloch A, Shinohara RT, Satterthwaite TD.
papers.abstract: The insula is a heterogeneous region associated with a range of functional domains including sensory, cognitive, and emotional processing. Cytoarchitectural and functional studies have described an antero-posterior axis of insula organization. However, the insula's functional development remains sparsely described. We delineated the development of insula resting-state functional connectivity across 562 individuals (6-22 years) using generalized additive models and population value decomposition. We show insulo-cortical functional connectivity development differs across the insula: anterior subregions have predominantly decreasing connectivity across the age range examined, whereas posterior subregions have variable connectivity that aligns with the sensorimotor-association axis. Vertex-level analysis revealed that age-related trajectories followed an antero-posterior axis that aligned with estimates of insula microstructure. Our results emphasize that the development of insula connectivity is spatially heterogeneous and aligns with known cytoarchitecture. The normative insula development described here provides a foundation for investigating how emerging psychopathology may be linked to variation in insula development.

papers.title: Tetrahydrobiopterin restores oligodendrocyte maturation after hypoxic white matter injury by reprogramming translational output
papers.authors: Sarić N, Antonios I, Heiser K, Ballard A, Miller K, Mansoor I, Rajtboriraks MT, Chandran S, Goldstein E, Ishibashi N.
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Complex congenital heart defects (CHDs) are frequently associated with chronic cerebral hypoxemia, leading to impaired white matter maturation. One proposed mechanism involves hypoxia-induced disruption of the nitric oxide synthase cofactor tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4), resulting in oxidative stress and impaired oligodendrocyte (OL) development. While our previous studies found BH4 supplementation improves hypoxia-induced white matter dysmaturation, the molecular mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Because OL maturation requires coordinated translational control, we hypothesized that BH4 promotes white matter maturation by restoring translation programs disrupted by hypoxia. Methods Translating Ribosome Affinity Purification sequencing (TRAP-seq) was performed on OL lineage cells isolated from transgenic ribosomal reporter mice exposed to chronic hypoxia (10.5% O₂, postnatal day 3–11) with or without daily BH4 treatment. Differential translation, weighted gene co-expression network analysis, pathway enrichment, RNAscope, and immunohistochemistry identified translational programs associated with hypoxia and BH4-mediated rescue. Results Developmental hypoxia extensively altered the OL translatome, suppressing transcripts associated with OL maturation while enriching pathways related to translational regulation and cellular stress. Network analyses identified BH4-responsive gene modules enriched for OL maturation, protein metabolism, and translation-related processes. BH4 partially reversed hypoxia-induced translational changes, restored OL maturation gene expression, and normalized nuclear localization of the lineage regulator OLIG1, consistent with recovery of maturation-associated regulatory programs. Conclusions Developmental hypoxia disrupts OL maturation through coordinated alterations in ribosome-associated gene expression and post-transcriptional regulatory pathways. BH4 promotes recovery of OL maturation programs, including restoration of translation-related networks and OLIG1 nuclear localization, providing mechanistic insight into BH4-supported white matter maturation under chronic hypoxic conditions. Research Perspective What New Question Does This Study Raise? Developmental hypoxemia in congenital heart disease remodels the oligodendrocyte translatome, raising the question of whether translational dysregulation represents a fundamental and therapeutically targetable mechanism underlying white matter dysmaturation in other forms of perinatal brain injury. What Question Should Be Addressed Next? Future studies should determine how BH4 restores ribosome-associated translation of oligodendrocyte maturation programs, establish whether these molecular changes increase myelin protein synthesis and improve long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes, and define the cross-species efficacy for clinical translation. Clinical Research Implication These findings provide a mechanistic rationale for evaluating BH4 as a neuroprotective adjunct therapy to preserve white matter development in fetuses and infants with congenital heart disease experiencing chronic cerebral hypoxemia.

papers.title: Brain Age Gap Associations with Externalising Behaviours in Youth: A Longitudinal Investigation in the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Cohort
papers.authors: Asikin A, Visontay R, Devine EK, Squeglia LM, Byrne H, Mewton L.
papers.abstract: Background Early adolescence is a period of heightened risk for the emergence of externalising psychopathology, making it an important window for identifying neurodevelopmental risk markers. Differences between predicted brain age and chronological age–termed the brain age gap –reflect variation from age-typical patterns of brain structure. While brain age gap has been closely linked with internalising behaviours in adolescence, less is known about its relationship with externalising symptoms. This study examined whether brain age gap in late childhood/early adolescence (9-11 years) is associated with current externalising symptoms and whether it predicts externalising trajectories over seven- year follow-up. Methods Participants were 10,516 adolescents (aged 9-11 at baseline; up to 18 years at follow-up) from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study who met inclusion/exclusion criteria. Brain age gap for each participant was derived from an external validated prediction model (Drobinin et al., 2022) applied to baseline measurements of cortical volume, area, and subcortical volume. Linear mixed-effects models were used to test cross-sectional and longitudinal associations between baseline brain age gap and externalising symptoms, as assessed using the Child Behaviour Checklist. Primary models were adjusted for age, sex, pubertal status, and prior to inclusion of sociodemographic covariates (ethnoracial identity and caregiver highest education). Results A higher/more positive brain age gap was associated with greater externalising symptoms at baseline ( B [SE]=0.067[0.033], p =.042), but this association was removed following sociodemographic adjustment ( B [SE]=0.056[0.033], p =.088). Longitudinally, a significant brain age gap × age interaction was identified that remained evident after sociodemographic adjustment, with this relationship weakening across adolescence ( B [SE]=- 0.007[0.003], p =.033). Conclusions These findings suggest that a more positive brain age gap, indicating more mature-appearing brain structure for age, in late childhood/early adolescence may be associated with externalising psychopathology, but this relationship is likely to be age- and context-dependent rather than a stable marker of persistent behavioural risk.

papers.title: Scalable hardware and software for high-density, multi-regional electrophysiology in non-human primates
papers.authors: Dubey A, Xu Q, Khazali M, Choi J, Wingel K, Haggerty J, Stefanowicz J, Pesaran B.
papers.abstract: Understanding how distributed neural circuits generate complex behaviors requires long-duration recordings from populations of individual neurons across multiple brain regions. High-density Neuropixels probes have revolutionized rodent systems neuroscience. Extending these capabilities to non-human primates (NHPs) for chronic, multi-regional recordings requires compact, implantable microdrive hardware and reliable automated spike-sorting software. NHPs provide access to complex and flexible behaviors that are difficult to study in other model systems. Extending the Neuropixels revolution to NHPs therefore depends on integrating hardware and software for long-duration, multi-regional recordings. Here, we present a scalable hardware–software platform co-designed for high-density neural data acquisition and reliable single-unit identification in NHPs. The Multi-regional Implantable NeuroDrive (MIND) is a lightweight, implantable microdrive that provides stable recordings from multiple independently positioned Neuropixels probes and is designed to support chronic, ambulatory, head-free recordings. We paired MIND with UnitAssay, an automated post-sorting curation framework that identifies and curates characteristic spike-sorting errors with minimal computational cost. Together, MIND and UnitAssay provide an integrated platform for implanted, multi-regional recordings in NHPs performing complex and naturalistic behaviors. We tested MIND and UnitAssay across parietal, prefrontal, and motor cortices in rhesus macaques performing reaching and eye-movement tasks. MIND enabled stable multi-probe recordings across cortical regions and durations. UnitAssay enabled automated curation of large-scale spike-sorting output and improved reliable single-unit identification relative to Kilosort 4 labels and standard SpikeInterface quality control. Together, MIND and UnitAssay provide a scalable solution for high-density, multi-regional, long-duration electrophysiology in NHPs. Graphical Abstract

papers.title: Neuroscience in Conversation: Tracking Scientific Change Through an Open Seminar Archive
papers.authors: Bellin I, Tulner LK, Beyh A, Wearn A, Forkel SJ.
papers.abstract: Scientific talks capture how researchers frame questions, debate ideas, and communicate emerging methods, providing a complementary record of scientific change to the published literature. We investigated whether an open neuroscience seminar archive could reveal shifting scientific attention and contain predictive information about subsequent discourse. We analysed 470 English-language transcripts from the Clinical Neuroanatomy Seminars YouTube channel, spanning 2010–2026 and approximately 2.6 million words, using longitudinal vocabulary analysis, unsupervised topic clustering, conceptual comparisons, and rolling temporal forecasting. The archive captured sustained discussion of language, white matter anatomy, connectivity, clinical neuroscience, and neurobiological mechanisms, alongside changes in their relative prominence. Network-related terminology became more prominent than localisation-related terminology, references to individual variability and computational approaches increased, and open science practices became more visible in scientific discussion. Beyond retrospective description, a regression model predicted keyword frequencies one and two years ahead with approximately 12% and 17% lower mean absolute error, respectively, than a persistence baseline. This modest gain is better explained by smoothing of year-to-year fluctuations than by genuine prediction: terms showing the strongest recent growth tended to fall back rather than continue rising. These findings suggest that spoken scientific discourse shows clear longitudinal change but offers limited evidence of information about subsequent shifts in attention. Interpretation remains grounded in the archive’s curated scope and changing content composition. By making nearly two decades of freely accessible neuroimaging education amenable to systematic analysis, this study connects open educational practice with the study of science itself. Open seminar archives can serve as reusable research resources, preserving the conversations through which scientific communities develop and revise their ideas.

papers.title: Familiarity synchronizes brain rhythms during natural viewing
papers.authors: Noad KN, Kaiser D.
papers.abstract: Our perception of the world is shaped not only by sensory information, but also by prior experience. However, how familiarity alters the coordination of neural representations across distributed brain networks remains unclear. Rhythmic neural activity provides a potential mechanism for coordinating information across sensory and higher-order brain regions in the light of previous experience. Here, we thus investigated whether familiarity alters the coordination of brain rhythms during naturalistic viewing. Participants who were either familiar or unfamiliar with the television series Game of Thrones viewed clips from the series while EEG or fMRI was recorded. We calculated the intersubject correlations of neural activity across EEG frequency bands and related this rhythmic activity to fMRI BOLD responses. Across participants, all brain rhythms showed reliable intersubject synchrony and related to activity across large-scale brain networks. Familiarity selectively enhanced intersubject synchronisation in beta and gamma rhythms, with these effects reflected in visual and default mode brain regions. Moreover, beta and gamma band activity were modulated by similar aspects of the movie, suggesting coordinated familiarity-related processing. These findings show that familiarity selectively shapes rhythmic neural dynamics across the cortex, providing a mechanism through which prior experience alters the coordination of neural representations during naturalistic perception.

papers.title: Anterior Versus Posterior Circulation Acute Ischemic Stroke and 3-Month Cognitive Profiles: A Single-Center Cohort Study.
papers.authors: Zhang Y, Zhang Y, Dong S, Li J, Gu Y, Chu H, Wang H.
papers.abstract: Post-stroke cognitive impairment (PSCI) is common, but its pattern may differ between vascular territories. This single-center cohort included adults with first-ever, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-confirmed acute ischemic stroke admitted between May 2022 and June 2024. Infarcts were classified as anterior or posterior circulation, and cognition was assessed in person at 3 months using the Beijing version of the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA). The primary PSCI definition was an education-adjusted MoCA score <26, with a sensitivity analysis using <22. Of 173 enrolled patients, 167 completed follow-up (91 anterior and 76 posterior circulation infarctions). PSCI occurred in 50/91 (54.9%) and 27/76 (35.5%) patients, respectively (p = 0.012). The unadjusted odds ratio was 2.21 (95% confidence interval, 1.18-4.14), and the adjusted odds ratio was 2.18 (95% confidence interval, 1.06-4.49; p = 0.035). With the <22 cutoff, the corresponding prevalences were 31.9% and 15.8%, and the adjusted odds ratio was 2.43 (95% confidence interval, 1.06-5.54; p = 0.035). After false-discovery-rate correction, differences in visuospatial/executive, naming, delayed-recall, language, abstraction, and orientation performance remained, whereas attention did not differ. Cognitive outcomes differed between vascular-territory groups despite similar global disability scores; these group-level associations do not establish a causal effect of territory or a domain-specific diagnosis.

papers.title: Does the reading brain possess top-down connections from morphemes to letters?
papers.authors: Mlinarič M, Grainger J, Beyersmann E, Snell J.
papers.abstract: No psycholinguist will contradict the importance of morphemes in language processing. But as a cognitive construct, the morpheme and its operations are not fully mapped out yet. Here, we investigated whether morphemes provide top-down support for their constituent letters: a so-called morpheme superiority effect. In two experiments (N = 100 per experiment), French participants identified single letters in nonword strings that either comprised a French affix (e.g., 'o' in 'cojuste') or not ('o' in 'sojuste'). In Experiment 1 participants provided free-recall responses by typing letters seen at postcued locations. Experiment 2 was a Reicher-Wheeler (i.e., two-alternative forced-choice) version of the same task. Neither experiment evidenced better identification of target letters embedded in affixes than nonaffixes. On the other hand, we did observe an impact of the frequencies of embedding N-grams (i.e., letter chunks). Hence, while the brain learns and represents letter combinations, we did not observe evidence for morpheme representations partaking in the brain's feedback loop. Findings are discussed in light of the recent PONG model of word recognition.

papers.title: Introducing the “ASCENT” EEGLAB Plugin: Aperiodic Signal Complexity Estimation for Neurophysiological Time Series
papers.authors: Cannard C, Delorme A.
papers.abstract: Entropy- and complexity-based measures are promising tools to characterize neural dynamics beyond traditional linear and oscillatory analyses. However, their adoption in electroencephalography (EEG) and magnetoencephalography (MEG) research has been limited by methodological fragmentation, computational cost, and a lack of standardized implementations and visualization tools. Hence, we developed ASCENT, an open-source EEGLAB plugin for computing and visualizing a broad range of entropy, fractal, and aperiodic measures in neurophysiological time series. ASCENT integrates established single-scale, multiscale, and multivariate entropy algorithms, fractal dimension estimators, and aperiodic spectral parameterization within an optimized framework, accessible through both a graphical interface and a fully parameter-tunable command-line interface. To our knowledge, it is the first toolbox to combine these measures on independent component (IC) time series and on scalp channels, and to offer time-resolved estimation of both modified multiscale entropy and aperiodic parameters. Outputs are stored in a structured format for statistical analysis with external tools, as illustrated by an accompanying group-analysis script. As a usage example, we applied ASCENT to resting-state EEG from 40 participants recorded with eyes closed and eyes open. Condition differences were found for multiple measures and temporal scales. Their direction, spatial distribution, and scale extent depended on the measure, the coarse-graining operator and, for the power spectrum, aperiodic correction.
