Correlation analyses helped to indicate which measures were redundant. ASCENT aims to lower the threshold for researchers to apply these measures consistently and interpret them appropriately.

papers.title: Evaluating the mobile MUSE EEG headband for studying resting state EEG and event-related potentials
papers.authors: Godde B.
papers.abstract: We examined whether and how tactile EEG experiments could be done through self-assessments by participants at home or through online experiments with consumer-grade mobile EEG devices. As a first step towards this aim, we performed a Flanker task in an online scenario with a MUSE headband and similarly a conventional lab experiment with a standard EEG device.Five undergraduate students participated in a visual flanker experiment and associated ERP components were recorded with either a standard 32-channel EEG System or a 4-channel MUSE EEG headband. In addition, we performed a 2-minutes resting state recording.Resting state brain oscillations measured with the Muse device revealed a similar pattern as with a standard EEG machine, however, strength of alpha oscillations was significantly reduced. For the Flanker task, in the Muse data, the stimulus-locked ERP components were less visible as compared to standard EEG, still the N200 was clearly expressed for the correct trials. Interestingly, in the incorrect trials, time-locked to the response there was the same negative Ne component visible as for the standard experiment. Our results reveal that the Muse device is suitable to obtain event-related potentials – even from interpolated electrode channels. Advanced preprocessing and artifact removal algorithms specifically targeting such devices with only a few and peripheral channels might help to better isolate ERP components of interest. It remains the challenge to develop devices and procedures for online tactile testing.

papers.title: The Impact of Attention on Speech Entrainment in Clinical High-Risk for Psychosis Individuals
papers.authors: Poulton VR, Grent-'T-Jong T, Brickwedde M, gross j, Correll CU, Uhlhaas PJ.
papers.abstract: Language comprehension is disrupted in schizophrenia and early-stage psychosis, but the contributions of bottom-up and top-down processing remain unclear. In the current electroencephalography (EEG) study, we investigated speech entrainment in a sample of n=21 individuals at clinical high-risk for psychosis (CHR-P) and n=25 healthy controls (HCs). Continuous speech was presented through an audiobook in three listening conditions: (1) “Active”, in which participants attended to speech; (2) “Passive”, in which participants passively listened to the audiobook while performing a concurrent visual Flanker task; and (3) “Passive-reversed”, in which participants listened to an unintelligible time-reversed and noise-vocoded version of the audiobook while performing the Flanker task. Mutual Information (MI) analyses were used to assess shared information between the speech amplitude envelope and neural oscillations in the delta (0.25-3 Hz), theta (4.5-6.5 Hz), and alpha (7-10 Hz) frequency ranges. Sensor-level and source-level results indicate stronger delta entrainment in the Active vs. Passive conditions across groups. However, compared to controls, CHR-Ps showed reduced theta entrainment in auditory cortices, independent of condition, and decreased alpha entrainment in the Passive vs. Active condition. The findings point to theta entrainment deficits in CHR-Ps during continuous speech processing, indexing a bottom-up impairment. In contrast, delta and alpha entrainment in CHR-Ps were modulated by attention. Together, these findings highlight that both bottom-up and top-down impairments contribute to speech entrainment deficits in CHR-Ps.

papers.title: Estimating Functional Independence Measure Scores From Japanese Rehabilitation Notes Using a Large Language Model: Retrospective Study.
papers.authors: Nishiyama T, Mine Y, Itoh N, Ikenoue T, Nagasaka K, Matsuo N, Tatsuki O, Aramaki E.
papers.abstract: Background The Functional Independence Measure (FIM) is a standard functional assessment tool in rehabilitation medicine; however, formal assessments are often conducted only at limited intervals. Free-text clinical notes contain more frequent observations of patients' functional status and may complement these assessments. Objective This study aimed to estimate item-level FIM scores from Japanese free-text rehabilitation notes using a locally deployed large language model (LLM) and to evaluate estimation performance; item-level estimability; and differences across diseases, therapy types, and admission FIM severity groups. Methods We retrospectively analyzed free-text notes from physical therapy (PT), occupational therapy (OT), and speech-language pathology (SLP) for patients hospitalized with cerebral infarction (CeI), hip fracture (HF), or vertebral fracture (VBF) at Saiseikai Moriyama Municipal Hospital between October 2019 and September 2024. Using zero-shot prompting, an LLM estimated all FIM items from each note. Estimated scores were matched to reference FIM scores recorded for the same patient on the same calendar date. Performance was evaluated using the mean absolute error (MAE), root mean squared error, and quadratic weighted kappa. Estimation rates and comparisons with modal-score and last-observation-carried-forward (LOCF) baselines were also examined. Results Among 2,952,702 eligible note-item pairs from 164,039 retained rehabilitation-note-level outputs, the model produced 980,000 valid estimates, corresponding to an overall estimation rate of 33.2%. Among 170,744 note-item opportunities with an available same-day reference score, 57,246 (33.5%) were estimable, of which 77.7% (44,481/57,246) were within 1 point of the reference score. Estimates derived from OT notes had a lower MAE than those derived from PT notes in CeI and HF, whereas the difference was not significant in VBF. The LLM outperformed the modal-score baseline but had a higher MAE than the LOCF overall (0.825 vs 0.648). Conclusions The locally deployed LLM shows the potential to derive item-level FIM estimates from Japanese rehabilitation notes. Among estimable note-item pairs with a same-day reference FIM score, 77.7% were within 1 point of the reference score. These findings support the potential use of LLM-based estimation to structure functional information contained in routine rehabilitation notes and complement periodic FIM assessments. Further integration of multidisciplinary clinical records and external validation are needed to improve estimability and evaluate its value for longitudinal functional monitoring.

papers.title: Acanthamoeba granulomatous amoebic encephalitis mimicking tumefactive demyelination
papers.authors: Prakash R, K R, Reghukumar A.
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Acanthamoeba brain infection can cause ring-enhancing lesions that mimic neoplasm, abscess or demyelination on brain imaging. High-dose corticosteroids, the standard treatment for tumefactive demyelination, can be detrimental if infection is not systematically excluded. Case presentation: A 42-year-old immunocompetent woman presented with a two-week history of non-fluent aphasia, executive dysfunction, and progressive right hemiparesis. An MRI scan of the brain showed two left frontoparietal lesions with perilesional oedema, open-ring enhancement, and mass effect. Spectroscopy showed elevated choline and reduced N-acetyl aspartate. Based on the radiological differential diagnosis of tumefactive demyelination versus high-grade glioma, intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g daily was initiated at an outside hospital before referral to our centre. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) study on day 5 of methylprednisolone showed 6 cells/mm³, sugar 78 mg/dL, protein 79 mg/dL, and no oligoclonal bands. CSF 18S rRNA PCR detected Acanthamoeba spp. Combination anti-acanthamoeba therapy (doxycycline, fluconazole, co-trimoxazole, and miltefosine) was administered. The lesions regressed, and deficits improved; however, CSF Acanthamoeba PCR remained positive even after four months of treatment, with co-detection of parvovirus B19. Conclusion Acanthamoeba CNS infection can mimic the clinical, neuroradiological, and spectroscopic features of tumefactive demyelination, including the characteristic open-ring sign. When tumefactive lesions lack definitive features of established demyelinating disease, it is prudent to rule out infective etiologies, such as CNS infections with free-living amoebae, before administering immunomodulators.

papers.title: Giant High-Grade Myxofibrosarcoma of the Right Thigh Treated by Hip Disarticulation: A Case Report with Imaging–Pathology Correlation
papers.authors: Ibrahim M, Saif-aldeen M, Alrifai H, Shams-aldeen E, Mohmmed M, Alzain M, Alsir S.
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Myxofibrosarcoma (MFS) is a soft-tissue sarcoma of fibroblastic origin that typically presents as a slowly enlarging, painless mass. High-grade tumors are locally aggressive, and their diagnosis can be delayed by misleading clinical findings and by under-grading on initial biopsy. Case presentation: A 61-year-old man developed a small fatty-type swelling in the muscular region of the right lower limb in February 2024. It was initially diagnosed as a benign fatty cyst and excised in April 2024. The mass recurred and enlarged, and histology of the excised specimen listed liposarcoma, leiomyosarcoma and rhabdomyosarcoma as differential diagnoses. The patient was referred for chemotherapy, which he received only intermittently (seven cycles of MAID/ifosfamide-based chemotherapy in total). Over the following two years the tumor grew to approximately 31 × 25 × 26 cm. CT showed a cystic-solid necrotic mass eroding the femoral cortex and displacing the femoral vessels, with pelvic and inguinal lymphadenopathy and a small right upper-lobe pulmonary nodule. Pre-operative assessment showed rapid atrial fibrillation with a preserved ejection fraction (58%). Because of neurovascular encasement and bone destruction, limb salvage was not feasible, and a radical right hip disarticulation was performed in July 2026. Histopathology confirmed high-grade MFS with approximately 80% viable tumor after chemotherapy, and R0 margins were achieved. The patient received no adjuvant therapy and was in good condition at the time of writing. Conclusion Deep-seated MFS can remain clinically silent until it reaches massive dimensions. Core biopsy of myxoid-rich tumors may under-grade or misclassify the lesion, radiological stability may mask substantial viable tumor after chemotherapy, and radical amputation remains a valid option when neurovascular encasement and bone destruction preclude limb salvage.

papers.title: Neuroimaging Correlates of Adolescent Substance Use: A Systematic Review of the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study
papers.authors: Assari S, Ray J.
papers.abstract: Abstract Background: Neuroimaging may help characterize brain and contextual factors associated with substance use during development. The ABCD study supports investigation of developmental pathways relevant to substance use [1]. Objective: To synthesize original ABCD publications examining MRI measures in relation to substance use and substance-related exposures. Methods: The authors screened all 2,700 publications in the ABCD corpus. Original empirical articles reporting an MRI measure of any modality and a substance use variable were eligible; methodological, conceptual, review, and commentary articles were excluded. Imaging modality, brain measures, substances, design, and association direction were extracted for descriptive synthesis. Results: The evidence considered spans morphology, white matter microstructure, resting-state connectivity, and task activation. Findings concerning youth initiation, prenatal exposure, and familial liability address distinct developmental questions. Family history and stressful life events feature in the white matter literature [2]. Findings vary by modality, exposure definition, and temporal direction, and include null associations. Conclusions: The literature suggests distributed and context-dependent neuroimaging associations. Observational designs, overlapping participants, confounding, and analytic heterogeneity limit causal interpretation and assessment of independent replication. The findings support further longitudinal investigation but do not establish a validated MRI screening tool.

papers.title: Effectiveness of treatments for managing affective prosody deficits in adults with acquired brain injury: a systematic review
papers.authors: Teulon C, Baglione H, Monetta L.
papers.abstract: Abstract Affective prosody conveys emotional information through variations in the acoustic parameters of speech. Impairments in the production and/or comprehension of affective prosody may occur following acquired brain injury (ABI) and they significantly affect communication and social participation. Objective: This paper aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of interventions designed to target receptive and expressive affective prosody deficits in adults with ABI. Special attention was given to post-treatment improvement, generalization, maintenance of treatment gains, and transfer to everyday communication. Methods: A systematic review of the literature was conducted following the PRISMA protocol. Six databases were searched according to predefined eligibility criteria. Results: Nine studies involving 62 participants met the inclusion criteria. The identified treatments were grouped into four main approaches and analyzed with respect to treatment outcomes and methodological quality. Treatments targeting both expressive and receptive affective prosody deficits showed promising effects, although evidence was stronger for post-treatment improvement than for generalization, maintenance, or transfer to everyday communication. Conclusions: Current findings suggest that affective prosody deficits following ABI can be treated through rehabilitation. Nevertheless, the evidence base remains limited, highlighting the need for larger and more rigorous studies to establish evidence-based recommendations for clinical practice.

papers.title: Investigating the Association of Physical Activity and Muscular Fitness with Structural Brain Changes and Cognitive Performance
papers.authors: Schellin J, Herden M, Neumann M, Petersen M, Nägele FL, Bischoff LL, Cheng B, Twerenbold R, Thomalla G, Jensen M, Schumacher N.
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Physical activity (PA) is a modifiable factor linked to cognitive decline, but its relationship with structural brain changes remains inconsistent. We studied associations of self-reported PA and handgrip strength with brain structure and cognition. Methods We examined middle-aged to elderly participants from the population-based Hamburg City Health Study, who underwent brain MRI and cognitive testing. PA was assessed via questionnaires (overall PA, sport participation, strength training frequency), and handgrip strength indexed muscular fitness. MRI markers included among others peak width of skeletonized mean diffusivity (PSMD), cortical thickness, and structural connectivity metrics. Cognition was assessed with CERAD-Plus subtests. Associations were examined using multivariable linear regression and mediation analysis. Results Among 2,618 participants (mean age 64 ± 8.3 years; 44% female), higher handgrip strength was associated with lower PSMD (β=-0.117, 95% CI [-0.194, -0.041]), greater cortical thickness (β = 0.100, 95% CI [0.019, 0.181]), and faster processing speed (β=-0.155, 95% CI [-0.234, -0.076]). Self-reported PA showed no associations with brain structure. Sport participation was associated with faster processing speed (β=-0.059, 95% CI [-0.105, -0.014]), better executive function (β=-0.045, 95% CI [-0.088, -0.002]), and better verbal memory (β = 0.052, 95% CI [0.007, 0.097]). PSMD partially mediated the association between handgrip strength and processing speed (ab=-0.008, 95% CI [-0.019, -0.001]). Conclusions Handgrip strength, unlike self-reported PA, was associated with brain structure and cognitive performance, highlighting the importance of PA assessment modality in brain health research. Mediation of associations between handgrip strength and cognition by PSMD suggest white matter microstructural injury as one pathway linking neuromuscular and cognitive function. Clinical Trial Registration: ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT03934957.

papers.title: Bilateral accessory posterior cerebral arteries (hyperplastic anterior choroidal arteries): a case diagnosed by magnetic resonance angiography
papers.authors: Uchino A, Tsuzuki N.
papers.abstract: Abstract Purpose To describe a case of bilateral accessory posterior cerebral arteries (PCAs) incidentally diagnosed by magnetic resonance angiography (MRA). Methods A 33-year-old woman with a pituitary microadenoma underwent MRA using a 3-Tesla scanner. MRA was performed using a standard three-dimensional time-of-flight technique. Results MRA of the intracranial region revealed no pathological lesions. The right anterior choroidal artery (AChA) was hyperplastic and supplied the temporal branch of the right PCA. The left AChA was also slightly hyperplastic and supplied the hypertrophic uncal branch covering the anterior temporal branch of the left PCA. Conclusion A hyperplastic AChA that supplies a branch of the PCA is termed an accessory PCA, and three types have been described. When the entire PCA territory is supplied by a hyperplastic AChA, the artery is termed a replaced PCA. The prevalence of a hyperplastic AChA has been reported to be 2.3% on catheter angiography and 0.55% on MRA. However, to our knowledge, a type 1 accessory PCA, which supplies a hypertrophic uncal branch covering the anterior temporal branch of the PCA, has not previously been reported on MRA, and bilateral accessory PCAs have not been reported in the English-language literature. Because of the relatively low spatial resolution of MRA, small arteries such as a type 1 accessory PCA may be easily overlooked. Because numerous arteries are located around the circle of Willis, careful evaluation of volume-rendered MRA images is important for the accurate diagnosis of this vascular variation.

papers.title: Synchronized Dual-Task Training During Robot-Assisted Gait Training After Stroke: A Three-Arm Randomized Controlled Trial
papers.authors: Chen H, Qiu D, Zhao Y, Li J, Wang J, Zhang B, Li P.
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Robot-assisted gait training (RAGT) and dual-task training (DTT) each improve walking after stroke, but whether delivering dual tasks synchronously during RAGT confers additive benefit is unknown. We compared synchronized robot–dual-task training (RDT) against each component alone. Methods In this single-center, three-arm, assessor- and statistician-blinded randomized controlled trial, 99 patients with post-stroke walking dysfunction were allocated to RDT (n = 33), RAGT (n = 33), or DTT (n = 33) (after removal of one duplicate data-entry record), each added to conventional rehabilitation (20 min/day, 5 days/week, 8 weeks). The primary outcome was the Fugl-Meyer Assessment of the Lower Extremity (FMA-LE); secondary outcomes were the Berg Balance Scale (BBS), activities of daily living (ADL; Modified Barthel Index), and six-minute walk test (6MWT) categories. Between-group change scores were compared by ANCOVA adjusted for baseline values, with pairwise post hoc comparisons. Results All groups improved significantly on all outcomes (all within-group P < 0.001). FMA-LE gains were greatest with RDT (Δ14.27 ± 4.99) versus RAGT (Δ8.55 ± 2.72; adjusted mean difference 4.87, 95% CI 3.39–6.35; P = 1.1×10⁻⁸; d = 1.43) and DTT (Δ6.39 ± 2.84; adjusted mean difference 5.99, 95% CI 4.38–7.61; P = 3.8×10⁻¹⁰; d = 1.94); RAGT also exceeded DTT (adjusted mean difference 1.54, 95% CI 0.40–2.69; P = 0.009). BBS and ADL improved most with RDT (Δ21.67 and Δ31.52, respectively); all nine pairwise comparisons across outcomes were statistically significant, including ADL RDT versus RAGT (adjusted mean difference 5.33, 95% CI 1.03–9.62; P = 0.016, not surviving Bonferroni correction). Week-8 6MWT categories favored RDT (P = 0.006 vs RAGT; P < 0.001 vs DTT); 66.7% of RDT participants walked > 300 m, and none were unable to complete the test. Findings were robust in baseline-stratified analyses, in a sensitivity analysis excluding 13 over-age participants, and in an ordinal logistic regression of 6MWT categories adjusted for baseline grade. Conclusions In this completed three-arm randomized trial, synchronized dual-task training during RAGT was associated with greater improvements than dual-task training alone across all evaluated outcomes—lower-limb motor function, balance, activities of daily living, and walking endurance—and with greater improvements in FMA-LE, BBS, and ADL than robot training alone, although the ADL contrast versus RAGT was modest and did not survive Bonferroni correction. Diffusion tensor imaging correlates of these clinical gains and longer-term follow-up will be reported separately. Trial registration Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR), http//www.chictr.org.cn/ registration number ChiCTR2500115695 date of registration 29 December 2025. National Medical Research Registration and Filing Information System record MR5025090484.

papers.title: RAVEN: Representation-Aware Reliability Validation under Data Distribution Shifts
papers.authors: Nguyen PHT.
papers.abstract: Abstract Deep classifiers can remain highly confident when inputs depart from the training distribution, making output confidence an incomplete proxy for reliability. This paper introduces RAVEN (Representation-Aware Reliability Validation), a post-hoc framework that evaluates reliability under controlled distribution shifts by jointly examining prediction confidence, semantic consistency, multi-level representation instability, and representation displacement. The central question is whether internal representation instability provides information about prediction failure beyond conventional confidence. The supplied experiments use a frozen ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-18 with a lightweight trainable head across six datasets, five corruption families, and five severity levels. Severity is strongly associated with representation instability (Spearman ρ = 0.7842), while MRI is associated with prediction failure (ρ = 0.4618) and remains associated after conditioning on severity, dataset, and corruption (partial ρ = 0.2643). In mixed-effect logistic regression controlling for confidence and severity, the MRI coefficient is 1.424 (SE = 0.031), corresponding to an odds ratio of 1.153 per +0.1 MRI. The proposed RARS score reaches failure-detection AUROC 0.812, compared with 0.750 for MRI and 0.8068 for Mahalanobis. Additional evaluations report natural-shift AUROC 0.788, a five-seed pooled AUROC of 0.8121 ± 0.0059, and matched tests across ResNet, EfficientNet, DINOv2, CLIP, MAE, and Swin representations. Cross-dataset transfer yields AUROC 0.767, while cross-backbone tests retain positive gains over confidence. The results support the narrower conclusion that representation instability is a complementary reliability signal under the evaluated shifts, while the extension analyses define its empirical boundary conditions.

papers.title: Functional Dysphagia in Anorexia Nervosa After Weight Restoration: Case Report
papers.authors: Brinegar MG.
papers.abstract: Abstract Most research on dysphagia in patients with anorexia nervosa (AN) suggests it results from muscle atrophy due to low body mass index (BMI) and nutritional status. This report highlights a case of new onset dysphagia in a patient with AN after significant weight restoration. A diagnostic evaluation demonstrated mild esophageal motility issues, but with no structural abnormalities or organic disease identified. The only medical treatment recommendations were lifestyle changes (e.g., small meals, soft foods). Eventually, a mind-body conceptualization of the swallowing difficulties provided a framework for change. A mix of acceptance-based skills and dysphasia compensatory strategies led to a complete resolution of swallowing difficulties. The conceptualization of this case as being both physical and psychological is consistent with the shift in framing functional gastrointestinal disorders as disorders of gut-brain interaction per the new Rome V guidelines. Mental health providers, speech-language pathologists, and gastroenterologists could all benefit from a working knowledge of how AN and dysphagia may co-occur. Future research could clarify effective treatments.

papers.title: Impairment of mental time travel in patients with depressive disorders: Neural mechanisms and individual-level identification based on default mode network connectivity
papers.authors: Ran W, Shi Q, Pan G, Yuan Y, Zhang T, Chen G.
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Mental time travel (MTT) enables re-experiencing past and pre-experiencing future events. Impairment in MTT is a core cognitive feature of major depressive disorder (MDD), but its neural mechanisms involving default mode network (DMN) functional connectivity remain unclear. Methods Thirty-six MDD patients and 36 healthy controls (HC) completed an adapted Autobiographical Memory Test to assess MTT. Resting-state fMRI examined DMN functional connectivity. Brain–behavior correlations used Spearman rank with Holm–Bonferroni correction. A support vector machine (SVM) classifier and support vector regression (SVR) evaluated individual discriminative and predictive values of identified connectivity features. Results Patients showed significantly reduced specificity in past recall and future imagination, with lower emotional valence, field perspective, and intensity. Resting-state connectivity revealed dissociated DMN patterns: weakened right anterior supramarginal gyrus–frontal pole, left frontal pole–posterior parietal, and hippocampus–lingual/cerebellar connections; enhanced left medial prefrontal–occipital and dorsal medial prefrontal–frontal pole connections. In HC, frontoparietal connectivity correlated with visual perspective; in patients, enhanced prefrontal connectivity negatively correlated with negative valence. Machine learning achieved 94.4% accuracy (AUC = 0.971) in classifying MDD vs HC, with frontal pole connections most discriminative. DMN connectivity significantly predicted individual specificity and neutral valence. Conclusions MTT impairment in MDD reflects system-level DMN imbalance and functional reorganization, providing neural targets for interventions. High individual classification accuracy supports DMN connectivity as a potential biomarker.

papers.title: Clinical biomarkers predictive of radionecrosis in patients with brain metastases treated with stereotactic radiotherapy. A monocentric experience
papers.authors: Lolli J, Pasqualetti F, Magni G, Paiusco M, Bellu L, Satragno C, Librizzi G, Manara R, Scarzello G, Krengli M.
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Reliable biomarkers predictive of Radionecrosis (RN) associated with stereotactic radiotherapy (SRT) for brain metastases are still lacking. This retrospective study aimed to analyze clinical, radiological, and dosimetric features associated with the development of RN after upfront SRT. Materials and methods We retrospectively analyzed 53 patients with 129 brain metastases treated with SRT at the Veneto Institute of Oncology between January 2021 and December 2022. The treated lesions were monitored for a median observation time of 11.0 months (range 3.2–34.2). Depending on the lesion size, treatment was delivered in 1, 3, or 5 fractions, with mean total doses of 20 Gy, 33.75 Gy, and 36.75 Gy, respectively. Evaluated risk factors included clinical variables, radiological features (lesion site, diameter, and extent on MRI), and radiotherapy parameters such as gross tumour volume (GTV), planning target volume (PTV), and brain V12 and V20. Results RN occurred in 17 patients (32.1%), involving 20 lesions (15.5%). Larger lesion diameter on MRI contrast-enhanced T1-weighted and FLAIR sequences was significantly associated with RN (p = 0.0028 and p = 0.0011, respectively). Additionally, RN incidence was significantly associated with larger GTV (p = 0.0055), PTV (p = 0.0091), brain V12 (p = 0.0096), and brain V20 (p = 0.0144). In multivariable GEE analysis accounting for within-patient clustering, lesion diameter ≥ 8 mm remained the only independent predictor of radionecrosis (OR 4.76, 95% CI 1.08–20.95; p = 0.039). Conclusion Pretreatment lesion size on contrast-enhanced T1-weighted MRI was independently associated with the development of RN after SRT for brain metastases. Pretreatment FLAIR extension may represent an additional imaging marker of RN risk and warrants further investigation in larger prospective cohorts.

papers.title: Evidential Safety-Gated Segmentation for Robust Brain Tumor Analysis with Missing MRI Modalities
papers.authors: Garikapati S.
papers.abstract: Accurate brain tumor segmentation from multi-parametric MRI is indispensable for clinical decision-making, yet real-world deployment is persistently challenged by missing or corrupted modalities arising from scanner failures, protocol variations, and patient-specific contraindications. Existing models tend to fail silently under such conditions, propagating high-confidence but clinically incorrect predictions into downstream workflows. We present Fail-SafeAI, a safety-gated, uncertainty-driven framework that integrates evidential deep learning with a learnable clinical safety gate for reliable segmentation under modality absence. The backbone operates on the two most discriminative MRI channels — FLAIR and contrast-enhanced T1 (T1ce) — and is trained with aggressive per-channel dropout to build inherent robustness. Network outputs are parameterized as a Dirichlet distribution over four semantic classes, enabling direct epistemic uncertainty (vacuity) estimation in a single forward pass. At inference, the clinical safety gate evaluates per-slice uncertainty statistics and dynamically decides whether to accept the prediction, escalate to a radiologist, or trigger a lightweight conditional U-Net inpainter for missing channel synthesis. On BraTS 2020, Fail-SafeAI achieves a whole-tumor Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) of 0.864 under complete data and ≥0.795 under single-modality dropout, outperforming AdaMM by 7.2 percentage points under missing T1ce while reducing the Unsafe False Acceptance Rate from 5.1% to 0.2%. Uncertainty maps are demonstrably calibrated: vacuity is statistically higher for incorrect predictions than for correct ones, and the accuracy-rejection curve shows that deferring the 30% most uncertain pixels to a human expert raises retained accuracy from 68.8%

papers.title: Retinal layer structure on optical coherence tomography in post-traumatic stress disorder.
papers.authors: Patel SD, Karthik N, Justin GA, Haystead A, Chiu SJ, Stinnett SS, Johnson KG, Grewal DS, Fekrat S.
papers.abstract: Purpose To assess individual retinal layer thickness and volume changes on optical coherence tomography (OCT) in individuals with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) compared to controls. Methods Adults ≥18 years with a PTSD diagnosis were identified. Age- and sex-matched controls (±5 years) without PTSD were recruited. Exclusion criteria included any cognitive disorder, brain injury, glaucoma, diabetes, optic nerve or vitreoretinal disease, uncontrolled hypertension, refractive error >±6 diopters, or best corrected visual acuity <20/40. Non-mydriatic OCT macular cube 512x128 images were obtained using Zeiss Cirrus HD-5000 AngioPlex. The Duke Reading Center DRCVisualizer software was used to segment the ganglion cell/inner plexiform (GC-IPL), inner nuclear (INL), outer plexiform (OPL), outer nuclear (ONL), photoreceptor, and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) layers. Mean retinal thickness and volume were calculated for all layers within the central 1-mm subfield and 3- and 6-mm ETDRS rings, further divided into nasal, superior, temporal, and inferior quadrants. Results 81 eyes of 42 PTSD patients and 81 eyes of 42 controls were analyzed. Average ages were 48 ± 15 years for PTSD and 51 ± 19 years for controls. Groups were 36% male. PTSD eyes showed significantly decreased photoreceptor thickness and volume and increased RPE thickness/volume across all ETDRS rings and quadrants (all p < 0.05). OPL thicknesses were decreased in PTSD eyes versus controls for temporal 3-mm (25.29 ± 1.36 µm vs. 26.64 ± 3.80µm) and temporal 6-mm (23.47 ± 0.88µm vs. 24.00 ± 1.54µm) rings (p < 0.05). OPL inferior 6-mm thickness was decreased in PTSD eyes (23.98 ± 1.58 µm vs. 24.78 ± 2.34 µm) versus controls (p < 0.05). The ONL nasal 6-mm thickness was decreased in PTSD versus controls (55.96 ± 7.90 µm vs. 56.74 ± 7.47µm) (p < 0.05). After adjusting for multiple testing, RPE differences remained significant across all evaluated regions, while photoreceptor differences remained significant within the central 1-mm and 3-mm ETDRS regions. Conclusions PTSD eyes demonstrated decreased photoreceptor layer and increased RPE thickness and volume.

papers.title: From Target to Trial: Artificial Intelligence in Psychiatric Drug Development.
papers.authors: Olisaeloka L, Nunez JJ, Shankaraiah RC, Lam RW, Vigo DV, Yatham LN.
papers.journal: Canadian journal of psychiatry. Revue canadienne de psychiatrie
papers.abstract: Plain Language SummaryHow Artificial Intelligence Could Improve Psychiatric Drug Development Developing new medicines for mental health conditions is difficult, expensive, and often unsuccessful. One reason is that people with the same diagnosis can differ greatly in their underlying biology and in how they respond to treatment. Clinical trials also rely heavily on symptom ratings and can be affected by placebo responses. This editorial explains how artificial intelligence (AI) could help at several stages of psychiatric drug development. AI can help researchers identify promising drug targets, design new treatment molecules, and use biological, brain-imaging, and clinical data to predict treatment response and improve clinical trials. Emerging approaches include digital twins, synthetic control groups, and digital measures of symptoms and behaviour. However, these technologies are still developing and should not be viewed as a solution to all the challenges of psychiatric drug development. Wider use will require representative datasets, strong data governance, transparent and interpretable models, rigorous clinical validation, and appropriate regulation.

papers.title: Metformin Preserves Regional Brain Glucose Uptake, Structure, and Functional Connectivity in Adults with Insulin Resistance.
papers.authors: Pataky MW, Ruegsegger GN, Jo HJ, Klaus KA, Sevits KJ, Leija RG, Prabha Kumar A, Lim S, Sinhawansa S, Carter RE, Stricker NH, Lowe VJ, Port JD, Nair KS.
papers.abstract: Background Dementia is a rapidly expanding public health problem with major socio-economic burden. Insulin resistance (IR) is a prevalent but modifiable risk factor for dementia, yet its effects on brain structure, functional connectivity, and metabolism remain incompletely understood. Methods Regional brain glucose uptake (PET), volumes (MRI), functional connectivity (fMRI), and cognition (NIH Toolbox) was measured in 72 adults with or without markers of IR. To evaluate reversibility of IR-associated brain deficits, forty older adults with IR were randomized to forty weeks of metformin or placebo, and brain measures were repeated. As a proof-of-concept experiment, we developed a conditional brain-specific insulin receptor knockout mouse and assessed brain mitochondrial function and cognition. Results In older adults with markers of IR is associated with diminished total and regional brain volumes in areas critical for neuronal connectivity, memory, and learning, including cerebral white matter and the hippocampus. Reduced functional connectivity between brain regions detrimental for cognition was also noted. Further, we demonstrated that ATP production, essential for neuronal connectivity, was diminished in neuron-specific insulin receptor knockout mice accompanied by deficits in hippocampal- and prefrontal-dependent tasks. Forty weeks of metformin improved systemic insulin sensitivity concurrent to preserved brain glucose uptake, volume, and functional connectivity within specific regions central to decision-making and learning. Metformin was also associated with an improved composite measure of processing speed and working memory. Conclusion These findings highlight IR as a key regulator of brain metabolism and support the concept that insulin sensitization can prevent neurobiological deficits in older people with IR.

papers.title: Substantial evidence against sex differences in bed nucleus of the stria terminalis volume in the human brain.
papers.authors: Berry SC, Suri HK, Lisi M, Ravenhill JP, Aggleton JP, Hodgetts CJ.
papers.abstract: "The bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BNST) is a sexually dimorphic basal forebrain region" is a claim prevalent across rodent and human neuroscience research, arising from the observation that it is substantially larger in male versus female brains. Despite the pervasiveness of this claim, which may have implications for understanding sex differences in anxiety and substance use disorders, inspection of the literature reveals a complex and nuanced picture. Research on volumetric human BNST sex differences comes from a handful of mostly small-scale post-mortem studies and two MRI studies, between them reporting no, moderate, or very large differences. This indicates the need for a more detailed systematic investigation. Addressing this, we developed a novel 3T T1-weighted (T1w) manual segmentation protocol for the BNST, which was applied to sub-millimetre resolution T1w structural MRI data in 170 young human adults. Using a Bayesian modelling approach, taking into account existing data and accounting for total brain volume, age, and sibship, we find substantial evidence favouring no sex difference in total BNST volume. We recommend that researchers exercise caution when reporting evidence of BNST sexual dimorphism, particularly when translating findings from rodent models in which the BNST may play a different, olfaction-focused, role.
keywords: Bed Nucleus Of The Stria Terminalis

papers.title: A generative framework for estimating brain energy landscapes from continuous neuroimaging observations.
papers.authors: Jeong SO, Kim E, Kang J, Eo J, Lee D, Park HJ.
papers.abstract: Pairwise maximum entropy models (pMEMs) are gaining increasing attention as a principled way to study nonlinear brain-state transitions. By representing each brain region as a binary active/inactive state and estimating the least-biased probability distribution over all such network configurations, pMEMs reconstruct an energy landscape in which local minima correspond to stable or metastable brain states and transitions reflect movement across attractor basins. However, neuroimaging recordings are continuous and spatially mixed, forcing conventional pMEM analyses to demean and hard-threshold each channel. This ad hoc binarization discards amplitude information and can conflate spatially correlated noise or source mixing with genuine neural coupling. We introduce a hierarchical generative pMEM that links latent binary network states to continuous observations. Node-specific baseline and gain parameters model amplitude modulation, compound-symmetry noise captures shared residual covariance, and, for electroencephalography/magnetoencephalography (EEG/MEG), the electromagnetic leadfield is included as a generative forward model rather than a preprocessing inverse. Model parameters and latent states are jointly estimated using exact posterior enumeration for the small networks analyzed here and a mean-field extension for larger networks. Controlled simulations demonstrated two complementary advantages of the proposed framework. Residual-covariance modeling improved recovery of pMEM fields, couplings, and latent states by accounting for shared fluctuations, with the clearest gains when residual spatial correlation was sufficiently strong. The generative leadfield model further improved sensor-space inference by avoiding inverse-first source reconstruction, including settings in which covariance modeling alone offered limited gains. Resting-state EEG validation showed higher residual correlation during eyes-closed than eyes-open rest, consistent with elevated and spatially coherent alpha activity. Applied further to propofol sedation EEG (alpha-band amplitude envelopes, 8-13 Hz), the fitted 6-node default mode network (DMN) model showed pipeline-dependent condition effects in residual spatial correlation and basin entropy, not apparent under the conventional demean-based pMEM.

papers.title: Longitudinal quantitative streamline tractography: Robust estimation of white matter connectivity differences.
papers.authors: Pruckner P, Mito R, Vaughan DN, Schilling KG, Morgan VL, Englot DJ, Smith RE.
papers.abstract: Longitudinal probing of structural connectivity via diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (dMRI) is experiencing uptake. However, the detection of biological effects is significantly hampered by the limitations of cross-sectional streamline tractography, where even small changes in the dMRI signal can produce drastically different trajectories and, therefore, quantitative parameterisation; if not properly dealt with, such effects will manifest as spurious longitudinal change, which can obscure subtle biological differences. To address this challenge, we here introduce a novel quantitative streamline tractography framework tailored for longitudinal analysis, wherein an individual's streamline trajectories remain fixed throughout the analysis, allowing only their ascribed density weights to vary between sessions. We present two strategies by which these quantitative streamline weights can be determined, both extensions of the widely adopted SIFT2 method. The performance of this framework is benchmarked against cross-sectional reconstruction with and without SIFT2 optimisation, in both in silico dMRI phantoms with known ground truths and three distinct human in vivo cohorts with clear a priori expectations of biological effects. We demonstrate that the proposed framework drastically reduces methodological imprecisions in synthetic dMRI phantoms and enhances statistical sensitivity and specificity to biological effects in human cohorts, enabling more robust quantification of longitudinal structural connectivity differences.

papers.title: Bayesian brain mapping: A population-informed framework for personalized functional network topography and connectivity.
papers.authors: Derman D, Silva Sanchez ND, Rutherford S, Pham DD, Butler ER, Nebel MB, Mejia AF.
papers.abstract: The spatial topography of functional brain organization is increasingly recognized to play an important role in cognition and disease. Accounting for individual differences in functional topography is also crucial for accurately distinguishing spatial and temporal aspects of functional brain connectivity. Yet, accurate estimation of personalized functional brain networks from functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) without extensive scanning remains challenging due to high noise levels. Here, we describe Bayesian Brain Mapping (BBM), a technique for personalized functional topography and connectivity informed by population information. BBM relies on population-derived priors on both spatial topography of networks and between-network functional connectivity to guide subject-level estimation and combat noise. These priors are based on existing spatial templates, such as parcellations or continuous network maps, providing correspondence to those templates. Yet BBM is highly flexible, avoiding strong spatial or temporal constraints and allowing for overlap between networks and heterogeneous patterns of engagement. BBM is designed for single-subject analysis, making it computationally efficient and translatable to clinical settings. Here, we describe the BBM model and illustrate the use of the BayesBrainMap R package to construct population-derived priors, fit the model, and perform inference to identify engagements. A demo is provided in an accompanying Github repo. We also share priors derived from the Human Connectome Project and provide code to support the construction of priors from different data sources, lowering the barrier to adoption of BBM for studies of individual brain organization.

papers.title: Hemisphere fingerprinting: Identifying left and right hemispheres using functional connectivity.
papers.authors: Day TKM, Turkeltaub PE, Newport EL, DeMarco AT.
papers.abstract: Many studies have analyzed what organizational features distinguish the left and right hemispheres of the human brain, with differences typically being found in language areas and in fine motor control (i.e., handedness). In this analysis, we test whether supervised learning can categorize ("fingerprint") an unseen hemisphere as right or left based on functional connectivity. Using data from the Human Connectome Project, we find success to be extremely high (accuracies > .90) in models trained on right-handed participants (Edinburgh Handedness Inventory [EHI] > 0) and in models trained on left-handed participants (EHI ≤ 0). In a second analysis, we test whether the same can be done to identify handedness alongside hemisphere left/right sidedness. While individuals' hemispheres are less distinct the more left handed they are, hemiconnectomes cannot be reliably classified as belonging to a left- or right-handed person. Our approach can inform developmental and post-injury work on hemispheric organization and reorganization.

papers.title: Age-Adjusted Exploratory Analysis of Spectral, Aperiodic, and Microstate EEG Features in Multiple Sclerosis.
papers.authors: Ren Y, Bi Y, Wang Y, Gong L, Li P, Kong L, Guo Y.
papers.abstract: Background Electroencephalography (EEG) can characterize functional brain alterations in multiple sclerosis (MS), but many EEG features vary with age. We therefore examined resting-state EEG associations with MS using age-adjusted models while explicitly accounting for the severe age imbalance in the available dataset. Methods Resting-state 128-channel EEG data from the BrainLat dataset were analyzed. Demographic files included 32 patients with MS and 32 healthy controls (HC); global-feature models included 29 patients with MS and 32 HC, and channel-level sample sizes varied by feature. Diagnosis and age were entered in linear models. Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction was applied separately to five global spectral/aperiodic tests, 16 global microstate tests, and the 128 channel-wise tests within each feature. Within-MS continuous age regression and exploratory age-stratified ANOVA were evaluated with the same family definitions. Results After correction, diagnosis coefficients were significant for global bandwidth (β = 1.928, q = 0.0287), global aperiodic offset (β = 1.816, q = 3.29 × 10⁻⁷), and offset at all 128 channels (β range = 1.52-2.41; q range = 3.56 × 10⁻⁸ to 7.43 × 10⁻⁵). Global central frequency, exponent, PSD, and all 16 microstate measures did not survive FDR correction. No within-MS continuous-age or age-stratified result survived FDR correction. Conclusions Aperiodic offset showed the strongest diagnosis association under the specified age-adjusted model. However, the MS and HC age ranges did not overlap (21-55 vs 56-83 years), so the diagnosis coefficient depends on extrapolation and cannot establish an MS-specific effect. The findings are exploratory and require age-matched replication with detailed clinical, vigilance, site, sex, and MRI characterization.

papers.title: Annual Research Review: A probe into sensitive periods - how the developmental timing of adverse childhood experiences influences brain structure and function - a systematic review.
papers.authors: Hartanto S, Rakesh D, Orr C, Forlano E, Khetan M, Whittle S.
papers.journal: Journal of child psychology and psychiatry, and allied disciplines
papers.abstract: It is proposed that adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) - potent predictors of mental illness - exert time-dependent effects on neurodevelopment, reflecting periods of heightened neuroplasticity and developmental sensitivity. We systematically reviewed neuroimaging studies examining the role of timing in the association of ACE exposure with brain structure and function across the lifespan. Across 43 studies spanning childhood to adulthood, findings most consistently implicate earlier onset and longer duration of adversity in alterations to limbic and paralimbic regions, including the hippocampus, amygdala, cerebellum and global brain measures. However, evidence for discrete sensitive periods is mixed and varies by brain system, outcome and analytic approach, with no consistent pattern of sensitive periods emerging across adversity types and functional neuroimaging studies remaining comparatively limited. Progress in the field is further constrained by substantial conceptual and methodological heterogeneity, including inconsistent operationalisation of sensitive periods, reliance on retrospective ACE measures and predominantly cross-sectional designs. Moving forward, we argue that advancing the field will require reconceptualising sensitive periods as probabilistic, system-specific and shaped by the nature, timing and chronicity of adversity, rather than as fixed developmental windows. Integrating longitudinal assessment of adversity and neurodevelopment with measures of the neurobiological processes underlying plasticity may help determine whether sensitive periods are better characterised by underlying neuroplasticity than chronological age alone. Improved understanding of these developmental processes may ultimately help inform the timing and targeting of preventive and therapeutic interventions for young people exposed to adversity.

papers.title: Motor-based interventions for brain structure and function in children with developmental coordination disorder: A systematic review.
Efficacy of a motor speech intervention in children with cerebral palsy: A randomized controlled trial.
papers.authors: Fiori S, Ragoni C, Podda I, Festante F, Puliti D, Scaffei E, De Masi S, Chilosi AM, Sgandurra G.
papers.abstract: Aim To evaluate the effects of an intensive motor speech intervention based on Motor Speech Intervention-Prompts for Restructuring Oral Muscular Phonetic Targets (MSI-PROMPT) on speech and perceived intelligibility in children with cerebral palsy (CP) aged 3 to 10 years. Method This was a waiting list-control randomized parallel clinical trial. Participants were randomized to a 3-week MSI-PROMPT programme or waitlisted to standard care (WL-SC). Primary outcomes were the Intelligibility in Context Scale, the Viking Speech Scale (VSS), and the Phonetic Inventory. After the intervention, group comparisons were performed using analysis of covariance, adjusting for baseline scores, age, and sex; results were reported as the adjusted mean difference (AMD) and 95% confidence interval (CI). Interactions with baseline severity were explored using simple-effect analyses. Results Sixty children (30 MSI-PROMPT, 30 WL-SC; n = 20 females; mean age 5 years 3 months, SD = 2 years 2 months; range = 3 years 0 months-9 years 11 months) completed the trial. After the intervention, the MSI-PROMPT group showed significantly greater improvements than the WL-SC group in Intelligibility in Context Scale (AMD = 0.38; 95% CI = 0.23-0.53, p < 0.001), VSS (AMD = -0.31; 95% CI = -0.50 to -0.12; p = 0.002), and Phonetic Inventory (AMD = 1.21; 95% CI = 0.60-1.81; p < 0.001). VSS gains were larger in children with higher baseline severity (VSS = 3: AMD = -0.35, p = 0.001; VSS = 4: AMD = -0.64, p = 0.002). Exploratory within-group analysis in the MSI-PROMPT group suggested that observed gains were maintained at the 3-month follow-up. Interpretation Intensive MSI-PROMPT significantly improved perceived intelligibility and speech skills in children with CP compared to standard care. Follow-up observations at 3 months suggested potential stability of gains, although these within-group findings remain exploratory because of the lack of a parallel control group. Exploratory analyses also suggested that treatment effects may vary according to baseline severity, supporting further investigation of individualized intervention planning.

papers.title: Amygdala vulnerability in Pick disease with discrete frontotemporal dementia syndromes.
papers.authors: Keszycki R, Kawles A, Minogue G, Zouridakis A, Macomber A, Nelson C, Mao Q, Castellani RJ, Jamshidi P, Gill N, Weintraub S, Mesulam MM, Geula C, Gefen T.
papers.abstract: Frontotemporal lobar degeneration with tauopathy (FTLD-tau) typically manifests as either behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD) or primary progressive aphasia (PPA). Tau pathology in FTLD-tau is characterized by predominantly three-repeat (3R) tau, as in Pick disease (PiD), or four-repeat (4R) tau species of corticobasal degeneration (CBD) and progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP). FTLD-tau preferentially targets frontal and anterior temporal lobes, including the amygdala, contributing to severe neuropsychiatric symptoms. This study investigated whether bvFTD and PPA due to FTLD-tau exhibit distinct amygdalar histopathology and whether these patterns reflect their initially distinct clinical phenotypes, particularly in PiD. We examined 47 autopsy-confirmed FTLD-tau cases from the Northwestern Alzheimer's Disease Research Center Brain Bank using postmortem digital pathology analysis to quantify tau phosphorylation and HLA-DR immunoreactivity in the amygdala. In a subset of 19 PiD cases (10 bvFTD-PiD, 9 PPA-PiD), we assessed neuropsychiatric symptoms, tracked longitudinally using the Neuropsychiatric Inventory-Questionnaire (NPI-Q), and quantified neuronal and Pick body densities via unbiased stereology and neuronal sizes via digital pathology analysis. Across the FTLD-tau cohort, bvFTD exhibited greater amygdalar neuroinflammation than PPA, despite comparable tau burden. Interestingly, 3R cases also demonstrated higher levels of phosphorylated tau and MHC-II-positive microglia than 4R cases. In PiD, neuropsychiatric symptoms converged over time, with PPA cases evolving to show bvFTD-like symptoms with disease progression. BvFTD-PiD showed a trend toward greater MHC-II-positive microglia than PPA-PiD, despite similar neuronal size/density and Pick body burden. Increased HLA-DR immunoreactivity correlated positively with Pick body pathology. Neurons containing tau pathology (Pick cells) were notably larger than unaffected neurons, suggesting that early tau accumulation precedes overt neuronal degeneration. These findings underscore the potential role of neuroinflammation in shaping clinical phenotypes in FTLD and highlight the role of the amygdala in complex clinicopathologic relationships. Targeting neuroinflammatory processes may represent a viable therapeutic avenue for managing neuropsychiatric symptoms in tauopathies.

papers.title: First Experience With a New Active Bone Conduction Device in Pediatric Patients.
papers.authors: Prenzler N, Higgins M, Lenarz T, Maier H, Ghoncheh M, Busch S.
papers.journal: Otology & neurotology : official publication of the American Otological Society, American Neurotology Society [and] European Academy of Otology and Neurotology
papers.abstract: Objective The aim of this retrospective analysis was to evaluate the feasibility, surgical safety, and early audiological benefit of the new active transcutaneous bone conduction implant Sentio in pediatric patients. Design Retrospective case series. Study sample Seven children (8 ears), aged 3.6 to 9.7 years, underwent implantation of a Sentio system between December 2024 and March 2025 for congenital aural atresia (6 ears) or single-sided deafness due to cochlear nerve aplasia (2 ears). Results All surgeries were completed successfully using the Sentio Ti Implant. Limited exposure of the dura, sigmoid sinus, and/or mastoid air cells occurred during bone-bed preparation, but there was no laceration, bleeding, cerebrospinal fluid leak, compression, or clinical sequela. No perioperative or postoperative adverse events occurred through initial fitting. Bone conduction thresholds remained stable postoperatively, confirming preservation of cochlear reserve. Mean Sentio-aided free-field thresholds were 22.5, 20.0, 18.6, and 18.6 dB HL at 0.5, 1, 2, and 4 kHz, respectively. Word recognition scores at initial fitting averaged 96.3% in all patients (range: 85-100%) at a conversational level of 65 dB SPL. The relatively flat transducer and flexible band fixation facilitated safe implantation in young children with thin cranial bone. Conclusion Sentio Ti implantation was technically feasible in this selected cohort, with no clinical adverse events through initial fitting and favorable early aided outcomes. Larger prospective studies with standardized testing and longer follow-up are required to assess long-term safety, skull growth, implant stability, MRI-related limitations, and sustained benefit.

papers.title: Quantitative Measurement of White Matter Hyperintensities in Brain MRI using a Multimodal Boundary-Aware Dual-Task Segmentation Framework.
papers.authors: Yao S, Zhang Y, Wang L, Huang C, Liu J.
papers.abstract: White matter hyperintensity (WMH) subtype segmentation in brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) remains challenging due to heterogeneous lesion sizes, indistinct boundaries, and severe class imbalance. We propose a multimodal boundary-aware dual-task U-Net for segmenting periventricular (PVWMH), deep (DWMH), and subcortical (SWMH) lesions. The framework integrates FLAIR-T1-weighted feature fusion, Vision Mamba-based feature modeling, an SWMH-specific boundary loss, and auxiliary boundary detection. The method was evaluated using patient-level five-fold cross-validation on a private multicenter cohort (n = 75) and separately on 60 publicly annotated MICCAI WMH Challenge subjects for binary segmentation. On the private cohort, the proposed framework achieved an overall Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 0.6081 and a 95th-percentile Hausdorff distance (HD95) of 14.80 mm, compared with 0.5638 and 18.25 mm for the FLAIR-only ablation baseline. It also improved SWMH DSC from 0.4610 with nnU-Net to 0.5215 (p = 0.008). On the public dataset, the mean binary DSC and HD95 were 0.6812 and 12.91 mm, respectively.Given the relatively large through-plane voxel spacing (8.4 mm), the framework processes 2D axial slices independently and does not explicitly model inter-slice context, which may limit its ability to characterize lesions extending across adjacent slices.

papers.title: Combined voltammetry and optical brain imaging: toward high resolution neurochemical measurements.
papers.authors: Zavialov V, Tsytsarev V, Volnova AB, Gainetdinov RR, Inyushin M.
papers.abstract: The question of the mechanisms by which cellular interactions in the brain are converted into integrative behavioral phenomena is closely related to functional localization, and also to the relationship between spatial and temporal resolution when interpreting experimental data. Classical electrophysiology is usually limited in its ability to display information about the functioning of neural circuits with sufficient spatial resolution, although the temporal resolution is almost always very high. Other modern methods for recording the functional characteristics of neural activity in the brain vary considerably in spatial and temporal resolution. Voltammetry is one of the key instrumental methods used in neurobiology to measure neurotransmitter release and dynamicsin vivo . It is similar to electrophysiology in terms of temporal resolution, but spatial resolution remains low. This method records changes in the concentration of chemicals, typically neurotransmitters, in the brain's extracellular environment with sufficient temporal resolution to capture release peaks. However, as this monitoring is performed at a single location or target, the technique does not provide information about the spatial distribution of the recorded signal characteristics. Various techniques for functional optical imaging of brain structure and activity offer relatively high spatial resolution, often accompanied by adequate temporal resolution. Some of these methods are suitable for visualizing neural activity in both 2D and 3D. However, while functional brain imaging allows areas of neural activity to be identified, it typically does not provide quantitative information about changes in the concentration levels of specific molecules. A significant challenge would be to combine the key advantages of voltammetry and functional optical brain imaging, i.e. to obtain continuous quantitative information on the concentration of neurochemically active molecules across many areas of the investigated brain region with sufficiently high temporal and spatial resolution. This review discusses the current state of voltammetry and functional optical brain imaging techniques, as well as the hypothetical possibilities for combining them based on the experimental data obtained to date.

papers.title: Communication breakdown: Impaired pericyte KATP channels in a model of Alzheimer's disease.
papers.authors: Jackson WF.
papers.abstract: The brain requires a continuous supply of blood in proportion to its metabolic activity, a process that is disrupted in Alzheimer's disease. However, the mechanisms responsible for altered brain blood flow regulation in Alzheimer's disease remain poorly defined. In an earlier issue of JGP, Hariharan et al. (https://doi.org/10.1085/jgp.202614014) significantly add to our understanding of this pathology by showing that ATP-Sensitive K+ (KATP) channels in thin strand pericytes on cerebral capillaries are compromised at 6-8 weeks in the 5X-FAD mouse model of Alzheimer's disease. They also confirmed that cerebral capillary endothelial inward rectifier K+ (KIR) channels are crippled and importantly show that this defect occurs at 2-4 months, before significant cognitive defects have been reported. Combined, these channelopathies severely attenuate electrical communication along cerebral capillaries, dampening blood flow regulation. These novel findings present new therapeutic targets to slow or possibly prevent the reduced cerebral blood flow in Alzheimer's disease, perhaps delaying or preventing cognitive decline. Like all scientific advances, they also open the door for new areas of research.

papers.title: Perspectives on traumatic brain injury screening among intersecting underserved populations: an exploratory study.
papers.authors: Hanafy S, Estrella MJ, Colantonio A, Haag HL, Matheson FI, Omar S, Odorico N, Yin J, Bayley M, Hwang SW, Panenka W, Wiseman-Hakes C, Cullen N, Balogh R, Yadollahi A, Chan V.
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aimed to explore barriers and facilitators in traumatic brain injury (TBI) screening for underserved individuals and knowledge translation efforts to address challenges. Materials and methods Guided by qualitative description, we conducted four virtual focus groups: 10 people (7 female, 3 male) with lived experience of precarious housing, criminal legal involvement, and/or violence and 11 service providers (9 female, 2 male) supporting these populations with TBI. Data were analyzed using thematic analysis. Findings Barriers to TBI screening included (1) inconsistent implementation and competing priorities within organizations; (2) stigmatization and systemic challenges in service provision; and (3) a lack of a universal screening system and follow-up pathways. While potential facilitators to screening involved language, knowledge and resources, as identified in the following themes: (1) language matters: shaping conversations in TBI screening; (2) screening for all: knowledge and access; and (3) easy and engaging tools for screening. Conclusions Barriers to TBI screening persist. Systemic changes and targeted educational initiatives are needed to improve knowledge and awareness of TBI with sensitivity to potential circumstances of specific populations. Affirming conversational language in screening, along with providing tailored resources and access to follow-up support services that address social determinants of health, are essential.

papers.title: Calcium permeability-enhancing mutations in GluRIIC suppress sustained presynaptic homeostatic plasticity triggered by loss of GluRIIA.
papers.authors: Malak OA, Gray L, Aly A, Ball RW, Gustin-Murray J, Moujahidine M, Carrasco G, Rosko A, Isacoff EY, Haghighi AP.
papers.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
papers.abstract: Presynaptic homeostatic plasticity (PHP) stabilizes neural circuits by adjusting synaptic strength when faced with disturbances in postsynaptic activity. Despite identification of many genes and mechanisms required for PHP, the underlying trigger mechanisms remain elusive. Loss of GluRIIA, one of five glutamate receptor subunits at the Drosophila neuromuscular junction (NMJ), reduces quantal size and synaptic calcium influx and triggers a sustained PHP. Two common features of genetic manipulations that lead to the activation of this form of PHP are a drop in synaptic calcium influx and a reduction in quantal size; however, it is not clear that either of these features is absolutely necessary for PHP. We have generated a glutamate receptor transgene with mutations in the pore, which can largely restore calcium influx in GluRIIA-/- mutant larvae without affecting quantal size. We find that restoration of calcium influx in GluRIIA-/- mutant larvae blocks PHP without any detectable changes in synaptic structure. Our findings, therefore, indicate that a reduction in synaptic calcium influx is necessary for triggering and/or maintenance of the sustained PHP at the NMJ, a model that may be extendable to the vertebrate NMJ and neuron-neuron synapses.

papers.title: Stress-inducible WASF3 regulates brain metabolism and cognitive function.
papers.authors: Syed AM, Ma J, Wang PY, Son Y, Penjweini R, Mattu N, Knutson JR, Nakamori-Yamashita S, Springer DA, Ganguly A, Liu C, Hwang PM.
papers.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
papers.abstract: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein family member 3 (WASF3) disrupts mitochondrial respiration and is induced in association with endoplasmic reticulum stress in myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS). Because cognitive impairment is a hallmark of ME/CFS, we investigated the role of WASF3 in brain metabolism and function using WASF3 transgenic and knockout mouse models. WASF3 disrupted respiratory complex IV and localized to mitochondria-associated membranes, known to modulate cellular processes important for neuronal activity. Overexpression of WASF3 in the hippocampus, a critical region for memory formation, induced a metabolic shift toward glycolysis and promoted a "hypometabolic" state. Increased WASF3 also caused a reduction in ATPIF1, previously shown to facilitate cognitive function, and impaired learning. Conversely, WASF3 deficiency increased ATPIF1 level, enhanced oxidative metabolism, and preserved cognitive function under stress. Together, these findings demonstrate that WASF3 suppresses oxidative metabolism in the brain and contributes to cognitive dysfunction, providing mechanistic insights into the "brain fog" reported in ME/CFS.

papers.title: Neuromodulation-inspired gated associative memory networks: Extended memory retrieval and emergent multistability.
papers.authors: Goto D, Lopez Rios HM, Scholz M, Vaikuntanathan S.
papers.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
papers.abstract: Classical autoassociative memory models have been central to understanding emergent computations in recurrent neural circuits across diverse biological contexts. However, they typically neglect neuromodulatory agents that are known to strongly shape memory capacity and stability. Here we introduce a minimal, biophysically motivated associative memory network in which neuromodulator-like signals are modeled by a self-adaptive, activity-dependent gating mechanism. Using many-body simulations and dynamical mean-field theory, we show that such gating fundamentally reorganizes the attractor structure: the network bypasses the classical spin-glass transition, maintaining robust, high-overlap retrieval far beyond the standard critical capacity. Mechanistically, when the gates act as fully open or fully closed switches, the gate stabilizes transient "ghost" remnants of stored patterns even far above the Hopfield limit, converting a single memory fixed-point attractor into a cluster of fixed points. The retrieved state is set by the initial overlap rather than quantized to the stored pattern. This graded dependence may be exploited for input-driven computation with persistent activity. These results establish that neuromodulation-like gating alone-without modifying synaptic weights or introducing explicit higher-order couplings-can dramatically expand memory capacity, eliminate catastrophic breakdown, and reshape a discrete attractor landscape into a rich continuum, suggesting a general and biologically accessible route to enhanced computational capabilities in neural circuits and neuromorphic architectures.

papers.title: Intraventricular clindamycin enhances interstitial brain fluid drainage and the blood-brain barrier after a traumatic brain injury.
papers.authors: Ashby LS, Crowe MG, Chakravarty D, Medam S, Frampton G, Das AB, Hormuth DA, Yankeelov TE, Wang VYC, Noble-Haeusslein LJ, Umlauf BJ.
papers.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
papers.abstract: Despite advances in the acute clinical management of severe traumatic brain injuries (TBIs), treating injury-derived secondary pathogenesis remains challenging. We demonstrate intracerebroventricular (I.C.V.) administration of clindamycin alleviates TBI secondary pathogenesis in both focal and diffuse murine models of brain injury. I.C.V. administration of clindamycin increased the motility of ependymal cilia, which line the ventricles and spinal canal, by 30 to 60%, which correlated with interstitial brain fluid drainage through the cortex (r > 0.9 Pearson, n = 4 compounds tested). I.C.V. clindamycin treatment post-TBI also restored the blood-brain barrier (BBB), decreased lesion size, and lowered serum levels of glial fibrillary acidic protein by 2.8-fold. Consistent with these data, a novel objective recognition test revealed an improvement in recognition memory in brain-injured mice treated with clindamycin. These collective findings reveal a counterintuitive finding that I.C.V. clindamycin enhances drainage of toxins from the brain while simultaneously restoring the BBB, potentially providing a new solution for alleviating secondary pathogenesis in brain-injured patients.

papers.title: White matter fiber bundles enable robust conduction and time-critical signaling despite axon caliber variation.
papers.authors: Mordhorst L, Weiskopf N, Morawski M, Mohammadi S.
papers.abstract: Axon caliber determines signal conduction velocity and varies within and across the bundles that form the brain's wiring. Our knowledge of this organization derives largely from 2D histology, assuming cylindrical axons whose calibers are described by their radius. However, recent 3D histology reveals substantial along-axon variability in radius, calling into question 2D-derived insights into axon radius and conduction velocity. We show in 450,000 3D axon reconstructions from male rats that-despite this individual variation-axon bundles possess stable radius distributions at the ensemble level. These distributions are faithfully captured by 2D cross-sections and yield robust conduction velocity predictions, as along-axon variability has only a modest effect. Conduction in large axons is particularly stable, supporting time-critical signaling. With 2D sampling validated, we leverage 46 million human corpus callosum axons from 2D histology to determine sample size requirements across neuroscience applications. Our findings show how axonal organization gives rise to stable ensemble statistics and conduction, explaining and reinforcing decades of 2D histology-based research.

papers.title: A NEST-based framework unlocks massively parallel simulation of networks of multi-compartment neurons with customizable subcellular dynamics.
papers.authors: Wybo WAM, Ewert L, Linssen C, Babu P, Pastorelli E, Paolucci PS, Morrison A.
papers.abstract: While subcellular mechanisms in the dendrites of neurons govern the implementation of learning and memory in the brain, large-scale network simulations featuring such processes remain challenging to achieve. This can be attributed to a lack of appropriate software tools, as neuroscientific simulators focus on the one hand on highly detailed models, and on the other hand on massive networks featuring point neurons. Here, we fill this gap by implementing a framework for the massively parallel simulation of simplified dendrite models with customizable subcellular dynamics. We leverage the NEural Simulation Tool (NEST), the neuroscientific reference with respect to efficient massively parallel simulations of point-neuron networks. By co-opting the model description language NESTML, we generate C++ code implementing user-configurable subcellular dynamics. We show that the generated models run efficiently, leading to scalable NEST network simulations. To showcase relevant functionalities, we provide a proof-of-concept demonstration that a key sensory computation - the association of top-down context arriving at distal dendrites in layer 1 and feedforward sensory input arriving perisomatically - can be achieved in a single-shot fashion through apical calcium dynamics. Our work thus unlocks the study of how dendritic processes shape network function and learning at scale.

papers.title: Stimulus-specific recruitment of human amygdala neurons predicts episodic memory encoding success.
papers.authors: Xiao J, Daume J, Salimpour Y, Kurilenko N, Mosher C, Anderson WS, Valiante TA, Mamelak AN, Rutishauser U.
papers.abstract: Controlling whether an experience is encoded into long-term memory and thus later remembered is a crucial aspect of memory. Here we examined single-neuron activity in the human brain while participants formed memories for novel visual stimuli and later retrieved them with confidence ratings. Category-selective amygdala neurons exhibited elevated firing during encoding of later remembered items relative to later forgotten items. This effect was predictive of the episodic aspect of the memory, was restricted to the preferred category of each cell, emerged earlier and was stronger in the amygdala compared to the hippocampus, and did not depend on stimulus valence and arousal. Successful memory formation was accompanied by enhanced spike-field coherence between the activity of amygdala category cells and hippocampal field potentials. These findings demonstrate that stimulus-specific recruitment of the amygdala predicts memory formation and suggest category cells in the right amygdala as a target for interventions to treat disorders affecting episodic memory in humans.

papers.title: Circuit mechanisms for disentangled representations and generalization in the hippocampus.
papers.authors: Tang W, Chang H, Liu C, Perez-Hernandez S, Zheng WY, Park J, Karaba LA, Oliva A, Fernandez-Ruiz A.
papers.abstract: Understanding how the heterogeneous activity patterns of individual neurons give rise to coherent population dynamics and cognition is a central challenge in neuroscience. In the hippocampus, neurons are tuned to spatial location, yet their activity is also modulated by multiple external and internal variables and appears to drift randomly over time, making it difficult to link hippocampal computations to behavior. By analyzing hippocampal population dynamics in behaving mice, we reveal a structured organization underlying the diversity of single-neuron responses-the hippocampus encodes different aspects of experience as disentangled variables represented in the co-activity dynamics of cell assemblies. The temporal and contextual components of these representations are governed by local inhibitory interactions and input-driven cell-assembly dynamics, respectively. Our findings reveal the circuit basis of disentangled hippocampal representations, offering a unifying geometric principle of population coding that supports flexible memory representations and enables rapid generalization of prior knowledge to new situations.

papers.title: Mysterious flickering brain signals could help to unlock secrets of consciousness.
papers.authors: Lenharo M.

papers.title: Ultrasound-assisted formation of red rice bran fiber-anthocyanin complexes: Improved bioaccessibility and color stability.
papers.authors: Ahmed Z, Manzoor MF, Farooq U, Zhou Y, Aït-Kaddour A, Sheng T, Chen C, Aadil RM, El-Din Ibrahim ME.
papers.abstract: This study investigates the interactive mechanisms between ultrasound-treated red rice bran dietary fiber (URBDF) and anthocyanins to improve their physicochemical stability, bioaccessibility, and structural integrity via ultrasound treatment (300 W, 50 °C, liquid-to-solid ratio 30:1, 40 min). Ultrasound treatment increased the fiber's porosity and specific surface area, which significantly enhanced its adsorption capacity toward anthocyanins (42.54 ± 0.87 mg/g). Optimal adsorption conditions (pH 5, 37 °C, 95 min, anthocyanin concentration 3 mg/mL) yielded stable URBDF + RBA complexes with improved functional performance, as proved by spectroscopic and microscopic analyses. The hydrogen bonding and hydrophobic interactions were the dominant non-covalent forces mediating URBDF + RBA association and interactions effectively, which inhibited anthocyanin degradation and crystallization, resulting in markedly enhanced thermal and environmental stability. The anthocyanin retention up to 94.3 % under stress conditions induced structural modification of ultrasound treatment, reduced the particle size and increased the surface roughness and hydrophilicity of the fiber. The results on microstructure, rheological properties, water-holding, oil-binding, swelling capacities, and simulated gastrointestinal digestion demonstrated that URBDF binding substantially improved antioxidant activity and bioaccessibility as compared to untreated samples. Cell experiments showed that RBDF, URBDF, RBDF + anthocyanin and URBDF + anthocyanin had different degrees of proliferative effects on L-02 and RAW264.7. This work provides mechanistic insight into ultrasound-assisted red rice bran by-products and dietary fiber modification as a sustainable strategy for stabilizing anthocyanins. The findings establish a foundation for developing novel fiber anthocyanin complexes with improved stability and functionality for applications in natural systems, functional foods and nutraceuticals.
