papers.title: Lysosomal biophysics in CLN3 disease: Connecting membrane transport, molecular homeostasis, and tissue dysfunction.
papers.authors: Al Abdulsalam NK, Hamad RS, Elmorsy EA, Saber S.
papers.journal: Progress in biophysics and molecular biology
papers.abstract: CLN3 disease (CLN3 Batten disease) is a lysosomal neurodegenerative disorder characterized by early retinal degeneration and progressive neurological dysfunction, yet the mechanisms connecting CLN3-dependent membrane physiology to selective cellular and tissue vulnerability remain unresolved. This review integrates current evidence across four experimentally separable scales: membrane biophysics, molecular and organellar homeostasis, cell-specific function, and tissue pathology. Direct electrophysiological studies support a luminal pH-sensitive CLN3-dependent lysosomal chloride conductance associated, in tested systems, with changes in luminal chloride, pH, cathepsin activity, and protein degradation. Independently, CLN3 deficiency disrupts glycerophosphodiester clearance, phospholipid and cholesterol handling, cation-independent mannose 6-phosphate receptor trafficking, hydrolase delivery, and autophagic lysosomal reformation. These organellar abnormalities coexist with distinct phenotypes in retinal pigment epithelium, neurons, microglia, astrocytes, and brain endothelial cells, together with retinal, neural-circuit, and myelin abnormalities at the tissue level. Current evidence does not establish a universal chloride-first or storage-first cascade; instead, it supports interacting CLN3-dependent modules whose causal ordering may vary by cell type, model, and disease stage. We therefore propose a multiscale mechanistic framework that links measurable lysosomal physical variables to molecular homeostasis, cell-specific function, and tissue vulnerability while preserving the distinction between direct evidence and mechanistic inference. This framework defines testable priorities for causal ordering, rescue experiments, and mechanism-matched target engagement in CLN3 disease.

papers.title: Visuospatial attention modulates audiovisual temporal perception: Context-dependent associations between prestimulus alpha lateralization and perceptual reports.
papers.authors: Jiang Z, Zhao Y, Ren W, Zhang J, Liu X, Yu F, An X, Zhong W, Wu D, Zhang P, Zhang Z.
papers.abstract: Audiovisual temporal perception depends on the timing of sensory events and on preparatory attention. We examined how visuospatial cueing affects explicit synchrony judgments and sound-induced flash illusions, and how prestimulus EEG relates to these perceptual reports. In Experiment 1 (N = 39), participants judged beep-flash synchrony across auditory- and visual-leading stimulus onset asynchronies (SOAs). In Experiment 2 (N = 36), they reported flashes in fusion and fission conditions across SOAs and corresponding references. Experiment 1 showed a Cue validity × SOA interaction, with more synchrony reports on valid trials at -100 and +50 ms. Cueing shifted the point of subjective simultaneity among 21 participants with reliable fits. Trial-level posterior alpha lateralization was associated with synchrony reports as a function of Cue validity. In Experiment 2, valid cues reduced raw fusion reports at -100, -50, and +100 ms. A Cue validity × SOA interaction persisted for reference-adjusted fusion scores, whereas neither raw nor adjusted fission showed a corresponding interaction. The association between reference-adjusted alpha lateralization and fusion reports varied with Cue validity and SOA, although a direct comparison with the visual reference did not establish an illusion-specific association. These EEG-behavior associations were stable after accounting for temporal progression, preceding trials, cue side, and an ocular-sensitive EEG proxy. Together, the findings indicate timing- and context-dependent effects of visuospatial attention on audiovisual temporal perception and identify preparatory posterior alpha lateralization as a correlate of subsequent reports.

papers.title: Distinct neural patterns of valence and arousal in the developing brain: A representational similarity analysis of MEG.
papers.authors: Ntoumanis I, Papadelis C.
papers.abstract: How children and adolescents encode the affective meaning of visual stimuli remains poorly understood. A key reason is that valence and arousal are inherently correlated across affective stimuli and thus confounded in the categorical contrasts mostly used in emotion research. Here, in a secondary analysis of a previously collected MEG dataset, we dissociate the contributions of valence and arousal in emotional processing by applying partial representational similarity analysis (RSA) to magnetoencephalography (MEG) data from 57 typically developing children and adolescents (5 - 18 years old) viewing pictures from the Nencki Affective Picture System. Source-localized responses were first estimated on a volumetric grid, after which we tested, across regions and time windows, whether similarity in neural activity patterns tracked similarity in valence or arousal ratings while controlling for their shared variance. Valence emerged as the primary organizing dimension of neural representations in this sample, with effects detectable in frontotemporal and salience regions within the first 100 ms and sustained over time in the lateral prefrontal cortex. These responses formed a distributed representational network that progressively engaged higher-order evaluative regions. In contrast, arousal contributed transiently through a distinct network that only intermittently overlapped with valence-related activity. Together, these findings indicate that valence predominantly structures affective representations in this pediatric sample, whereas arousal exerts a weaker and more limited influence. This work provides an initial characterization of affective representational structure in this sample of children and adolescents, that if replicated, may inform future reference framework for identifying deviations associated with conditions such as autism spectrum disorder.

papers.title: Spectral-spatial Modeling of Neural Couplings in Functional Connectivity of Motor Networks.
papers.authors: Abbaspour H, Wade MH, Hurt CP, Gonzalez CL, Walker HC, Irwin ZT.
papers.abstract: Background Functional neural connectivity reflects coordinated interactions within brain networks in both health and disease. Phase-amplitude coupling (PAC) is widely used for this purpose, but its pairwise formulations overlook spatially distributed, spectrally correlated structures in neural activity that arises from complex brain circuits. New method We developed a spectral-spatial generalized linear model (SS-GLM) to characterize the high-frequency response as the integrated outcome of multiple low-frequency phase sources across channels and frequencies. Our method also utilizes a regularization strategy to mitigate predictor collinearity and spurious effects for stable attribution of network-level coupling estimates. Results Validation was performed using both synthetic data and human motor network recordings from 25 patients with Parkinson's disease undergoing deep brain stimulation (DBS) surgery. In synthetic analyses, SS-GLM accurately recovered ground-truth coupling configurations under multiple plausible scenarios. In real data, the framework revealed coherent cortico-subthalamic coupling patterns across distinct motor tasks that aligned with clinically effective DBS contacts and their anatomical organization. Comparison with existing methods Conventional pairwise PAC metrics, such as the modulation index and GLM assess interactions in isolation. In contrast, SS-GLM jointly models distributed predictors and yields spatially localized, spectrally specific coupling estimates that also achieve stronger correspondence with clinical stimulation outcomes. Conclusions This work offers a principled and extensible framework for advancing functional connectivity analyses, with improved interpretability of network-level interactions, enhanced robustness to confounds, and broad potential for future applications in systems neuroscience and neuro-engineering research.

papers.title: Pediatric Leukodystrophy Classification from 3D MRI: A Comparative Study of Radiomics-Based Machine Learning, Deep Transfer Learning, and Hybrid Models.
papers.authors: Saraji Z, Heidari M, Rashidi S, Ashrafi M.
papers.journal: Journal of neuroradiology = Journal de neuroradiologie
papers.abstract: Background Pediatric leukodystrophies are rare inherited white matter disorders characterized by heterogeneous neuroimaging patterns that complicate accurate and early subtype classification. Despite their clinical importance for treatment planning, genetic counseling, and prognosis assessment, automated artificial intelligence-based diagnostic tools remain limited for these disorders. Methods In this study, we propose a comprehensive machine learning and deep learning framework for the classification of five clinically relevant leukodystrophy subtypes using multimodal axial brain MRI, including T1, T2, and FLAIR sequences acquired from 115 pediatric patients. Following image pre-processing and atlas-based segmentation, region-level representations were extracted and three complementary classification strategies were investigated: (i) radiomics-based machine learning models using handcrafted imaging features; (ii) an end-to-end 3D transfer-learning approach employing pre-trained CNN architectures, including ResNet18, ResNet50, and DenseNet121; and (iii) hybrid models in which CNN-derived deep features were used either independently or in combination with radiomic descriptors for supervised classification. Results The results demonstrated that fine-tuned transfer learning models outperformed radiomics-based and hybrid approaches across all evaluation metrics. Among the evaluated architectures, the best-performing end-to-end model, DenseNet121, achieved an accuracy of 95.50%, a precision of 89.62%, a recall of 89.19%, an F1-score of 88.88%, and a specificity of 97.12%. Conclusion These findings indicate that 3D transfer learning can effectively capture complex spatial and hierarchical volumetric MRI patterns for multiclass pediatric leukodystrophy classification and may serve as a promising decision-support tool in clinical settings with limited data availability.

papers.title: The Entangled Loop: Emotion, interference and hierarchy in the architecture of consciousness.
papers.authors: Kringelbach ML, Rosas FE, Laukkonen R, Chandaria S, Perl YS, Deco G.
papers.abstract: Why does consciousness feel like something, and why is experience unified rather than fragmented? We propose that these properties arise from an entangled trefoil of emotion, interference-based inference and hierarchical orchestration, shaped by the thermodynamic constraint that living systems must remain far from equilibrium using limited energy. Emotion compresses actions into valenced signals of what matters, while a pleasure cycle schedules competing biological needs through predictive wanting and satiety organised around the true hedonic outcome of liking. Hierarchical orchestrating regions integrate and broadcast information through interference between classical coupled oscillators, shaped by the spectral gaps of the connectome driven by long-range exceptions to local cortical wiring. The architecture of the Entangled Loop consists of three inseparable strands, each continually constraining the other two, with the one operator linking computational possibilities to the arrow of time and energetic cost of running them. Evidence suggests that the same three signatures emerge independently in large language models trained on human language, but as shadows of the generating architecture rather than evidence of consciousness. The trefoil predicts a distinctive human vulnerability because our abundance of rare long-range connections promotes more computation for less energy while making the architecture more fragile. Neuropsychiatric disorders could therefore arise from perturbations entering through any strand and propagating through the others, while the more robust architecture of other species may help explain why animal models reproduce human psychiatric disorders poorly. Sustaining and restoring flexible entanglement in the Entangled Loop may provide mechanistic routes towards flourishing.

papers.title: Repetitive low-level blast exposure and brain health: State-of-the-science and clinical priorities in 2026.
papers.authors: Meabon JS, McEvoy C, Crabtree A, Ditzel R, Benedict BA, Ivory RA, Hebert JR, Flarity K, Buckey JC, Geimer S, Mihalik JP, Peskind ER.
papers.abstract: Low-level blast (LLB) exposures generated by weapons systems and explosives use are now recognized as an occupational hazard for many military and law-enforcement communities. Although individual exposures often fall below thresholds for clinically diagnosable concussion, accumulating data from human and animal studies suggest that repetitive LLB can produce subtle but durable changes in neurobehavioral function, neuroimaging markers, and blood- and CSF-based biomarkers, as well as cardiovascular and neurovascular health. At the same time, the field remains fragmented, with heterogeneous exposure metrics, characterized by non-standardized exposure quantification methods, variable outcome measures, and inconsistent longitudinal follow-up intervals. This state-of-the-science review synthesizes current evidence on LLB with a deliberate emphasis on clinical aspects that matter to Servicemembers, Veterans, and clinicians focusing on posttraumatic outcomes (e.g., psychological, cognitive, physical), reduction of risk of neurodegenerative disease, and practical pathways for exposure prevention and mitigation. We first describe contemporary definitions and patterns of LLB exposure across operational communities, followed by a critical appraisal of epidemiological studies linking LLB to symptoms, functional outcomes, and health-care utilization. We then summarize converging evidence for neurodegenerative and neurovascular risks, integrate mechanistic insights from neuroimaging, neuropathology, and animal models, and highlight emerging biomarker and computational approaches. Finally, we outline pragmatic strategies for exposure assessment, screening, and follow-up in clinical settings and identify high-priority research and policy directions. Rather than asking whether LLB is "safe" or "unsafe" in absolute terms, we focus on vulnerability and context as a roadmap for scientific and clinical development while balancing mission requirements with long-term brain health.

papers.title: Perivascular space imaging marker and glymphatic function in obstructive sleep apnea: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
papers.authors: Tanayapong P, Numthavaj P, McKay G.
papers.abstract: Background and objectives Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is a recognized cardiovascular and dementia risk factor that has been previously reported in association with enlarged cerebral perivascular spaces (PVS) indicative of cerebral small vessel disease (CSVD) and impaired glymphatic function. We aimed to evaluate associations between OSA and neuroimaging-visible PVS and Diffusion Tensor Imaging Analysis Along the Perivascular Space (DTI-ALPS), as a surrogate marker of glymphatic function. Methods A systematic search of MEDLINE, Scopus, and Embase was conducted through Oct 11, 2026. The meta-analysis included observational studies exploring associations between OSA severity and PVS burden and DTI-ALPS. Reported effect estimates for PVS or glymphatic parameters across OSA disease severity were pooled using a random-effect model. Results Sixteen studies (N = 2618) met the inclusion criteria. Results showed that patients with OSA had a significantly higher odds of documented PVS compared to those without OSA (OR = 4.97, 95% CI 2.51 to 9.82). Each per unit increase in apnea-hypopnea index corresponded to a 3% increase in the odds of PVS (OR = 1.03, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.04). OSA was linked to a significant decrease in glymphatic-related diffusion as indicated by DTI-ALPS index (mean difference = -0.2, 95% CI -0.35 to -0.06). This reduction persisted across all OSA severities, including mild (mean difference = -0.17, 95% CI -0.32 to -0.02), and moderate-to-severe (mean difference = -0.10, 95% CI -0.17 to -0.04) OSA. Conclusions Our meta-analysis demonstrated a strong link between OSA and both increased PVS burden and impaired surrogate of glymphatic function, potentially implicating OSA in the pathogenesis of both CSVD and dementia. Further prospective studies are necessary to confirm causality and direction of effect of the observed association. Registration PROSPERO registration number, CRD420261279540. ABBREVIATIONS AND ACRONYMS.

papers.title: The inferior parietal lobule is associated with suicidal outcomes in adolescents and youths with non-suicidal self-injury.
papers.authors: Cao Y, Wang J, Liu X, Wang X, Chen W, Yu Y, Gou M, Li W, Li N, Tong J, Xie T, Yu T, Li Y, Chen S, Yang X, Wang Z, Pan S, Luo X, Zhang P, Tian L, Li CR, Tan Y.
papers.abstract: Non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI) is a leading predictor of suicidal thoughts and behaviors in adolescents and youths, yet the neurobiological mechanisms underlying this transition remain unclear. The Integrated Motivational-Volitional (IMV) model links NSSI to suicidal outcomes, but its phases have rarely informed neuroimaging work. We examined 173 adolescents and youths (117 NSSI, 56 non-NSSI) recruited from a psychiatric hospital who underwent structural MRI. Nine theory-driven regions of interest (ROIs) informed by IMV phases were analyzed using ANCOVA, bootstrap mediation, sequential path analysis, and machine-learning classification. Sensitivity analyses controlled for borderline personality disorder, depression, anxiety, image quality, and age range. Four ROIs showed significant group differences after false discovery rate (FDR) correction: transverse temporal gyrus, putamen, posterior corpus callosum, and inferior parietal lobule (IPL). Only IPL thickness showed an FDR-corrected indirect association with suicidal ideation through NSSI frequency (behavior-frequency composite score); its group difference was modest, whereas transverse temporal thickness was the most robust across sensitivity analyses. In an exploratory path model informed by the IMV framework (IPL thickness → NSSI frequency → suicidal ideation → suicide attempts), the serial indirect effect was significant; anxiety and depression were each associated with the IPL-NSSI link. Exploratory machine learning classified NSSI at modest accuracy but not suicidal outcomes. This study provides preliminary IMV-informed structural neuroimaging findings in adolescents and youths. The IPL emerges as a candidate neural correlate associated with suicidal outcomes through affective symptoms, NSSI, and ideation. Brain features classify NSSI but not suicidality outcomes.

papers.title: Hippocampal subfield functional connectivity alterations in major depressive disorder: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
papers.authors: Liu Y, Chen Y, Kong M, Xu Z, Jiang W.
papers.abstract: Background Major depressive disorder (MDD) is increasingly conceptualized as a disorder of distributed neural network dysfunction. The hippocampus comprises functionally distinct subfields, yet evidence on subfield-level functional connectivity (FC) abnormalities in MDD remains heterogeneous, partly because studies use different segmentation approaches. Methods Following PRISMA 2020, we systematically searched PubMed and Scopus for English-language studies published from January 2020 to August 2026 examining FC involving hippocampal subfields or subregions in depression. We summarized segmentation methods, compared atlas-level spatial overlap, performed random-effects meta-analyses where data were comparable, and narratively synthesized case-control and treatment-related findings. Results Eighteen studies including 1366 patients with MDD and 935 healthy controls were included. Segmentation approaches differed substantially in hippocampal coverage and granularity. Five studies contributed to exploratory network-specific meta-analyses. FC was lower in MDD for hippocampal subregion-default mode network connections (g = -0.74, 95% CI -0.98 to -0.50) and visual network connections (g = -0.64, 95% CI -0.94 to -0.34). Estimates for salience, limbic, and sensorimotor networks were imprecise and heterogeneous. Narrative findings were bidirectional, while longitudinal studies suggested treatment-related connectivity changes. Conclusions MDD is associated with heterogeneous, subregion-specific hippocampal dysconnectivity. Atlas non-equivalence may contribute to variability across studies, supporting more harmonized and method-aware segmentation approaches.

papers.title: Do nanoplastics reshape microglial support of neuronal resilience? A study of microglial bioenergetics and microglia-neuron communication in vitro.
papers.authors: Brunialti E, Villa A, Meda C, Parolini M, Ciana P, Casati L.
papers.abstract: Nanoplastics (NPs) are emerging environmental contaminants able to cross biological barriers, disrupt cellular and organelle homeostasis, and alter the brain microenvironment. This study investigated whether NPs affect microglia-neuron communication, a key mechanism underlying neuronal resilience, via the nuclear factor erythroid 2-like 2 (NFE2L2) pathway. Using an in vitro model, we evaluated the effects of polystyrene nanoplastics on microglial metabolic fitness and microglia-mediated neuronal stress responses. Increasing NP concentrations induced a dose-dependent biphasic effect. Low- to intermediate-concentration treatments increased intracellular adenosine triphosphate (ATP) levels in microglia and enhanced microglia-mediated activation of neuronal NFE2L2. In contrast, high NP concentrations impaired microglial metabolism, reduced ATP availability, and decreased microglial-neuronal communication. These findings indicate that NPs alter microglial energetic status and modulate neuroprotective signaling, potentially contributing to impaired neuron-microglia interactions and increased susceptibility to neurotoxicity.

papers.title: Quantitative in vitro PET/MRI and kinetic modelling of imaging agent release from a thermoreversible intranasal sol-gel.
papers.authors: Almahmoud A, Gulzar A, Paterson BM, Parekh HS, Cowin GJ, Ali M, Hawker RR, Tupally KR, Vegh V.
papers.journal: European journal of pharmaceutics and biopharmaceutics : official journal of Arbeitsgemeinschaft fur Pharmazeutische Verfahrenstechnik e.V
papers.abstract: Intranasal phase-transforming thermoresponsive gels can prolong nasal residence and enable controlled release of diagnostic or therapeutic payloads. However, quantitative real-time release characterisation of multimodal imaging probes remains limited. Here, we developed a poloxamer-based sol-gel and established a hybrid PET/MRI framework to quantify the release of PET tracers and an activatable MnO2 nanoflower into simulated nasal fluid. The formulations transformed from solution-to-gel at ∼ 28-29 °C with a storage modulus of 8.2-9.5 kPa attained at typical nasal cavity temperature (34 °C), while maintaining a nasal-compatible pH. PET imaging with an extended time window demonstrated diffusion-dominated release with clear size dependence: ionic [64 Cu]Cu2+ reached 30.0 ± 3.0 % cumulative release at ∼42 h, whereas [64 Cu]Cu-Sar-OP showed 15.6 ± 3.1 % cumulative release under the same simulated conditions. PEGylated MnO2 nanoflowers exhibited negligible apparent release in simulated nasal fluid without reductant due to the absence of redox-triggered MnO2 dissolution to soluble Mn2+ and electrolyte-induced nanoparticle aggregation trapping, which restricts diffusion out of the gel; but with GSH-supplementation, quantitative T1/T2 mapping enabled relaxivity-calibrated tracking of apparent Mn-equivalent accumulation, reaching 13.9 ± 0.7 % of the nominal loaded Mn (T1-based) at ∼24 h. The cytocompatibility of MnO2 NFs-PEG was also evaluated in an RPMI 2650 human nasal epithelial cell model following 24-h exposure. Kinetic modelling (Higuchi and Korsmeyer - Peppas) supported diffusion-dominated transfer of the PET tracers, whereas the MnO2 profile reflected coupled redox and transport processes under limited-GSH conditions. Overall, our integrated PET/MRI approach provides a quantitative framework for comparing in vitro depot release kinetics and informing intranasal PET/MRI formulation design; however, the findings should not be interpreted as direct evidence of mucosal retention or in vivo nose-to-brain transport.

papers.title: Primary cilia mediate specific neuron-glia attachments in C. elegans through the secreted protein BUG-1.
papers.authors: Wexler LR, Griffin B, Dutta P, Sengupta P, Kolotuev I, Ringstad N, Heiman MG.
papers.abstract: Primary cilia are signaling hubs that influence nearly every aspect of cell physiology. Neuronal primary cilia were recently found to form extensive attachments to glia in the mammalian brain, but it is not known how these attachments form or what functions they serve. Defects in cilia cause profound neurological disorders, highlighting the importance of understanding the specialized functions of neuronal cilia. Here, we use a genetic screen in Caenorhabditis elegans to determine how a stereotyped cilia-glia attachment forms and how the attachment affects ciliary calcium signaling. We find that two sensory neurons (URX and BAG) use their cilia to attach to a specific glial partner (ILsoL/R). This attachment requires BUG-1, a large secreted protein that localizes precisely to the cilia-glia attachment site. In the absence of BUG-1, neuronal cilia are present but always fail to attach to the glial cell. As a result, the URX cilia do not undergo activity-dependent remodeling seen in wild-type neurons and the BAG cilia exhibit reduced sensory stimulus-evoked calcium entry and defects in calcium clearance. Our work shows that cilia can select specific glial partners for attachment, identifies a novel protein that mediates these attachments, and demonstrates the functional consequences of loss of cilia-glia attachment on neuronal signaling. We propose that neuronal primary cilia act not only as antennae to receive long-range signals but also as points of close-range cell-cell contact, through which glia could modulate neuronal signaling.

papers.title: Performance of MRI-based synthetic CT for detecting spinal new bone formation in patients with inflammatory arthritis and healthy controls: a comparison with MRI, CT, and radiography.
papers.authors: Willesen ST, Møller JM, Gosvig KK, Pedersen SJ, Hadsbjerg AEF, Georgiadis S, Østergaard M.
papers.abstract: Objectives This study aims to compare magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-based synthetic computed tomography (sCT), T1-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (T1wMRI), low-dose CT (ldCT), and radiography for detecting spinal new bone formation (NBF) in participants with axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA), psoriatic arthritis (PsA), rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and healthy controls (HCs). Methods All participants underwent whole-spine ldCT and MRI in addition to cervical/lumbar spine radiography (not HCs). sCT was reconstructed using BoneMRI. Images were independently assessed for NBF by 2 readers blinded to other imaging and clinical information. One reader repeated ldCT and sCT reads after 6 months. Sensitivity and specificity were calculated using ldCT as the reference standard. Inter-reader and intra-reader reliability were assessed using intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) and Cohen's kappa. Results Sixty-nine participants (36 males, mean age 51.4 years) were included: 30 axSpA, 19 PsA, 10 RA, and 10 HCs. The mean number of NBFs per participant was 25.8 on ldCT, 24.0 on sCT, 9.3 on T1wMRI, and 6.9 on radiography. Sensitivity for NBF detection was highest for sCT (70%), followed by radiography (50% cervical/lumbar and 21% whole-spine) and T1wMRI (28%); specificity was ≥93% across modalities. Inter-reader reliability was high for sCT and ldCT (excellent ICCs, substantial kappas), whereas radiography and T1wMRI showed good ICCs with substantial/moderate kappas. Intra-reader reliability and inter-modality agreement for sCT and ldCT were excellent/substantial (ICCs/kappas). Conclusions Using ldCT as a reference standard, sCT demonstrated substantially higher sensitivity than T1wMRI and radiography. Intra- and inter-reader reliability and inter-modality agreement between ldCT and sCT were comparable, suggesting that discrepancies in lesion detection primarily reflect reader variability rather than inter-modality differences.

papers.title: Impact of Epileptiform Abnormalities on Functional Phenotype in a Cohort of Autism Spectrum Disorder Patients With or Without Epilepsy: A Monocentric Retrospective Study.
papers.authors: Garotti R, Aiello S, Riccio MP, Pezone M, Fiorile AMF, Marani N, Bravaccio C, Terrone G.
papers.journal: Journal of autism and developmental disorders
papers.abstract: Purpose Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) and epilepsy frequently co-occur, suggesting shared neurobiological underpinnings. While no specific seizure type or epilepsy syndrome is consistently associated with ASD, Epileptiform Abnormalities (EAs) are commonly observed in affected individuals, though their clinical significance remains unclear. Methods This study examined the impact of EAs and epilepsy on the functional phenotype of 338 individuals with ASD, assessed through video-EEG (v-EEG) and standardized psychometric tools (ADOS-2, Leiter-R, WISC-IV, VABS). Results Results showed that ASD individuals with epilepsy exhibited significantly lower cognitive performance compared to those with ASD alone or with EAs. Additionally, greater symptom severity was observed in the ASD-+EA group. However, no significant differences emerged in adaptive functioning or language abilities. Conclusion These findings highlight the potential influence of epileptiform activity on cognitive and behavioral outcomes in ASD. Further longitudinal research is warranted to elucidate the prognostic implications of EAs in ASD and better characterize its impact on functional profile.

papers.title: Deep-learning-based contrast synthesis in knee magnetic resonance imaging: performance across multiple target contrasts.
papers.authors: Nykänen O, Nikki M, Casula V, Lattanzi R, Nissi MJ, Nieminen MT, Nevalainen MT.
papers.abstract: Introduction Quantitative MRI has been held back, because it increases scan time on top of clinical protocols. In this cross-sectional study, we explore how accurately unmeasured contrasts can be synthesized from magnetic resonance fingerprinting (MRF) data. Materials and methods MRF, T1-weighted (T1w), gadolinium-enhanced T1w fat-saturated (Gd T1w fs), and double-echo steady-state (DESS) data were acquired at 3 T from volunteers having knee joint symptoms (n=88). Ten subjects were excluded due to missing MRF-data. U-Nets were trained to synthesize the other contrasts out of the MRF data, and the image quality was evaluated for both the synthetic and conventional by two radiologists. Presence of synovitis was evaluated from Gd T1w fs images. Wilcoxon signed-rank test was utilized to test differences in the image quality scores. Results Synthetic images overall had only slightly lower image quality in radiologists' evaluation for T1w (3.54 vs 3.88, p<0.01), DESS (3.22 vs 3.90, p<0.01), and Gd T1w fs images (3.40 vs 3.76, p<0.01). Synovitis could not be reliably observed from synthetic Gd T1w fs images. Conclusions The image quality gap observed earlier persisted in this study and manifested itself steadily across all the joint tissues. Synovitis assessment was not possible from the synthetic contrast-enhanced images.

papers.title: Altered developmental trajectories in neurodevelopmental disorders: mechanisms, human models and translational perspectives.
papers.authors: Desprez F, Ung DC.
papers.abstract: Neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) are clinically and genetically heterogeneous conditions often studied through diagnostic categories, causal genes, synaptic dysfunction or end-stage phenotypes. Although these approaches remain essential, they do not fully capture the developmental nature of NDD pathophysiology. This review proposes a trajectory-first framework in which NDDs are interpreted as disorders of altered developmental progression. From this perspective, the key question is not only which gene, pathway, cell type, or synapse is affected, but when, where and how neurodevelopment begins to diverge. We discuss mechanisms of trajectory divergence, including altered developmental timing, cell-state and lineage disruption, selective cellular vulnerability, epigenetic and signaling dysregulation, cytoskeletal and morphogenetic abnormalities, synaptic maturation defects, excitability changes and network-level alterations. We then examine how human systems, including fetal and post-mortem atlases, iPSC-derived models, cortical organoids, assembloids, functional readouts and patient-level phenotypes, can be integrated to reconstruct developmental trajectories across biological scales. Representative NDD genes and syndromes illustrate that distinct divergence points may later converge on shared functional or clinical outcomes, including altered excitation/inhibition balance, abnormal network activity, epilepsy, language delay, intellectual disability, autism spectrum disorder features or motor dysfunction. Finally, we discuss limitations and perspectives for trajectory-based stratification and biomarker discovery. Rather than acting as static diagnostic readouts, future biomarkers should aim to capture developmental state, timing, divergence, convergence, compensation and response to intervention.

papers.title: Imaging classification of pancreatic cystic lesions: a radiologist's guide.
papers.authors: Boraschi P, Cervelli R, Donati F.
papers.abstract: Pancreatic cystic lesions (PCLs) are increasingly encountered in clinical practice owing to the widespread use of high-resolution cross-sectional imaging. These lesions comprise a heterogeneous group of entities ranging from benign cysts to pre-malignant neoplasms and invasive cancers, making accurate characterization essential for appropriate patient surveillance and therapeutic management. Imaging plays a pivotal role in lesion detection, differential diagnosis, and assessment of malignant potential. This review presents a practical imaging-based classification of PCLs founded on lesion morphology, relationship to the pancreatic ductal system, enhancement patterns, and associated imaging features. Using a stepwise diagnostic approach, pancreatic cystic lesions are categorized according to their increasing risk of malignancy into non-neoplastic cysts, serous cystic neoplasms, mucinous cystic lesions, and cystic degeneration of solid pancreatic tumors. Characteristic imaging findings, relevant differential diagnostic considerations, and imaging features associated with increased malignant potential are comprehensively reviewed, with particular emphasis on the role of MRI and MR cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) in lesion characterization. A structured pattern-recognition flowchart is proposed to facilitate routine image interpretation and enhance diagnostic confidence. In addition, a practical reporting template is presented to promote standardized assessment and effective communication within multidisciplinary teams. Emerging techniques, including diffusion-weighted imaging, quantitative MRI biomarkers, radiomics, artificial intelligence, and molecular analysis of cyst fluid, are discussed as promising tools for improving diagnostic accuracy and refining risk stratification. By emphasizing readily recognizable imaging features and a systematic diagnostic workflow, this review provides radiologists with a practical and clinically applicable framework for the evaluation, diagnosis, risk assessment, and multidisciplinary management of pancreatic cystic lesions.

papers.title: Externally validated MRI radiomics machine learning models for differentiating between myxoid liposarcoma and myxoma.
papers.authors: Chen YH, Bazanjani S, Wang Z, Bauer F, Sharp A, Hung YP, Ossiani T, Saraee M, Smith G, Viator M, Gonzalez M, Chen A, Kerimo E, Palmer W, Pianykh O, Lozano-Calderón SA.
papers.abstract: Objective To develop and externally validate a radiomics-based machine learning model for differentiating myxoid liposarcoma (MLS) from myxoma on MRI and compare its diagnostic performance with that of experienced musculoskeletal radiologists. Methods In this retrospective study, T1-weighted and fluid-sensitive MRI sequences from 109 patients with histologically confirmed MLS or myxoma were used to train support vector machine (SVM), random forest (RF), and XGBoost (XGB) classifiers. Models were evaluated in an independent external cohort of 32 patients from a second institution using different scanner hardware and protocols. Diagnostic performance was compared with that of two fellowship-trained senior musculoskeletal radiologists. Secondary analysis assessed MLS grading. Results The T1-weighted SVM achieved the strongest external binary performance (accuracy, 0.84; AUC, 0.91), outperforming RF and XGB (p = 0.005 and p < 0.001, respectively). Its performance did not differ significantly from that of radiologists (AUC, 0.88-0.94; p > 0.05), although the study was not powered to establish equivalence. Fluid-sensitive SVM performance was limited (accuracy, 0.56; AUC, 0.60), indicating sequence-dependent generalizability. Models and radiologists demonstrated limited MLS grading accuracy, reflecting tumor heterogeneity. Conclusion Externally validated radiomics-based machine learning supported noninvasive differentiation of MLS from myxoma primarily on T1-weighted MRI. T1-weighted SVM performance was not significantly different from that of experienced radiologists, although equivalence was not established, whereas fluid-sensitive performance was substantially weaker. T1-weighted quantitative imaging biomarkers may complement soft tissue tumor characterization, but extrapolation to fluid-sensitive sequences requires caution.

papers.title: MUSIC-PD: A Delphi-Derived, Culturally Adaptable Music Therapy Protocol for Parkinson's Disease Rehabilitation.
papers.authors: Udupa M, R S, Falup-Precurariu C, Mukherjee BB, J JCR, Chandrasekar B, Phielipp NM, Ojha R, Germaine CHF, Ganguly J, Garg D, Manharlal PK, Kulkarni H, Caldera M, Sarangamat N, Gupta RK, Dastidar SBG, Venkatapathy R, Hegde S, Vines BW, Heidersceit A, Mestre T, Chaudhuri KR, Kukkle PL.
papers.abstract: Background Music-based interventions have shown promise in Parkinson's disease (PD) rehabilitation. However, variability in intervention design, delivery, dose, and documentation limits clinical translation. Objective The aim of the study was to develop a consensus-based music therapy protocol for PD, designed to permit cultural and linguistic adaptation. Methods A PRISMA-informed evidence-mapping review identified music-based and rhythm-based interventions relevant to PD rehabilitation. Findings informed a modified Delphi process involving a multidisciplinary expert panel of movement disorder neurologists, qualified music therapists, and people with PD. Round 1 generated qualitative inputs on therapeutic domains, safety, feasibility, and cultural adaptation. These were synthesized into 36 structured statements and rated in Round 2 using a 5-point Likert scale. Consensus was predefined as ≥80% agreement. Results The evidence map included 32 studies and identified 3 therapeutic clusters: motor/gait rehabilitation, voice-respiratory communication, and nonmotor cognitive-affective engagement. Of the 36 Delphi statements, 33 reached consensus. High-convergence domains included patient-preferred familiar music, cultural adaptation, rhythmic auditory stimulation for gait rehabilitation, multidomain symptom targeting, and vocal rehabilitation. The final framework was organized into LAYA-Locomotor Auditory Yielding Activation Module, NADA-Neurocognitive and Affective Domain Activation Module, and RAGA-Respiratory Aerodynamic Glottal Activation Module. The protocol incorporated session-selection rules, safety screening, difficulty levels, active and/or receptive therapy components, flexible pragmatic session guidance, caregiver-supported practice, and a proposed session-planning/documentation resource. Conclusion MUSIC-PD provides a structured, Delphi-derived, and panel-approved framework for integrating music-based interventions into multidisciplinary PD rehabilitation. It translates evidence and multidisciplinary consensus into a protocol intended for prospective feasibility, fidelity, safety, and efficacy evaluation.

papers.title: Monitoring Remyelination and Its Association With Disability Improvement in Multiple Sclerosis Using APART-QSM: A Longitudinal Cohort Study.
papers.authors: Wang Z, Tang M, Yao J, Ai K, Li Y, Wang J, Xu X, Ren W, Dang W, Liu G, Jiang Y, Kang S, Yang W, Li H, Yang D, Han Y, Liu J, Jia F, Jiang J, Ding Y, Zhang J.
papers.journal: Journal of magnetic resonance imaging : JMRI
papers.abstract: Background Conventional MRI has limited specificity for myelin quantification. IterAtive magnetic suscePtibility sources sepARaTion quantitative susceptibility mapping (APART-QSM) quantifies myelin-sensitive (χdia ) and iron-sensitive (χpara ) susceptibility components, but its value for longitudinal assessment of remyelination in multiple sclerosis (MS) remains unclear. Purpose To characterize longitudinal χdia in MS and assess its associations with clinical characteristics. Study type Prospective, longitudinal. Population One hundred forty-five patients with MS and 65 healthy controls (HCs). Field strength/sequence 3.0T; 3D T1-weighted, 3D FLAIR, 3D DIR, and multi-echo gradient-echo imaging sequences. Assessment APART-QSM generated χdia and χpara maps, with susceptibility quantified in lesions and non-lesional regions, and the Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS) assessed at baseline and follow-up. Statistical tests Chi-square, Mann-Whitney U, Wilcoxon signed-rank, Friedman tests, linear mixed-effects models, linear and nonlinear regression. A p value < 0.05 was considered significant. Results One hundred one patients with MS and 20 HCs completed follow-up after a median (IQR) interval of 1.0 (0.8) and 1.25 (0.2) years, respectively. At baseline, white matter lesions (WMLs) exhibited lower χdia (0.0131 [IQR 0.0087] ppm) and higher χpara (0.0058 [IQR 0.0049] ppm) than corresponding normal-appearing white matter (NAWM) (0.0191 [0.0088] ppm; 0.0036 [0.0038] ppm; both p < 0.001). Over 1 year, χdia in WMLs increased (0.0122 [IQR 0.0069] vs. 0.0152 [IQR 0.0065] ppm, p < 0.001), particularly in ofatumumab-treated patients (0.0114 [IQR 0.0085] vs. 0.0158 [IQR 0.0081] ppm, p < 0.001). Greater increases in χdia were significantly associated with female sex, ofatumumab treatment, relapsing-remitting phenotype, and EDSS improvement (all Bonferroni correction p < 0.01). Δχdia showed a nonlinear decline with increasing disease duration (effective degrees of freedom (edf) = 1.83, p = 0.002). Conclusion APART-QSM may enable longitudinal monitoring of remyelination-related changes in MS, with declining Δχdia over disease duration potentially informing individualized treatment strategies. Level of evidence: 2 Stage of technical efficacy 2.

papers.title: Mapping the neural basis of the perception of “flow of time”: interval timing and mental time travel in the human brain
papers.authors: Ochi R, Kawamura M.

papers.title: The transcription factor BCL11A restores differentiation potential to aged oligodendrocyte progenitor cells.
papers.authors: Ghosh T, Baror R, Zhao C, Sharma A, Au WH, Lakatos A, Goldman N, Franklin RJM.
papers.abstract: In young animals, oligodendrocyte progenitor cells (OPCs) in the CNS efficiently differentiate into myelinating oligodendrocytes (OLs), whereas ageing reduces this capacity, impairing remyelination following demyelinating injury and adaptive myelination involved in learning. To identify factors that restore resilience in aged OPCs, we developed gSWITCH (https://altoslabs.shinyapps.io/gSWITCH/, https://github.com/Tanay-math/gSWITCH), a computational pipeline that captures dynamic gene-expression patterns to identify 'switch' genes during lineage progression and ordered biological transitions, including time-series experiments. gSWITCH identified OPC-characteristic switch genes, which we compared between young and aged OPCs to determine whether their regulation is altered with ageing. This revealed several transcription factors with reduced expression in aged OPCs. Transcription-factor binding-site enrichment highlighted Bcl11a as a potential master-regulator of multiple switch genes. Bcl11a inhibition reduced OPC differentiation into OLs, whereas its overexpression in aged OPCs significantly enhanced OL differentiation without affecting proliferation. In aged mice subjected to demyelination injury in spinal cord white matter, Bcl11a overexpression increased OPC differentiation within lesions. We found that Bcl11a has undergone pervasive purifying selection throughout vertebrate evolution, preserving its amino acid sequence by eliminating deleterious mutations. Our study shows that reversing the age-related decline of this evolutionarily conserved factor in aged OPCs restores their impaired capacity for differentiation.

papers.title: Heterogeneous responses to embryonic critical period perturbations within the Drosophila larval locomotor circuit.
papers.authors: Krick N, Davies JJ, Coulson B, Sobrido-Cameán D, Miller M, Oswald MCW, Zarin AA, Baines RA, Landgraf M.
papers.abstract: As developing neural circuits become functional, they undergo a phase of heightened plasticity that facilitates network tuning in response to intrinsic and/or extrinsic stimuli. These developmental windows are termed critical periods (CPs) because perturbations during but not outside the CP can lead to lasting changes, such as the formation of sub-optimal or unstable networks. How separate but connected elements within a network might respond differently to a CP perturbation is not well understood. To study this, we used the locomotor network of the Drosophila larva as a model and heat stress as a CP stimulus that has ecological relevance. When embryos experienced heat stress, the subsequent development of their locomotor network was changed, creating larvae with reduced crawling speed and decreased network stability. Developing body wall muscles and central neurons are sensitive to heat stress perturbations during distinct, consecutive phases of embryogenesis. Within the CNS, transient embryonic CP perturbation leads to increased synaptic drive from premotor interneurons to motoneurons, which in turn adopt reduced excitability. In contrast, the peripheral neuromuscular junction maintains normal synaptic transmission, despite significant structural changes. Thus, connected elements respond differentially to a CP perturbation, suggesting a sequence, or hierarchy of network adjustment during the CP.

papers.title: PACAP engages distinct signaling programs across cortical neuronal and non-neuronal cell types
papers.authors: Heimbach SN, Collazos Matute Á, Dolman B, Bald V, Melzer S.
papers.abstract: Neuropeptides form modulatory communication channels that tune neuronal circuits and their functions, often through selective targeting of distinct cell populations. Pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide (PACAP) is an important neuropeptidergic regulator of fear and stress. However, its receptors are surprisingly ubiquitous across most brain areas and cell types, making the physiological roles and functional mechanisms difficult to predict. Here, we investigate the cell type-specific effects of PACAP in the temporal association cortex (TeA), a brain region implicated in fear learning and memory. Adcyap1r1 , encoding the PACAP receptor PAC1, was broadly expressed across the majority of neuronal and non-neuronal cells. Yet, PACAP engaged highly diverse molecular pathways across functionally distinct cell types that were differentially recruited during auditory fear learning and retrieval, providing a framework for how broad receptor expression can yield specific network modulation. Our data underscore the importance of dissecting cellularly resolved peptidergic signaling to understand functional mechanisms of neuropeptides.

papers.title: High-dimensional hippocampus representation facilitates learning of low-dimensional abstract representation and supports generalization
papers.authors: Wang B, Johnston WJ, Fusi S.
papers.abstract: Semantic knowledge encompasses facts, concepts, and their relationships. Recent work has proposed that some forms of semantic knowledge could be encoded in low-dimensional neural representations, such as the abstract, disentangled representational geometries observed in many cognitive brain areas. Experimental work has shown that hippocampal (HPC) lesions impair the formation of flexible and generalizable semantic knowledge. However, HPC representations are often high-dimensional and sparse. How can these representations contribute to the formation of low-dimensional abstract representation across these cognitive cortical areas? Here, we reconcile these observations using multiregional neural network models. Modeling HPC as a sparse, decorrelating autoencoder, we show that its high-dimensional representations promote the robust and efficient formation of low-dimensional abstract representations in downstream regions such as prefrontal cortex. This effect is most pronounced when the geometry of sensory inputs is misaligned with the geometry of desired outputs, requiring a more complex input-output transformation. Mathematical analysis shows that hippocampal expansion recoding suppresses misleading low-dimensional input structure and reshapes the loss landscape of downstream networks, allowing abstract semantic geometry to emerge reliably. The resulting abstract representations provide an inductive bias for sample-efficient learning of novel semantic-to-action mappings. Finally, we show that consolidating hippocampus-dependent representations into a hippocampus-independent pathway improves out-of-distribution generalization based on input structure. Together, these results suggest a circuit mechanism by which high-dimensional hippocampal representations can support, rather than oppose, the emergence of low-dimensional abstract representations.

papers.title: Network Localization of Anxiety as an Early Manifestation of Alzheimer’s Disease-related Neurodegeneration
papers.authors: Lee S, Ha J, Garimella AH, Baratono SR, Burt GT, Karim HT, Andreescu C, Sperling R, Donovan N, Fox M, Siddiqi S.
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Objective Anxiety is a prominent neuropsychiatric symptom in preclinical Alzheimer’s disease (AD), but the neural circuitry linking anxiety and AD remains uncharacterized. We assessed whether anxiety in preclinical AD is independently associated with AD-related neurodegeneration and localizes to a common anxiety network. Methods In cognitively unimpaired (CU) older adults with 3T MRI and amyloid-β PET (N=1,775), we examined whether an established AD-related atrophy network is associated with anxiety (STAI-6). Then, using Atrophy Network Mapping (ANM), which maps individual cortical atrophy patterns onto a normative functional connectome (N=1000), we derived an anxiety network. We tested its 1) spatial convergence with the AD network and with a causal anxiety network derived from lesion and neuromodulation data, 2) specificity relative to depression, 3) generalizability in samples from independent cohorts with AD and Parkinson’s disease (total n=878), and 4) association with longitudinal outcomes. Results In CU older adults, greater AD-network atrophy was associated with higher anxiety, independent of depression, cognition, cortical atrophy, and amyloid burden. Anxiety localized to a network closely resembling the AD network (r=0.74, p=0.04) and the causal anxiety network (r=0.72, p=0.02). This convergence extended across the AD continuum and to the Parkinson’s disease cohort and was specific to anxiety relative to depression. Greater anxiety-network atrophy was associated with cognitive decline over 4.6 years. Conclusion Anxiety localizes to a brain circuit resembling the AD-related atrophy network, is consistent across the AD continuum and may extend beyond AD. These findings support anxiety as an independent marker of early AD-related neurodegeneration.

papers.title: The path from brain to words is rerouted in opioid addiction
papers.authors: Pais S, Tikochinski R, King SG, Calderon N, Goldstein RZ, Reichart R.
papers.abstract: Whether spontaneous speech preserves how the brain encoded an experience is unknown. We tested this question in opioid use disorder (OUD), in which drug cues outweigh other rewards. Eighty-two people with OUD and 34 controls watched the opening of the film Trainspotting during functional magnetic resonance imaging, then retold it in their own words. Language-model analyses showed that people with OUD dwelt on craving, personal identification and recovery, devoting more of their retelling to drug scenes. In 65 participants with imaging, this speech bias tracked how strongly the brain had distinguished drug from non-drug scenes during viewing, in left frontoparietal cortex in controls but left temporal cortex in OUD. Direct comparison showed left accumbens coupling positive in OUD and negative in controls, and left superior frontal coupling weaker in OUD. Spontaneous speech thus carries a trace of neural encoding whose route depends on what the experience meant to the speaker.

papers.title: Beyond reduced alpha power: a weaker temporal link between alpha and other brain rhythms in Alzheimer’s disease
papers.authors: Wei J, Zhou C.
papers.abstract: Background Reduced alpha power is among the most consistently reported resting electroencephalography (EEG) features of Alzheimer’s disease (AD). However, alpha activity also interacts with other rhythms over time, a dynamic aspect that power measures do not capture. Whether AD weakens this temporal interaction, and whether such a change carries information beyond reduced alpha power, remains unclear. Methods We analyzed public eyes-closed resting EEG from 29 healthy controls (HC), 36 patients with AD and 23 with frontotemporal dementia (FTD). After separating periodic from aperiodic activity, we tracked the aperiodic exponent and periodic theta, alpha, beta and gamma activity in consecutive 1-s windows. A vector autoregressive model predicted these five measures from the preceding window. Alpha’s predictive contribution ( G α ) was the increase in prediction error for theta, beta and gamma when the model was refitted without alpha as a predictor, with training and testing on separate time blocks of each recording. AD–HC differences were adjusted for age and sex, then for alpha expression (periodic alpha power) and signal quality (dynamic range and spatial reliability), with alpha self-persistence (alpha’s carry-over between windows) as a benchmark. We also tested whether expression and G α each added information about AD beyond the other. An exploratory Jansen–Rit-family circuit model examined whether expression and G α can change partly independently. Results G α was lower in AD than in HC (adjusted difference in 10³ G α , −3.19; 95% confidence interval −5.25 to −1.13; p = 0.0035), with a consistent direction across sensitivity analyses. Adjustment for alpha expression and signal quality retained 75.8% of this difference but only 4.4% of the self-persistence difference. Expression and G α each added information beyond the other (Holm-adjusted p = 0.012 for both). FTD contrasts were inconclusive. In the circuit model, reducing local recurrent excitation lowered alpha expression without an estimated decrease in G α , whereas reducing downstream input lowered G α with a smaller change in expression. Conclusions At the group level, the resting alpha abnormality in AD comprises two partly nonredundant dimensions: reduced expression and a weaker temporal link between alpha and subsequent multi-rhythm activity. Quantifying this temporal link may complement conventional spectral markers of AD.

papers.title: Posterior-anterior striatal reorganization after weight restoration in anorexia nervosa is associated with remission outcome: from mice to longitudinal human study
papers.authors: Zarrabi AA, Cachia A, Tolle V, Costa CD, Lebrun N, Debacker C, Charron S, Chakravarty MM, Daumas S, Mestikawy SE, Oppenheim C, Gorwood P, Duriez P.
papers.abstract: Anorexia nervosa (AN) is a severe psychiatric disorder with high relapse rates despite successful weight restoration. Altered reward processing and an imbalance between goal-directed and habitual control within the striatum have been proposed to contribute to the persistence of maladaptive behaviours, but the striatal mechanisms underlying recovery and relapse remain unclear. Here, we combined cross-species structural MRI, including cross-sectional analyses in mice and longitudinal neuroimaging and clinical assessments in patients with AN, to investigate striatal alterations associated with recovery. Male mice with deletion of the vesicular acetylcholine transporter (VAChTcKO; n = 9), a model of maladaptive eating behaviour, showed reduced dorsolateral striatal volume compared with wild-type mice (n=9). At baseline, women with AN (n = 71) showed reduced striatal volumes compared with healthy controls (n = 30). Longitudinally, patients with AN (n = 41) and healthy controls (n = 28) were reassessed, revealing substantial recovery of striatal volumes following weight restoration in AN. Posterior-anterior putamen gradient changes differed according to subsequent remission status, with changes in the right putamen gradient predicting relapse. Striatal gradient changes were also associated with goal-directed and habitual behaviour during the slip-of-action task, response consistency during delay discounting, and circulating ghrelin and desacyl ghrelin concentrations. These findings identify longitudinal putamen reorganization as a candidate marker of vulnerability to relapse and link striatal plasticity, goal-directed and habitual control, reward processing, and metabolic processes in AN.

papers.title: From micro-architecture to networks: canonical neurobiological architecture of functional brain organization across the lifespan and in psychopathology
papers.authors: Feng G, Chen J, Iraji A, Sendi MS, Fu Z, Calhoun VD.
papers.abstract: Understanding how macroscale functional network connectivity (FNC) across the lifespan and in psychopathology is spatially organized with respect to microscale neurobiological architecture remains a challenge. Here, we constructed a cross-omics mapping framework by linking resting-state fMRI data (5,349 individuals, 6–80 years) with 49 neurobiological markers (24 cell types, 19 neurotransmitters, 6 mitochondria). We show that FNC development and aging unfold along cellular and molecular gradients. Specifically, spatial correspondence between age-related FNC changes and neurobiological microprofile networks varied by life stage, peaking for cell types in adolescence, neurotransmitter systems in mid-young adulthood and mitochondrial phenotypes in early adulthood. Applying normative modeling to 5 psychiatric disorders (schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, major depressive disorder, autism, and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder), we identified disorder-specific and cross-disorder FNC phenotypes spatially associated with neurobiological architecture. Together, these findings provide a hypothesis-generating framework linking functional brain organization and dysfunction to canonical neurobiological architecture across the lifespan and psychiatric disorders.

papers.title: Cumulative Prenatal Adversity and Fronto-Limbic White Matter Development Across Adolescence
papers.authors: Costello LA, Garavan H, Makowski C, Ahern J, Potter AS, Reid BM, Johnson ME, Albaugh MD, Gonçalves PD.
papers.abstract: Importance The prenatal period is a critical window for intergenerational transmission of adversity, yet the neural substrates through which cumulative prenatal stress becomes biologically embedded in offspring brain development remain poorly understood. White matter microstructure is a candidate mechanism linking prenatal adversity to downstream emotional dysregulation. Objective To examine associations between cumulative adverse prenatal exposure (APE) burden and fronto-limbic white matter fractional anisotropy (FA) at baseline and across adolescent developmental trajectories, and to test whether white matter FA mediates prenatal APE effects on emotional dysregulation. Design, Setting, and Participants Cohort study using data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study, Release 7.0, a diverse longitudinal cohort of US children recruited at ages 9 to 10 years across 21 sites. After diffusion tensor imaging quality control exclusions and retention of one twin or triplet per family, the final cross-sectional analytic sample comprised 10 483 participants. Longitudinal analyses included participants with data at one or more follow-up timepoints across four imaging waves. Exposures Cumulative APE burden, operationalized as a sum of six binary adverse prenatal exposures (unplanned pregnancy; early alcohol, tobacco, and cannabis use before pregnancy recognition; complicated pregnancy; complicated birth; range, 0-6) following Zhi et al. (2026). Main Outcomes and Measures Fractional anisotropy in 11 a priori fronto-limbic white matter tracts at baseline (ages approximately 10 years) and across four imaging timepoints (ages approximately 10, 12, 14, and 16 years). Exploratory outcomes included Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL) dysregulation profile and Emotion Regulation Questionnaire (ERQ) subscales. Results Higher prenatal APE burden was associated with lower baseline FA in left uncinate fasciculus (b = −0.00096; 95% CI, −0.00151 to −0.00042; FDR-corrected P = .006), corpus callosum (b = −0.00079; 95% CI, −0.00125 to −0.00032; FDR-corrected P = .006), and right uncinate fasciculus (b = −0.00071; 95% CI, −0.00120 to −0.00021; FDR-corrected P = .019). This association was stable across visits and robust to stringent adjustment for two complementary image-quality metrics (framewise displacement and frame censoring); prenatal burden was itself unassociated with image quality. Higher APE burden was additionally associated with steeper FA increases across adolescence (positive APE × Age interaction in 5 of 11 tracts); positive across all 11), these trajectory effects were more sensitive to image quality, though the right uncinate fasciculus association survived stringent adjustment. Post hoc analyses indicated that pregnancy complications and prenatal cannabis exposure were the most consistent contributors. White matter FA partially mediated the association between prenatal APE burden and involuntary emotional dysregulation, with no association with voluntary emotion regulation strategies. Conclusions and Relevance Cumulative prenatal APE burden was associated with lower fronto-limbic white matter FA —particularly in the uncinate fasciculus and corpus callosum—an enduring association that was stable across adolescence and robust to rigorous image-quality adjustment. Evidence for altered developmental trajectories was more sensitive to image quality and should be interpreted as a more tentative, complementary finding. These findings identify fronto-limbic white matter as a candidate neurobiological correlate of cumulative prenatal adversity, while underscoring that this pathway reflects a bounded set of prenatal exposures. Key Points Question Is cumulative adverse prenatal exposure burden associated with fronto-limbic white matter microstructure across adolescence? Findings In this cohort study of 10 483 adolescents from the ABCD Study, higher adverse prenatal exposure burden was associated with lower fractional anisotropy in bilateral uncinate fasciculus and corpus callosum —a stable association across adolescence that was robust to rigorous image-quality adjustment. Higher burden was additionally associated with steeper fractional anisotropy increases in 5 of 11 tracts, and white matter partially mediated associations with involuntary emotional dysregulation. Meaning These findings identify fronto-limbic white matter microstructure as a candidate neurobiological correlate of cumulative prenatal adversity, consistent with early biological embedding through prenatal programming.

papers.title: Using Diffusion Similarity Networks to Identify, Track, and Predict Movement Disorders
papers.authors: Shalaby A, Chitta KK, Alijanpourotaghsara A, Choi JW, Hitti FL, Chiang FL, Sharma VD, Kim WH, Pouratian N, Lee J.
papers.abstract: Characterizing individual structural brain alterations in movement disorders like Parkinson’s disease (PD) and Essential Tremor (ET) remains a significant challenge in clinical neuroscience. While brain structural connectivity (SC) derived from Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) tractography maps physical white matter pathways, it fails to capture localized microstructural remodelings within gray matter structures. In this study, we use Diffusion Similarity Networks (DSNs) as a novel framework to estimate microstructural connectivity from diffusion weighted imaging (DWI). First, we evaluate the ability of DSNs to differentiate individuals with PD from healthy controls (HC). We used Similarity Network Fusion (SNF) to visualize differences between the fused networks of both groups as well as the Brain Connectivity Toolbox (BCT) to quantify changes in network topology, including transitivity, clustering coefficient, global efficiency, and betweenness centrality. Second, to evaluate the capacity of DSNs to track disease progression over time, we utilized longitudinal data extracted from the Parkinson’s Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI) database, mapping distinct functional subnetwork degeneration trajectories in PD patients. Finally, we developed a predictive Graph Neural Network (GNN) framework on a locally collected cohort to address the challenging task of differentiating PD from ET, utilizing DSNs as highly discriminant input features. Our results demonstrate that DSN metrics successfully capture distinct structural signatures that reliably separate clinical phenotypes, while longitudinal modeling reveals an accelerated, progressive decay in specific motor and basal ganglia subnetwork topologies over time. Furthermore, the GNN model achieved high classification performance (Balanced accuracy = 0.8684, AUC= 0.9420) in distinguishing PD from ET globally, with local explainability analysis successfully showing the specific brain Regions of Interest (ROIs) driving the differential diagnosis. Overall, these findings demonstrate that Diffusion Similarity Networks serve as a robust, non-invasive biomarker for movement disorders, offering deep insights into disease progression and an explainable AI tool for clinical decision support.

papers.title: Current gaps in downstream applications of fMRI foundation models: lessons learned from BrainLM & BrainHarmonix on Prevent-AD
papers.authors: Wang H, Pichet Binette A, Sainath P, Farrugia N, Villeneuve S, Bellec L.
papers.abstract: Foundation models have driven major advancements in the language and vision domains, as seen in the popularity of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools, and a growing number of studies are bringing the approach to human brain imaging. Whether these models are ready for independent researchers to use on clinical datasets has yet to be examined. We evaluated two recent fMRI foundation models, BrainLM and BrainHarmonix, on PreventAD, a dataset on adults with a family history of Alzheimer’s disease. We compared features from frozen and fine-tuned models against two baselines: functional connectivity and a dummy classifier that always predicts the most common class. The sample includes 343 subjects who passed quality control, with a subset of 218 who had amyloid PET imaging. We tested four prediction targets: sex, age, progression to mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and β-amyloid burden. Both models required substantial changes to the released code. BrainLM’s own data preparation workflow did not produce stable fine-tuning, which we achieved only after switching to a standard workflow implemented with the library Nilearn. BrainHarmonix’s documentation did not specify how to normalize new data, so we resolved this by testing different alternatives. For sex, functional connectivity outperformed all foundation model features. For age group, the best foundation model feature, taken from BrainHarmonix’s structural (T1-weighted) encoder, slightly exceeded functional connectivity, but the difference was not significant. For MCI and β-amyloid, no feature exceeded the dummy classifier in accuracy, and the area under the curve (AUC) stayed near chance for all features. For both clinical targets, the most precise feature came from fine-tuned BrainLM, meaning a larger share of its positive predictions were correct than for functional connectivity, but neither difference reached statistical significance. These results suggested that the strong transfer to new tasks seen in large language models cannot yet be assumed for fMRI foundation models, and that both models required code adaptation that would preclude their streamlined adoption by independent groups. We recommend that future studies provide standardized data workflows and always report functional connectivity and dummy classifier baselines. For clinical targets with strong class imbalance, studies should report several metrics, including precision.

papers.title: Proteogenomics captures a midlife biological state of Alzheimer’s disease susceptibility
papers.authors: Perry AS, Adegboye HA, Bledsoe X, Archer D, Tiwari A, Lin P, Farber-Eger E, Perera BLA, Zhao S, Sheng Q, Ma S, Hutchins E, Zhang P, Alexander MW, Sale R, Chen Y, Colangelo L, Bahorik A, Tanriverdi K, Risitano A, Freedman JE, Nayor M, Das S, Liu D, Pechman KR, Shashikumar N, Bolton C, Davis LT, Landman BA, Hou L, Cruchaga C, Saloner R, Yaffe K, Wells QS, Hohman TJ, Jefferson AL, Keuren-Jensen Kv, Shah RV, Gamazon ER.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) develops over decades, but biological processes underlying susceptibility during midlife remain poorly understood. Using multimodal neuroimaging and plasma proteomics in UK Biobank participants, we identified circulating proteomic signatures of brain structure and organization. This ‘neurostructural proteome’ predicted future cognitive decline, incident dementia, and later-life AD pathology across independent cohorts spanning two decades of follow-up. Genetic and single-nucleus transcriptomic analyses demonstrated convergence of the neurostructural proteome and AD genetic architecture, highlighting enrichment in astrocyte, microglia, and endothelial pathways beyond the APOE region. Collectively, these findings identify a circulating neurostructural proteome detectable in midlife that captures molecular processes associated with future AD susceptibility and provide a framework for uncovering an early biological landscape of disease susceptibility that precedes conventional biomarkers and clinical onset.

papers.title: Multimodal Prediction of Distressing and Persistent Psychotic-Like Experiences in Adolescence across Environment, Genetics, and Neuroimaging
papers.authors: Lal A, Karcher NR, Ahern J, Rigby A, Rai S, Cadenhead K, Linkersdörfer J, Hagler DJ, Pecheva D, Barch DM, Jernigan TL, Parekh P, Dale AM, Makowski C.
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Adolescent psychotic-like experiences, particularly those that are distressing and persistent (dpPLEs), may elevate risk for a range of psychiatric disorders, yet the relative predictive contributions of brain structure, genetics, and environment to dpPLEs remain unknown. Using four timepoints from 7,399 children in the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study, we developed stacked ensemble machine-learning models integrating cortical morphometry and whole-brain microstructural properties, polygenic risk scores, family psychiatric history, and childhood environmental factors to predict adolescent dpPLEs. Environmental predictors alone, driven by area deprivation index, neighborhood drug-related crime, and cumulative early adversity, were the strongest predictive domain (ROC-AUC = 0.687 ± 0.003), outperforming genetic (0.619 ± 0.020) and all imaging models (0.588-0.650). Adding genetic risk to environmental features produced the best-performing model overall (ROC-AUC = 0.697 ± 0.007), whereas adding neuroimaging yielded no further incremental gain (ROC-AUC=0.683-0.696). Beyond environmental exposures, family history of psychosis, cross-disorder polygenic risk, and both globally distributed and regionally specific imaging components contributed to prediction. Childhood environmental factors thus capture a core predictive signal preceding dpPLEs, while genetic and neuroimaging features added comparatively modest discriminative prediction value, but may offer complementary biological insights.

papers.title: Heavy-tailed connections support robust neural communication
papers.authors: Betancourt JM, Varanasi V, Clark DA, Lynn CW.
papers.abstract: In the synaptic wiring between neurons, some rare connections are orders of magnitude stronger than most. This heavy-tailed connectivity is ubiquitous across different species, brain regions, and cell types, suggesting that it serves a general purpose for neural function. Here, we show, both analytically and in simulations, that heavy-tailed connections reduce communication errors in the presence of synaptic noise. In minimal models of individual neurons, noisy connections induce errors at a rate that depends only on a simple network statistic, which we refer to as robustness. For a fixed number of incoming synapses, neurons with broader distributions of connection strength are more robust and, therefore, admit fewer errors. Across several connectomes, we find that real neurons are consistently more robust than comparable null networks. In the whole brain of the fruit fly Drosophila, robustness increases with distance from the sensory periphery, such that central neurons are more robust than those involved in sensory processing. Together, these results indicate that heavy-tailed connections may arise universally to fortify the brain against noise in communication.

papers.title: NeCS-Flow: Necrosis-Guided Contrast-Enhanced MRI Synthesis with Rectified-Flow Refinement
papers.authors: Alzaga Goñi E, Zhao W, Adams R, Moinian S, Xiong Y, Wu T, Yan K, Shpanskaya K, Vasireddi A, Houk J, Calabrese E, Ma D.
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Gadolinium-based contrast agents raise concerns about tissue deposition, adverse reactions, and increased costs. Purpose To develop and validate a deep learning pipeline for gadolinium-free post-contrast T1w brain MRI synthesis incorporating necrotic scaling and Posterior-Mean Rectified Flow (PMRF) refinement, and to evaluate diagnostic utility through a blinded multi-reader study. Study Type Retrospective. Population 454 patients with adult-type gliomas (grade 2-4) from four publicly available datasets. Training used 374 patients; internal testing used 60 held-out patients; external validation used 20 patients. Field Strength/Sequence 1.5-3.0 T; pre-contrast T1w, T2w, and FLAIR as inputs; post-contrast T1w as synthesis target. Assessment A three-stage pipeline comprising nnU-Net Necrotic core segmentation, necrotic-scaling-guided U-Net Contrast Synthesis, and PMRF perceptual refinement (NeCS-Flow) was evaluated using whole-brain and tumor-region similarity metrics, enhancing tumor Dice scores, perceptual quality metrics, and a blinded three-reader study assessing diagnostic accuracy, enhancement detection, image quality, and real-versus-synthetic discriminability. Statistical Tests Paired t-tests and two one-sided tests for model comparison; Fisher’s exact test and two-sample t-tests for reader study comparisons, with p < 0.05 considered significant. Results Necrotic scaling consistently improved real versus synthetic enhancing tumor Dice internally (HGG: 0.793 to 0.816) and externally (HGG: 0.465 to 0.612). NeCS-Flow outperformed two benchmark architectures on all quantitative metrics in internal and external testing, although absolute enhancing tumor accuracy declined for all models on the external cohort. PMRF refinement improved perceptual realism across gliomas, reducing both FID and KID. Readers distinguished synthetic from real images only modestly above chance (overall accuracy 61.7%), and no significant differences between real and synthetic images were found for any clinical metric. Data Conclusion NeCS-Flow synthesizes perceptually realistic and diagnostically equivalent post-contrast T1w brain MRI, with necrotic scaling improving enhancing tumor delineation and PMRF refinement improving perceptual realism across gliomas. Performance on an external cohort was preserved relative to benchmark methods, though reduced in absolute terms.

papers.title: Joint reconstruction of multi-contrast relaxation-diffusion imaging
papers.authors: Wang Y, Liu Q, Consagra W, Ning L, Setsompop K, Rathi Y.
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Diffusion MRI across multiple gradient directions, b-values and echo times (TEs) provides complementary tissue contrast but requires extensive sampling. Joint k-space and q-space undersampling requires reconstruction that preserves diffusion- and TE-dependent signal variation while exploiting shared anatomical information. Here we introduce DIFFUSE (Diffusion-relaxometry Implicit Field Fitting from Undersampled k – q Space across Echoes), a subject-specific joint k – q –TE image reconstruction framework. It fits a single implicit neural representation (INR) directly to complementary undersampled multi-coil k -space measurements across diffusion encodings and echo times. The INR (a self-supervised neural network) maps spatial location, b-value and TE to baseline b0 signals and spherical harmonic coefficients for directional diffusion-weighted image reconstruction. The measurement-specific forward model incorporates phase, coil sensitivities and motion and eddy current related transforms. We evaluated DIFFUSE using retrospective Human Connectome Project data, controlled motion simulations and in vivo multi-shell and multi-TE acquisitions. At sixfold in-plane acceleration, DIFFUSE reduced normalized mean squared error by 57–73% relative to SENSE across two diffusion shells in the retrospective experiment. In the controlled motion experiment, motion-aware DIFFUSE reduced normalized mean squared error by 66–72% relative to static DIFFUSE. The prospective study demonstrated multi-shell reconstruction at 1.3 mm isotropic resolution with significantly high signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). In a separate multi-TE experiment, a single representation jointly reconstructed all nine contrasts corresponding to 3 b-value/TE combinations. DIFFUSE thus provides a common reconstruction strategy for accelerated protocols spanning multiple diffusion encodings and echo times.
