papers.title: Dissociating Resting-State Networks of Pedohebephilic Preference and Child Sexual Offending Using Network-Based Prediction
papers.authors: Serin E, Khan KR, Krueger THC, Sinke C, Beier KM, Walter M, Schiffer B, Amelung T, Walter H.
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Pedohebephilia (P+), the sexual preference for prepubescent and early pubertal minors, regularly causes distress in those affected. While associated with child sexual offending (CSO), P+ is not a prerequisite for CSO. Limited neuroimaging studies have identified alterations associated with P+, while these may primarily reflect offending history. The correlates of P+ independent of CSO therefore remain unclear. We examined this distinction using intrinsic functional networks within a multivariate predictive framework. Methods Using resting-state functional connectivity (rsFC) and network-based prediction (NBS-Predict), we performed pairwise classifications among non-offending pedohebephilic men (P+CSO-, n =35), pedohebephilic men with CSO (P+CSO+, n =38), and non-pedohebephilic controls without CSO (P-CSO-, n =63). Classification-relevant subnetwork nodal strength was associated post hoc with trait impulsivity within P+ groups. Results P+CSO-were significantly distinguished from P-CSO-(balanced accuracy [BAC]=0.621, p FDR =.041), and showed reductions between default-mode hubs and temporoparietal somatomotor and ventral attention regions. P+CSO+ were also significantly distinguished from P+CSO-(BAC=0.645, p FDR =.032) and yielded a smaller subnetwork centered on the substantia nigra. Against P-CSO-, P+CSO+ showed widespread reductions, particularly across subcortical, default mode, visual, limbic, and somatomotor regions (BAC=0.640, p FDR =0.032). Right precentral gyrus nodal strength correlated with impulsivity in P+CSO+ only ( r =0.57, p FDR =0.024). Conclusions Whole-brain rsFC contains information distinguishing pedohebephilic preference in the absence of known CSO, while P+CSO+ show additional and more widespread network alterations involving systems implicated in action selection and behavioral regulation. These findings open new avenues for integrating pedohebephilia into broader neurobiological research frameworks.

papers.title: Whole-brain normative modeling across multiple functional connectivity metrics in MEG
papers.authors: Kobbersmed JRL, Gohil C, Woolrich M, Vidaurre D.
papers.abstract: Normative modeling has recently emerged in structural and functional neuroimaging as a promising approach to characterize neuropathology at the individual level. Trained on large healthy cohorts, these models predict expected measurements from covariates such as age and sex while quantifying normal population variability. Individual measurements can then be compared against the model to identify deviations associated with pathology. While most normative models of brain function have been based on functional MRI, EEG and MEG offer more direct measurements of brain activity at higher temporal resolution. Despite the promise, how to adequately perform normative modelling at the whole-brain level on these modalities remains challenging. We here propose M/EEG-FUNCOIN to identify age- and sex-related dimensions of change in functional connectivity from a plethora of FC measures from electrophysiology: amplitude envelope correlation, phase-locking value, and time-delay embedding covariance. Using resting-state MEG data from the Cambridge Centre for Aging and Neuroscience (Cam-CAN) dataset, we show that M/EEG-FUNCOIN can: (i) characterize age- and sex-related whole-brain functional connectivity patterns in greater detail than existing methods; and (ii) effectively capture meaningful deviations in connectivity in individuals that rank high and low in cognitive ability. Altogether, these results show great potential for applications in complex, network-level brain pathology.

papers.title: Functional and Structural Brain Age Gaps as Complementary Predictive Markers for Cognitive Performance
papers.authors: Crocetta A, Morandini M, Bittner N, Caspers S, Cauda F, Brovelli A, Gilson M.
papers.abstract: Cognitive decline is characterized by substantial inter-individual variability across the lifespan, even among clinically healthy adults. However, it is unclear how structural and functional brain organization jointly relate to differences in cognitive performance within the typical populations. We considered a multimodal brain age framework by predicting for each subject its age from either structural MRI or resting-state functional MRI, after training on the 1000BRAINS cohort (901 participants, 18-85 years). Following, a structural and a functional brain age gap markers were defined as the deviations with respect to the real chronological age. We then used the markers to characterize the interplay between structure and function in shaping cognitive performances. Our findings reveal that the functional marker is as important to predict global cognitive performance as the structural marker. The most accurate prediction was found for global cognition, executive functions and episodic memory, followed by working memory, attention and language. In particular, the structural marker was contributing to all domains, except for working memory, whereas the functional marker had the highest contribution. Overall, structural and functional brain age models together provide a meaningful subject-level summary of brain information for predicting cognition, supporting a multidimensional view of typical aging.

papers.title: Prediction of Unfavorable Functional Status at Hospital Discharge in Older Adults with Traumatic Brain Injury : Model Development and Internal Evaluation.
papers.authors: Tunthanathip T, Intawong P, Songsiriphan N, Jintasawin P, Chiwangkull A, Sangsukwow C, Jirapattanapong T, Chotwiwattanakul T, Kanurak P, Srangrai S.
papers.journal: Annals of geriatric medicine and research
papers.abstract: Background Traumatic brain injury (TBI) in older adults is an increasing public health burden. An early risk assessment of poor functional outcome can help guide prognosis and communication. The objective of the present study was to develop and internally validate a prediction model for poor functional status at discharge from the hospital for older adults with TBI. Methods A retrospective cohort study included 3,193 patients aged ≥65 years with TBI. The Glasgow Outcome Scale (GOS) was used to evaluate the functional status of the patient at hospital discharge and was dichotomized as favorable (GOS 4-5) or unfavorable (GOS 1-3). Logistic regression was used to analyze candidate predictors; then, backward selection with the Akaike Information Criterion was used for multivariable analysis. The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) was used to measure discrimination, and the calibration intercept, calibration slope, and Brier score were used to measure calibration. Optimism-corrected performance was estimated using 1,000 bootstrapped resamples in the internal validation. Bootstrap inclusion frequencies were used to evaluate the predictor-selection stability. Results Among 3,193 patients, 224 (7.0%) had poor functional outcomes. Warfarin use, motor weakness, hypotension, category of GCS, pupillary response, basilar skull fracture, acute subdural hematoma, contusion/intracerebral hematoma, intraventricular hemorrhage, and basal cistern obliteration were predictor variables retained in the final model. The model achieved an apparent AUC of 0.964 (95% CI, 0.948-0.979). After 1,000 bootstrap resamples, the optimism-corrected AUC was 0.962 with a calibration intercept of -0.001 and the calibration slope of 0.959. Conclusion The model demonstrated strong discrimination with limited optimism after bootstrap internal validation. External validation in independent populations is required before clinical implementation.

papers.title: Electroconvulsive Therapy and the Long-Term Risk of Dementia: Conceptual Issues, Methodological Issues, and Recent Findings.
papers.authors: Andrade C.
papers.abstract: Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) induces changes in brain functioning. It requires a generalized seizure to be effective and is associated with anterograde and retrograde amnestic deficits that are mostly mild and short-lasting. For these and other reasons, the treatment has been claimed to cause brain damage and has fueled the consequent question of whether it increases the long-term risk of dementia. The question related to dementia risk is important because ECT-treated cohorts tend to be older rather than younger. This article examines conceptual issues, methodological issues, and findings related to the long-term risk of dementia in patients treated with ECT. In summary, ECT-associated amnestic deficits bear no resemblance to the chronic, deteriorating, global impairment that characterizes dementia. There is no evidence that ECT is associated with macroscopic, microscopic, or biomarker indices of brain injury. ECT is not associated with cortical atrophy, medial temporal lobe atrophy, white matter changes, or cerebral microbleeds. Rather, ECT increases neuroplasticity; there is a dose-dependent increase in neurogenesis, dendritic arborization, and new synapse formation in the hippocampus. ECT also increases rather than decreases hippocampal volume in depressed patients. As a further consideration, because ECT is an effective treatment, it may favorably modify illness-magnified lifestyle risk factors for dementia. With this background, 4 cohort studies published in the last decade (ECT total, 8,994 patients; control total, 277,871 patients) examined the risk of dementia in ECT-treated patients. These studies had an average of 5-25 years of follow-up, modestly adjusted for confounding, including confounding by indication and confounding by severity of indication, as well as considered death as a competing risk. No study found evidence that ECT was associated with an increased risk of dementia.

papers.title: Shared control-network recruitment and task-dependent brain-behavior associations in bilingual language and rule switching.
papers.authors: Guo T, Wu YJ, Chen J, Liu X, Chen S, Peng P, Li Y, Xie X, Wen R, Guo T.
papers.abstract: Bilingual language control is thought to draw on domain-general cognitive control, yet it remains unclear whether cross-task overlap in neural recruitment is accompanied by similar brain-behavior relationships. Previous connectivity studies have typically estimated functional connectivity (FC) across entire tasks or blocks, obscuring network changes specific to switch trials. We combined hierarchical drift-diffusion modeling, regional activation, and beta-series FC in 126 Chinese-English bilinguals (123 with usable fMRI data) who completed language- and rule-switching tasks. Both tasks reduced drift rates and prolonged nondecision times on switch trials. They also recruited a common 28-region switch-sensitive control core and showed increased switch-related FC within this core and between the core and default mode, subcortical, and cerebellar systems. At the individual-difference level, generalized estimating equations revealed task-dependent brain-behavior relationships: core-within and core-subcortical FC were more positively associated with drift-rate switch cost during language switching than during rule switching. Together, the results identify partial overlap in regional recruitment, similarly directed system-level FC changes, and distinct FC-evidence-accumulation relationships across tasks.

papers.title: Delayed intraparenchymal pneumocephalus causing internal capsule injury after endoscopic transsphenoidal surgery for recurrent Rathke's cleft cyst: illustrative case.
papers.authors: Tsukiyama A, Tahara S, Ishisaka E, Adachi K, Murai Y.
papers.abstract: Background Pneumocephalus is a rare but serious complication after endoscopic transsphenoidal surgery (ETSS), usually associated with CSF leakage and occasionally progressing to tension pneumocephalus. Delayed intraparenchymal pneumocephalus causing focal brain injury after ETSS for recurrent Rathke's cleft cyst (RCC) is exceptionally rare. Observations A 74-year-old woman underwent ETSS for recurrent RCC and was discharged on postoperative day (POD) 10 after an uneventful early course. On POD 37, she developed sudden left hemiparesis and mild dysarthria. Head CT demonstrated pneumocephalus extending from the sella toward the right internal capsule without rhinorrhea. With conservative management, the pneumocephalus gradually resolved, revealing parenchymal injury involving the posterior limb of the right internal capsule on CT and MRI. She later reported repeated nose blowing after discharge, including on the morning of symptom onset. Intraoperative endoscopic review revealed a depression in the anterior perforated substance, anatomically corresponding to the ruptured RCC and subsequent injury site. Lessons In recurrent or ruptured RCCs, occult communication between the sellar region and adjacent brain may permit air entry after postoperative Valsalva maneuvers. Strict counseling, recognition of high-risk parenchymal findings, and airtight multilayer reconstruction with a vascularized mucosal flap may reduce this risk. https://thejns.org/doi/10.3171/CASE26647.

papers.title: Management of a progressive post-Gamma Knife thalamic cyst using an Ommaya reservoir: illustrative case.
papers.authors: Gragg A, Failla Mulone M, Siler DA, Raslan AM.
papers.abstract: Background Delayed cyst formation is a known complication of Gamma Knife (GK) stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS). Estimates of this phenomenon occurring after GK-SRS for arteriovenous malformation are 1.6%-3.6%. Management strategies include aspiration, craniotomy, and shunt placement. This case report describes the placement of an Ommaya reservoir for recurrent symptomatic thalamic cyst formation after GK thalamotomy for essential tremor. Observations A 74-year-old female underwent left ventral intermediate nucleus GK thalamotomy for a medically refractory essential tremor in 2013 using a single 135-Gy shot. Eight years later, she developed right-sided motor symptoms and slurred speech. MRI demonstrated a left thalamic cyst with mass effect on adjacent thalamic structures and the posterior limb of the internal capsule. Initial burr hole biopsy and aspiration led to complete symptom resolution, but the cyst recurred. Her symptoms progressed and she underwent placement of a left Ommaya reservoir. She did well for approximately 1 year and then presented to the clinic with similar symptoms and worsened head tremor. CT showed a 2.8 × 2.1 × 1.5-cm cyst. Cyst aspiration via the Ommaya reservoir provided improvement in speech, gait, and head tremor. Lessons Ommaya reservoir placement may provide a minimally invasive and repeatable treatment option for recurrent symptomatic thalamic cysts after GK-SRS, particularly when intermittent decompression is preferred over permanent shunt placement or open surgical intervention. https://thejns.org/doi/10.3171/CASE26595.

papers.title: Hidden Neural Variability and the Unexplained Cochlear Implant Outcome
papers.authors: Strelnikov K.
papers.abstract: Cochlear implants work, but not equally. After decades of cohort studies, the familiar predictors of outcome (age, duration of deafness, residual hearing, etiology) still leave most of the spread between patients unexplained. Research on how the brain handles degraded speech, audiovisual cues and everyday sounds shows that implant outcome measures test the brain at least as much as the ear. Yet candidacy assessment still examines the cochlea, the auditory nerve and inner-ear anatomy, and rarely the cognitive and structural state of the brain that must learn to use the device. This article argues that undetected neural variability, including cognitive decline, hearing-related atrophy and incidental pathology in brains assumed to be normal, is a plausible and largely unmeasured contributor to the missing variance. It proposes routine cognitive and volumetric phenotyping of implant candidates, and of the control groups against which they are judged. Because the brain restores much of the degraded implant signal through its predictive mechanisms, the article also calls for a new line of work: the development of dedicated tests of predictive brain capacity, a measure currently absent from both candidacy assessment and outcome research.

papers.title: Rethinking Consciousness: The Self-Organising Information-Processing Systems Hypothesis
papers.authors: Potas JR.
papers.abstract: Across biology, artificial intelligence and social systems, interacting components develop specialised functions and collective capabilities that were not individually specified in advance. Examples range from reorganised living cells to functionally differentiated neural networks and collective decisions in animal groups. What organisational principles might account for these outcomes—and for consciousness?We propose the Self-Organising Information-Processing Systems (SOIPS) Hypothesis. Within physical and environmental constraints, causally accessible, information-mediated interactions among changeable components can generate organisational structures that alter subsequent interactions and enable new functions. SOIPS distinguishes a generative engine from Dimension A, describing informational organisation from functional signalling to context-sensitive coordination, and Dimension B, comprising the elementary functional families of retention, inference and regulation. Particular configurations of these elements support composite capabilities, including perception, memory, learning, agency and cognition. Developed capabilities can reshape their own organisational conditions, combine with other functions and contribute to systems at new organisational scales.Within this framework, consciousness is proposed as a configuration in which awareness-related information participates in flexible cognition. Awareness refers to the organised availability of information about relevant internal or external conditions. Consciousness is thus neither an inevitable endpoint of increasing complexity nor a capability restricted by definition to human biology. If experience is constituted by particular organised neural activity, SOIPS may also help investigate the origins of phenomenal experience.SOIPS offers a shared language for interpreting biological development, learned organisation in AI and collective behaviour. It also motivates testable predictions: changing information access, constraints or elementary functional contributions should alter the capabilities they support. Cross-domain interventions could assess whether analogous organisational relationships produce comparable outcomes, informing both scientific explanation and the design of artificial agents and institutions.

papers.title: Beyond Behavioral Adaptation: Evaluating the Added Value of EEG in Personalized Language Interfaces
papers.authors: Fernandes J, Bruno C, Santos LR.
papers.abstract: Neuroadaptive interfaces personalize human–computer interaction using brain activity, but whether neural measurements provide useful information beyond behavioral indicators remains unclear, particularly in language comprehension tasks. We propose a framework to investigate the added value of EEG in adaptive communication support. Written messages are presented through combinations of sentence segmentation, pictograms, and keyword labels, with presentation choices informed by individual preferences and task performance. A behavior-adaptive policy serves as the baseline for comparison with a neuroadaptive policy incorporating calibrated EEG estimates under signal-quality and uncertainty constraints. The research plan includes interface validation, behavioral feasibility testing, and an EEG-based comparison using held-out sessions. Evaluation focuses on comprehension accuracy, response time, subjective effort, and adaptation behavior. The objective is to determine whether neural information improves assistance decisions and user outcomes beyond behavioral adaptation.

papers.title: Resting-state alpha scale-free dynamics predict individual differences in the balance between reward-learned and preference-based values during free choice
papers.authors: Zhu J, Hashimoto J, Honda T, Yamamoto K, Anno M, Northoff G, Nakao T.
papers.abstract: Values learned through reward can continue to influence choices guided by one's own preferences, such as which painting to hang, to an extent that varies across individuals. Because such preferences build up gradually across choices, their expression may depend on how well internally generated states are sustained over time, a property indexed by long-range temporal correlations (LRTC) in intrinsic brain activity. We tested whether resting-state alpha-band LRTC predicts individual differences in the balance between reward-learned and preference-based values. Eighty-one participants learned through probabilistic feedback which of four abstract shapes tended to be rewarded, and then judged their preferences among these shapes and 11 new shapes without feedback. Alpha LRTC was estimated by detrended fluctuation analysis of resting-state electroencephalography recorded before, between, and after the tasks. A trial-level mixed-effects model showed that reward history influenced preference judgments and that this influence decreased with resting-state alpha LRTC: participants with weak LRTC chose high-reward shapes over new shapes on 75% of trials, whereas those with strong LRTC were close to indifference (54%). The relationship was distributed across the scalp, stable across recordings, and not explained by spectral power or learning performance. Resting-state alpha LRTC is thus related to how strongly reward-learned values are carried into preference-based choice. Given the view that stronger LRTC reflects a longer window over which internally generated states are integrated, the observed relationship could arise because the window is biased toward values built up through one's own choices, or because it attenuates values learned under a criterion that no longer applies; which account holds remains to be determined.

papers.title: HP-GSBS: Accelerating greedy state boundary search with reusable interval statistics
papers.authors: Zhao Y, Ji Y.
papers.abstract: Abstract Greedy State Boundary Search (GSBS) identifies transitions between relatively stable neural activity patterns in continuous recordings. Repeated template reconstruction and correlation evaluation make analyses across recordings and parameter settings computationally expensive. We present HP-GSBS, an open-source implementation that expresses the matching objective as additive interval contributions and computes t-distance from reusable correlation statistics. Streaming candidate reduction, sequential local refinement, and active-block reuse complement CPU, PyTorch CUDA, and Triton execution paths. Across seven controlled workloads with two input realizations each, median same-input speedups range from 154 to 1,730. All 168 optimized executions reproduce complete reference boundary histories and selected state counts, with a maximum absolute t-distance difference of $1.88\times10^{-11}$. Four publicly supplied BBBD EEG analysis matrices provide complementary cross-backend validation. A naturalistic fMRI application segments 4,230 angular-gyrus voxels in a group response and 16 participants; the 17 CPU fits total 213.10 seconds. Mean pairwise boundary alignment exceeds a circular-shift baseline, illustrating cohort-level use of the saved segmentations. Versioned results, recording-level parallelism, and optional low-memory execution support varied analysis scales. HP-GSBS connects an explicit mathematical reformulation of repeated computation to efficient and reproducible neural-state analysis.

papers.title: Endoscopic ultrasound in the diagnosis of chronic pancreatitis: a structured state-of-the-art review.
papers.authors: Iglesias-García J, Domínguez Novoa Y, Lariño Noia J, Domínguez-Muñoz E.
papers.abstract: Chronic pancreatitis (CP) is diagnosed by integrating clinical probability, structural imaging and, when required, pancreatic function. Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) is proposed as a first-line investigation in selected patients evaluated in expert centers when the principal question is early or minimal-change CP in a high-probability clinical setting, or when a known focal pancreatic lesion requires detailed characterization or tissue acquisition. This proposed sequence is an individualized alternative to guidance recommending CT or MRI as initial imaging in the general population with suspected CP; cross-sectional imaging remains complementary for alternative diagnoses, complications and lesion staging. EUS also has an established role after inconclusive CT or MRI/MRCP. This structured state-of-the-art review addresses predefined clinical questions and separates established practice from adjunctive and investigational EUS technologies. Conventional B-mode EUS with standardized morphologic reporting is the established endoscopic technique, although interobserver variability and imperfect specificity limit its use as an isolated reference standard. Strain elastography, contrast-enhanced EUS and secretin-stimulated EUS pancreatic function testing can add stiffness, perfusion or functional information in selected patients. Shear wave elastography and detective flow imaging remain emerging technologies requiring multicenter validation and standardized thresholds. Tissue acquisition is not recommended solely to prove CP and should be reserved mainly for suspected malignancy or autoimmune pancreatitis. A stepwise pathway distinguishes selected first-line EUS assessment from the guideline-based CT/MRI-first sequence and integrates complementary imaging and selective functional testing.

papers.title: One-shot learning of paired association navigation with biologically plausible schemas.
papers.authors: Kumar MG, Tan C, Libedinsky C, Yen SC, Tan AYY.
papers.journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
papers.abstract: After learning a multiple paired-association (MPA) navigation task, rodents can rapidly learn new cue-location associations after a single exposure, a phenomenon proposed to be facilitated by cognitive schemas. However, it remains unclear what schemas support this behavior and how they could be implemented in biological neural circuits. Here, we identify a set of schemas sufficient for gradual then one-shot paired-association navigation, and implement them in a fully neural agent using biologically plausible plasticity rules. The agent gradually acquires a low-dimensional spatial metric representation using a path-integration based temporal-difference error, enabling self-localization across different environments. It also contains a memory network that forms one-shot associations between sensory cues and goal locations, implemented using reward-modulated exploratory Hebbian (EH) plasticity. A third network performs vector subtraction between the agent's current and goal location to compute goal-directed actions. Supplementing these schemas with an actor-critic enables one-shot navigation past obstacles. Lastly, learning a working-memory gating mechanism using the temporal-difference error enables one-shot learning even with brief cue and distractor presentation. The model reproduces key behavioral features of rodent learning in the MPA task and generates testable predictions about the neural mechanisms underlying schema-based one-shot learning.Significance Statement Schema-dependent learning is exemplified by better recall of a lecture when one already has a schema for understanding. A rodent navigation task showing a shift from slow to rapid learning has been proposed to reflect such schema use, yet how schemas are neurally implemented and enable faster learning is poorly understood. We clarify this gap in this computational study by describing several schemas and implement them as neural networks with biologically plausible learning rules. Composing them into an agent reproduces schema-dependent rodent learning behavior. Because schemas also shape self beliefs, clarifying their neural basis has implications for psychopathology. At the same time, understanding how biological schemas support rapid learning may inform advances in machine learning.

papers.title: Emotional Content Enhances Attentional Tracking of Conversations through Context-Sensitive Modulation of Auditory-Language Networks.
papers.authors: Heikkinen P, Lepistö S, Wikman P, Koskinen E, Peräkylä A, Ravaja N, Harjunen VJ.
papers.journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
papers.abstract: Engagement in conversation often requires continuous monitoring of relevant speech in a continuously evolving auditory environment. Emotional salience of semantic content may influence this process, but its role in attentional tracking of continuous speech remains unclear. We address this question using an audiovisual "Cocktail-party" paradigm combined with source-localized magnetoencephalography and encoding-decoding analyses. Participants (18 female, 14 male) selectively attended to one dialogue while ignoring a concurrent distractor dialogue, with both emotional salience and semantic coherence of the conversations manipulated independently. Decoding analyses revealed that negatively valenced, high-arousal, and socially relevant semantic content strengthened neural speech tracking, but only for attended dialogues. This effect depended on semantic structure, emerging earlier in semantically coherent than incoherent dialogues. Encoding analyses further showed latency- and region-specific effects across temporal, parietal, and frontal cortical regions. Emotional salience and coherence jointly modulated mid-latency (100 - 250 ms) responses, whereas late-latency (270 - 450 ms) responses were driven primarily by emotional salience. These findings demonstrate that emotional meaning enhances neural prioritization of attended speech and semantic coherence shapes the temporal dynamics of this enhancement. Together, these results indicate context-sensitive emotional modulation of auditory-language processing during selective listening of continuous speech.Significance Statement Understanding how the brain prioritizes and selectively processes information in naturalistic, continuously evolving audiovisual scenes such as conversations is a central challenge in neuroscience. Here, we show that conversations conveying negatively valenced, high-arousal, and socially relevant content enhance neural tracking of attended speech in a noisy cocktail-party setting. This enhanced tracking depends on the semantic structure of the conversation, emerging earlier for coherent dialogues that are easy to follow. Furthermore, we show that emotional content strengthens mechanisms related to speech comprehension and sharpens segregation of relevant from irrelevant talk. These findings demonstrate that emotional meaning and semantic continuity jointly shape cortical processing of continuous speech, providing new insight into how the brain selects and processes meaningful information during a conversation.

papers.title: Neurocognitive characteristics of perceptual feedback processing differ in autism.
papers.authors: Zuk NJ, Slobodskoy-Plusnin JY, Weiss Y, Sampath V, Düsterwald KM, Akrami A, Ahissar M.
papers.journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
papers.abstract: Autistic individuals often show reduced adaptation to changing environmental demands, but the neurocognitive mechanisms underlying this difference remain unclear. We asked whether it may be explained by reduced sensitivity to external feedback and changes in task difficulty. Autistic and non-autistic adults of either sex, matched for cognitive ability, performed a pitch discrimination task in which their response was immediately followed by feedback. Accuracy was similar between the two groups, yet autistic participants exhibited a markedly reduced feedback-related negativity (FRN), an event-related EEG potential differentiating explicit negative versus positive feedback. They also showed weaker modulation of feedback-evoked EEG responses by perceptual difficulty. Lastly, they showed reduced trial-by-trial behavioral updating of perceptual bias following recent correct and easy trials. These effects were replicated in a follow-up experiment conducted 1-2 years later. When combined they classified autistic and non-autistic participants with about 80% accuracy. Together, our findings indicate that multiple processes for evaluating perceptual decisions and adjusting subsequent behavior differ in autism and likely contribute to slow updating in changing contexts.Significance Statement Autism is associated with reduced adaptation to changing environments in both behavior and neural signals, but the underlying neurocognitive mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we show that autistic individuals exhibit a reduced feedback-related negativity (FRN), an EEG component that is present when receiving negative instead of positive feedback. They also show weaker neural modulation by perceptual difficulty and reduced trial-by-trial behavioral updating of perceptual bias following recent correct and easy trials. These effects were replicated in a follow-up study. When combined, they classified autistic and non-autistic participants with high accuracy. These findings suggest that reduced flexibility in autism is associated with reduced processing of external feedback and task difficulty.

papers.title: An integrative computational approach for obstacle avoidance during action selection.
papers.authors: Zhong S, Pouratian N, Schrater P, Christopoulos V.
papers.abstract: Action selection in cluttered environments, where individuals must simultaneously pursue goals and avoid obstacles, presents a significant challenge for the brain. To understand the underlying mechanisms of action selection in such contexts, we propose a computational model that extends stochastic optimal control theory through a novel framework for obstacle avoidance. The model decomposes action selection into a weighted combination of individual control policies, each generated for either target approach or obstacle avoidance. By integrating value information from goals, obstacles, and actions into a unified measure of "relative desirability", the model dynamically determines the contribution of each policy to the overall action selection process. We evaluated the framework using simulated target-reaching tasks in cluttered environments based on previous human studies. The results showed that the model qualitatively captures key features of human motor behavior, including the influence of obstacle properties on movement trajectories and the transient tendency to initiate movements toward obstacles before avoidance. This work offers new insights into the dynamic interaction between approach and avoidance behaviors, providing a basis for future studies of action selection in more complex and naturalistic settings.

papers.title: Characterization of airway mucus using quantitative MRI: an in vitro proof-of-concept study.
papers.authors: Sedaghat S, Park JI, Fu E, Piran M, Ghasemiesfe A, Jung Y, Jang H.
papers.abstract: Objectives A characteristic of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is mucus hypersecretion. In this proof-of-concept study, we aimed to characterize airway mucus using a quantitative ultrashort echo time (UTE) magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) sequence in a controlled in vitro synthetic mucus model to establish a technical foundation for future in vivo studies. Materials and methods UTE double-echo steady-state (UTE-DESS) was performed to acquire the signal from free induction decay-like signal and spin/stimulated echo-like signal echoes; quantitative MRI parameters (T1, T2, and diffusivity) were estimated. Synthetic mucus phantoms were prepared using mucin (0.20%, 0.50%, and 1.0%) mixed with xanthan gum (0.10%, 0.25%, and 0.50%) to replicate the viscoelastic properties of human laryngeal mucus, and samples were embedded in 1% agar for imaging. Results The mucus phantoms with varying concentrations of mucin and xanthan exhibited visual differences in color and opacity. Estimated T1 values were 2.23 ± 0.16, 2.37 ± 0.20, and 2.09 ± 0.18 s (mean ± standard deviation) for the three tubes with relative mucus concentrations of 1, 2.5, and 5, respectively. Corresponding T2 values were 806.6 ± 105.6, 687.4 ± 78.0, and 475.0 ± 41.3 ms, while diffusivity values were 2.36 ± 0.14, 2.31 ± 0.18, and 2.33 ± 0.18 µm2 /ms for the three tubes. Only the T2 relaxation times showed a significant linear correlation with mucus concentration (r = -0.9998, p = 0.0112). Conclusion UTE-DESS MRI could be feasible for characterizing airway mucus. T2 relaxation time showed a strong inverse correlation with increasing mucus concentration, indicating its sensitivity to mucus content. Key points Question Can a novel quantitative ultrashort echo time MRI sequence noninvasively characterize airway mucus properties and overcome conventional lung imaging limitations in muco-obstructive diseases? Findings In this controlled in vitro model, UTE-DESS MRI mapping demonstrated that T2 relaxation times alone showed a strong inverse correlation with increasing mucus concentrations. Relevance statement This exploratory proof-of-concept establishes a technical foundation for radiation-free, noninvasive T2 mapping to monitor and phenotype chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and other mucoobstructive lung diseases in future in vivo studies.

papers.title: Multiparametric MRI radiomics model for preoperative prediction of IDH1 R132H immunopositivity status in adult diffuse Glioma.
papers.authors: Nguyen HD, Le MHT, Tran HT, Nguyen TP, Nguyen VT, Dinh HT, Nguyen TV, Vuong NK.
papers.abstract: Gliomas are the most common primary brain tumors, and isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) mutation status is a critical molecular marker influencing prognosis and treatment planning. This study aimed to evaluate the value of a multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) radiomics model in predicting IDH1 R132H immunopositivity status in patients with gliomas. A retrospective analysis was conducted on 94 adult glioma patients at Viet Duc University Hospital from June 2024 to January 2026. All patients underwent preoperative MRI including conventional sequences, diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI), and dynamic susceptibility contrast perfusion imaging (DSC-MRI). Radiomics features were extracted from apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) and relative cerebral blood volume (rCBV) maps within the tumor region, followed by correlation filtering and LASSO (Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator)-based feature selection, retaining 5 ADC and 10 rCBV features for logistic regression model construction. The ADC-based model achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.875, the rCBV-based model reached 0.943, and the combined model achieved the highest numerical AUC (0.955), with an accuracy of 89.5%, sensitivity of 87.5%, and specificity of 90.9%, although the differences between models were not statistically significant. These findings suggest that multiparametric MRI radiomics demonstrates promising discriminatory performance for preoperative prediction of IDH1 R132H immunopositivity status in glioma patients, although these estimates derive from a single-center cohort with a small held-out test set and therefore require external validation in larger, prospective cohorts.

papers.title: Repeated Head Impacts May Compromise White Matter Integrity and Bimanual Coordination in American Football Players.
papers.authors: D'Amario S, Magee B, Champagne AA, Wilson ME, Ramírez-García G, Coverdale NS, Cook DJ.
papers.abstract: Background Repeated head impacts (RHI) in American Football may contribute to subtle white matter (WM) abnormalities and functional deficits even in the absence of clinically diagnosed concussion. Hypothesis Contact athletes would demonstrate tract-specific differences in fractional anisotropy (FA) and mean diffusivity (MD) compared with noncontact controls, and high-exposure (HE) athletes would show greater within-season diffusion change, worse bimanual coordination, and greater symptom burden than low-exposure (LE) athletes. Study design Prospective cohort study. Level of evidence Level 3. Methods Twenty-two male varsity American Football players and 13 male noncontact controls underwent preseason diffusion tensor imaging. Football athletes were monitored over a single season using helmet-mounted accelerometers and stratified into HE and LE groups. Tract-specific FA and MD were derived using probabilistic tractography. Pre-post SCAT3 symptom and severity checklist data were collected from all football athletes, and pre-post Kinarm Ball-on-Bar (BOB) bimanual coordination data were available for 12 athletes. Results At preseason, contact athletes demonstrated higher FA in 15 of 16 tracts compared with noncontact controls, with lower FA in the forceps minor. MD was lower in 10 of 16 tracts, higher in the bilateral inferior longitudinal fasciculus, and similar in the corticospinal tract and superior thalamic radiation. Over the season, HE athletes sustained more impacts (P < 0.001) and greater cumulative g -force (P = 0.001) than LE athletes. On the BOB task, LE athletes showed modest improvement, whereas HE athletes worsened, yielding a between-group difference in change of 0.59 (95% CI, 0.22-0.96; P = 0.005). Generalized estimating equation models accounting for within-athlete tract correlations did not detect HE-versus-LE differences in FA change (Wald χ²(1) = 0.14; P = 0.71) or MD change (Wald χ²(1) < 0.01; P > 0.99), and SCAT3 symptom and severity scores remained low with no meaningful between-group differences. Conclusion In 22 contact athletes, repeated head-impact exposure was associated with preseason WM differences and worsening bimanual coordination across a single season, while longitudinal tract-level DTI and symptom-based clinical measures showed limited between-group change. Clinical relevance Objective motor assessment and advanced neuroimaging may help characterize subtle consequences of RHIs that are missed by routine symptom-based tools.

papers.title: Mind the Gap: How Velopharyngeal Gap Size Influences Consonant Accuracy.
papers.authors: Snodgrass TD, Alvarez-Montoya E, Donner M, Nett Cordero K, Perry JL, Philp J, Singh DJ, Sitzman TJ, Chee-Williams JL.
papers.journal: The Cleft palate-craniofacial journal : official publication of the American Cleft Palate-Craniofacial Association
papers.abstract: ObjectiveAssess if velopharyngeal gap size during speech is associated with consonant accuracy and whether hypernasality severity and compensatory misarticulation errors (CMAs) mediate this relationship.DesignCross-sectional.SettingMetropolitan hospital.ParticipantsEighty-one patients undergoing assessment for velopharyngeal insufficiency (VPI).Assessment(s)Each patient completed a preoperative magnetic resonance imaging protocol during sustained /i/ production and a perceptual speech evaluation. Velopharyngeal gap size was measured in millimeters. Hypernasality was rated using the Cleft Audit Protocol for Speech-Augmented-Americleft Modification. Percent consonants correct (PCC) and percent of CMAs used were derived from transcriptions of the American English sentence or phrase sample.Main Outcome Measure(s)A generalized structural equation model was used to examine whether velopharyngeal gap size is associated with PCC indirectly through hypernasality severity and CMA use.ResultsLarger velopharyngeal gap sizes were associated with more severe hypernasality (P < .001), greater hypernasality severity was associated with increased CMA use (P < .001), and greater CMA use was associated with lower PCC (P < .001). Velopharyngeal gap size was not directly associated with PCC (P = .400). However, the full indirect pathway from gap size to PCC through hypernasality severity and CMA use was significant (P = .001); gap size was significantly associated with PCC when accounting for both direct and indirect pathways combined (P = .005).ConclusionsThese findings suggest hypernasality severity is the key mediator between gap size and speech accuracy. Patients with more severe hypernasality may benefit from timely surgical remediation of VPI to increase overall consonant accuracy.

papers.title: Motion-corrected structural realignment and quantitative voxel targeting in magnetic resonance spectroscopy.
papers.authors: Manting CL, Takahashi A, Ahveninen J, Mujica-Parodi LR, Ratai EM.
papers.abstract: Magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) non-invasively quantifies neurochemical metabolites within a prescribed voxel in the brain, but is highly sensitive to head motion that displaces the voxel from its intended anatomical location, and introduces spectral contamination as well as tissue estimation errors. In particular, voxel displacement into bone tissue severely degrades spectral quality due to lipid contamination, often rendering the data unusable. While promising solutions exist to address motion-related issues, many rely on specialized infrastructure and expertise available only at a limited number of research centers. To address inter-acquisition motion, we combine automatic voxel repositioning using an updated 18 s head scout MRI, acquired immediately before MRS, with realignment of the structural MRI to ensure that tissue correction is based on the updated voxel location. Furthermore to quantify anatomical targeting accuracy, we introduced a voxel-ROI overlap metric that measures the percentage intersection between the prescribed voxel and atlas-defined target regions, enabling objective evaluation of voxel positioning accuracy. Using voxels prescribed across three brain regions (prefrontal cortex, thalamus, left superior temporal gyrus; N = 31), realignment on average increased voxel-ROI overlap by 24%, reduced inter-subject variability in tissue composition by 8.1%, and eliminated bone contamination in all six affected cases. Our computationally efficient method executes in < 35 s per participant and requires no specialized hardware, offering an accessible solution that integrates inter-acquisition motion correction with quantitative assessment to achieve accurate voxel targeting.

papers.title: Somatotopic functional connectivity gradients in the monkey and human striatum.
papers.authors: Goda N, Chiken S, Koketsu D, Nambu A, Fukunaga M.
papers.abstract: Understanding the topographic and functional organization of the striatum-a key brain structure involved in motor control, learning, and cognition-is crucial for elucidating the pathophysiology of the neurological and psychiatric disorders associated to it, and for developing targeted therapies. While recent magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) studies in humans and non-human primates have noninvasively characterized the brain-wide connectivity patterns of the striatum, its detailed somatotopic organization and the homology across species remains to be fully elucidated. We aimed to comprehensively characterize the somatotopic organization of the striatum in macaque monkeys based on functional connectivity patterns, and to assess the extent of homology or divergence of this organization between macaque monkeys and humans. Resting-state functional connectivity data were obtained from 11 anesthetized macaques using an ultra-high-field 7-tesla MRI scanner. Using two complementary approaches-seed-based analysis and connectopic mapping-we successfully delineated a distinct, regular volumetric somatotopic map within the macaque posterior putamen, a motor-related subregion of the striatum. This map exhibited a gradient encompassing the lower limb, trunk, upper limb, and face representations, predominantly oriented along the dorsal-ventral axis. The somatotopic gradient identified in macaques demonstrated a remarkable similarity with the corresponding gradient in the human posterior putamen, characterized using a publicly available resting-state functional MRI dataset. Furthermore, cross-species decoding analysis revealed that the somatotopy of the human posterior putamen could be accurately predicted using the anatomically aligned macaque somatotopic map obtained in this study as reference. In addition to this shared gradient organization, our seed-based analyses suggested non-gradient-like features in the human posterior putamen. These findings offer compelling evidence for the high evolutionary conservation of the major topographic organization in the primate posterior putamen, while pointing to species-specific divergence.

papers.title: Oromotor functional networks in the marmoset monkey.
papers.authors: Jafari A, Dureux A, Zanini A, Eed AFK, Corigliano MR, Lin MK, Schaeffer DJ, Menon RS, Everling S.
papers.abstract: Primate communication relies on the precise coordination of the orofacial complex. While New World monkeys are growing models for vocal communication research, the neural basis underlying their oromotor control remains underexplored. Here, we used ultra-high-field fMRI in awake common marmosets (Callithrix jacchus ) to map the whole-brain neural networks engaged during spontaneous visible oromotor functions-including jaw and lip movements, tongue protrusion, swallowing, and vocalization-distinct from those recruited during the auditory processing of conspecific calls. The resulting oromotor maps reveal a widespread control substrate extending beyond primary sensorimotor cortices, encompassing dorsal prefrontal (areas 8aD, 8b), mid-cingulate, posterior parietal areas (PF, PFG, and PE), and auditory regions. The parietal engagement points to a role for sensorimotor integration in marmoset oromotor control. Subcortically, this network engages the thalamus, basal ganglia, and cerebellum, with additional activation in the medullary reticular formation and periaqueductal gray, brainstem regions implicated in rhythmic oromotor control. A predominantly dorsal pattern of activation, with limited ventral premotor engagement, defines this network and provides a foundational framework for future studies of vocal-motor control in this species and a comparative reference for the rhythmic oromotor substrates from which speech is hypothesized to have evolved.

papers.title: Disrupted brain network topology and structure-function coupling in non-specific low back pain.
papers.authors: Butry L, Junker F, Vickery S, Belavy DL, Döding R, Ehrenbrusthoff K, Angelova M, Buehring B, Fitzgibbon B, Karmakar C, Miller CT, Owen PJ, Schulte TL, Tagliaferri SD, Trudel G, Van Oosterwijck J, Wilke HJ, Enax-Krumova EK, Schlaffke L.
papers.abstract: Central nervous system mechanisms contribute to non-specific low back pain (LBP), with widespread alterations in brain function and structure reported. It remains unclear how these alterations propagate to brain network topology and structure-function coupling. In this cross-sectional study, 282 participants with non-specific LBP (mean ± standard deviation, pain intensity 4.3 ± 1.7 [0-10 numerical rating scale]; current pain duration 54 ± 105 weeks) and 71 pain-free controls underwent resting-state functional and diffusion-weighted MRI to derive functional and structural connectomes. Subgroups were analyzed by pain status during scanning and pain duration. The main graph-theory analysis revealed that participants with non-specific LBP had lower segregation (d = 0.39-0.45, P = 0.009-0.019) in the whole-brain functional network and higher integration (d = 0.30-0.38, P = 0.005-0.027) in the functional ventral attention network. Subgroup analysis showed that participants with chronic non-specific LBP had lower segregation (d = 0.48, P = 0.002) and higher integration (d = 0.45, P = 0.004) within the structural default mode network. By modeling functional connectivity using structural communication predictors in a multivariable linear regression, we identified structure-function decoupling in participants with non-specific LBP across the whole-brain (d = 0.25-0.28, P = 0.026-0.041), ventral attention (d = 0.28-0.32, P = 0.005-0.048), and default mode network (d = 0.22-0.24, P = 0.031-0.046), alongside complex regional patterns of both decoupling and hypercoupling. Explorative partial correlation analyses associated disability, rather than pain intensity, with differences in brain network topology and structure-function decoupling. These findings advance the mechanistic understanding of the severity and persistence of non-specific LBP, showing disrupted bottom-up attentional processing and self-referential circuitry, resulting in large-scale structure-function decoupling.

papers.title: Reconstructing Cenozoic grasslands in North America and western Eurasia: evidence for cold-season grasses from 3D phytolith morphology.
papers.authors: Hermans RM, Gallaher TJ, Brightly WH, Zender C, Snoeck C, Strömberg CAE.
papers.abstract: Pooideae, the largest grass subfamily, radiated in the Northern Hemisphere from the Paleocene onward and today dominates cold-season and high-altitude grasslands. Fossil phytolith assemblages suggest pooid-rich ecosystems during the Oligocene-Miocene, but the lack of quantitative phytolith identification has limited reconstruction of early grassland composition and ecology. We combined 3D geometric morphometrics of grass silica short-cell phytoliths (GSSCPs) with machine-learning classification and phylogenetically informed climate modelling. A dataset of modern GSSCPs was used to classify Eocene-Miocene phytoliths from Türkiye and the US Great Plains and reconstruct paleoclimate. 3D GSSCP morphology distinguished modern grass subfamilies and tribes. Fossil assemblages contained mainly phytoliths assigned to Bambusoideae and Pooideae (including Poeae I and II). In modern grasses, Crenate and Polylobate phytolith dimensions correlated with temperature and precipitation. Fossil Crenates and Polylobates yielded climate estimates warmer and wetter than today. Ancestral state reconstructions indicated milder winter conditions at early Pooideae nodes, with cold tolerance arising early. Major temperate grass lineages (Poeae I and II) were established earlier than previously recognized, and Pooideae-rich grasslands were present by the Oligo-Miocene under warmer, wetter climates than today. These findings demonstrate the value of 3D phytolith morphometrics for interpreting early grassland evolution.

papers.title: Analysis of Muscle Fibre Orientation in the Human Medial and Lateral Pterygoid Muscles Using Diffusion Tensor Imaging: A Methodological Study.
papers.authors: Kinomura S, Sugano T, Tatewaki Y, Oba K, Shobara K, Ogawa T, Taki Y, Niizuma K, Kawashima R, Sasaki K, Yoda N.
papers.abstract: Background Deep anatomical locations limit functional and morphological evaluation of the medial and lateral pterygoid muscles, which are vital for mandibular kinematics. The lateral pterygoid comprises superior and inferior heads with distinct anatomical and functional characteristics. Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) tractography non-invasively visualises in vivo muscle fibre orientation. Objectives This methodological study aimed to quantify 3D fibre orientation of the medial pterygoid and both lateral pterygoid heads using DTI tractography, comparing simulated mandibular rest and 25-mm open-mouth positions. Methods Healthy males (28.4 ± 4.6 years) underwent cephalometric radiography and 3.0-T MRI. T1-weighted and DTI sequences were acquired at both mandibular positions. Target muscles were segmented. MRtrix3 tractograms were reconstructed (fibre orientation distribution [FOD] amplitude cutoffs: 0.02-0.10). Fibre orientations, quantified via vector projection onto coronal and sagittal planes, were statistically compared. Results Tractography successfully visualised fibre orientation; optimal FOD amplitude cutoffs varied among individuals and muscles. The medial pterygoid showed no significant changes. During mouth opening, seven participants exhibited marked fibre reorientation in the superior head and seven in the inferior head, although the direction and magnitude varied among participants. However, group-level analyses revealed no significant orientation differences for any muscle. Conclusion DTI tractography enabled in vivo evaluation of medial and lateral pterygoid internal fibre architecture. Between simulated rest and 25-mm open-mouth positions, group-level differences were non-significant in either plane despite variable lateral pterygoid reorientation. Inter-individual variability and FOD cutoff dependence highlight the need for participant- and muscle-specific parameter adjustment. These findings provide a methodological basis for future DTI applications in temporomandibular disorders and masticatory dysfunction.

papers.title: Research advances on the role of glutamate AMPA receptors in the pathogenesis and treatment of migraine: A narrative review.
papers.authors: Fan Y, Ye W, Sun Y, Li D, Liu J, Li Z, Huang Y.
papers.abstract: Background Migraine is a prevalent neurological disorder with incompletely understood mechanisms. Glutamate, the primary excitatory neurotransmitter, and its AMPA receptors (AMPARs) have emerged as key players in migraine pathophysiology. Objective This study aimed to synthesize current evidence on the role of AMPA receptors in migraine pathogenesis and to evaluate the therapeutic potential of AMPA receptor antagonists in migraine management. Methods This is a narrative review. A literature search was conducted on PubMed using the terms "migraine" AND "glutamate" AND "AMPA receptor." Additional related terms (e.g., "AMPA receptor antagonist," "perampanel," "cortical spreading depression (CSD)," "trigeminovascular system (TVS)," and "central sensitization") were used to broaden the search and capture relevant mechanistic and therapeutic studies. Only "English-language" articles published from inception to 2025 were considered. Relevant preclinical and clinical studies addressing the role of AMPA receptors in migraine pathophysiology (including "CSD," "TVS activation," and "central sensitization") and/or the therapeutic potential of AMPA receptor antagonists, particularly "perampanel," were included. No restrictions were placed on publication type. Results AMPARs contribute to migraine through multiple pathways. Their role in CSD remains controversial, with conflicting evidence on whether they are essential for CSD initiation and propagation. In contrast, AMPARs clearly facilitate TVS activation by promoting the release of calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) and pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide (PACAP), driving neurogenic inflammation and nociceptive transmission. Moreover, phosphorylation of AMPAR subunits, particularly GluA1 at Ser81 and Ser845, is a critical molecular mechanism underlying central sensitization, leading to allodynia and migraine chronification. Although early AMPAR antagonists, such as BGG492, showed limited clinical efficacy, the selective noncompetitive AMPAR antagonist perampanel has demonstrated anti-migraine potential in preclinical models by inhibiting PACAP and CGRP release and has shown clinical benefit in patients with comorbid epilepsy and migraine. Conclusion AMPA receptors play a pivotal role in TVS activation and central sensitization in migraine. Perampanel is a promising candidate for migraine therapy, but further clinical trials are needed to confirm its efficacy and safety in patients with migraine without epilepsy.

papers.title: Gut consciousness: a perspective on visceral phenomenal awareness.
papers.authors: Hasler G.
papers.abstract: The proposition that the enteric nervous system sustains a form of consciousness is seldom entertained in mainstream neuroscience, yet it follows from a disciplined reading of contemporary theories of mind. We argue that the 400-600 million neurons embedded in the mammalian gastrointestinal wall, taken together with the vast interoceptive surface they supervise, the enteroendocrine-immune interface, and the microbial community they co-regulate, constitute a substrate that satisfies, on several of the leading theories of consciousness, the criteria those theories use to attribute experience elsewhere. We synthesize evidence on enteric autonomy, chemo- and mechanosensory resolution, vagal and humoral signalling, self/non-self-discrimination at the epithelial-immune boundary, comparative data from invertebrates whose nervous systems are dominated by gut-like plexuses, and convergent clinical signatures (irritable bowel syndrome, food intolerances, psychedelic nausea, glucagon-like peptide-1 signalling) that are difficult to accommodate under a purely sensorimotor account. Throughout we distinguish two claims that are easily conflated: that the gut makes a large and underappreciated contribution to the single consciousness of the whole animal, and that enteric processing constitutes a second, much simpler locus of experience of its own. Most of the available evidence bears on the first, and we set out five lines of investigation that would discriminate between them. We conclude that gut consciousness is a testable hypothesis, likely corresponding to an 'animal' mode of consciousness dominated by interoceptive feel, drive and affect, and we propose empirical directions for its further investigation.

papers.title: Do psychiatrists have a spider-sense? Clinical impressions as violations of interpersonal Bayesian expectation.
papers.authors: Amad A, D'Hondt F, Gauld C, Bertoux M, Daoudi M, Fovet T.
papers.abstract: Psychiatric diagnosis depends on the clinician's ability to infer mental states from complex and dynamically evolving interpersonal signals. During the psychiatric interview, clinicians do not only collect explicit symptoms; they continuously sample a rich array of non-verbal and paralinguistic cues including gaze, prosody, affective reciprocity, and interactional timing. These signals are central to psychiatric assessment, yet their contribution to diagnostic reasoning remains poorly formalized. In this Review, we propose a computational account of clinical impressions in psychiatry. We integrate evidence from phenomenological psychopathology, social cognition, and computational neuroscience. We argue that such impressions may arise when the clinician's generative model of social interaction is persistently disconfirmed by subtle deviations in interpersonal behaviour, generating high-level social prediction errors experienced as a sense of incongruity or failed attunement. We formalize this process as VIBE: Violation of Interpersonal Bayesian Expectation. VIBE denotes a pre-reflective epistemic signal generated when observed interpersonal cues deviate from the clinician's expected model of social reciprocity. It is not a diagnostic criterion but orients hypothesis generation by drawing attention to disturbances in interpersonal predictability. We hypothesize that VIBE may constitute a transdiagnostic mechanism: different disorders, from schizophrenia to autism spectrum disorder and mood disorders, may disrupt distinct dimensions of interpersonal prediction. The Praecox Feeling, first described by Rümke in 1942, can be read as the earliest clinical formalization of this process and as its schizophrenia-spectrum instance, in which the profile of interpersonal violations is consistent enough to be clinically recognizable. This framework recasts the diagnostic impression as an embodied inferential process rather than an opaque subjective faculty. Teaching clinicians to articulate, examine, and recalibrate these impressions could strengthen diagnostic reasoning, reduce bias, and improve therapeutic attunement. VIBE provides a bridge between phenomenological psychopathology and computational neuroscience, and offers a tractable, empirically testable model for studying the neurocomputational basis of psychiatric clinical judgement.

papers.title: REFS: Robust EEG feature selection with incomplete labels for multi-dimensional emotion recognition.
papers.authors: Xu X, Dong W, Wei F, Zhuo L.
papers.abstract: Objective Compared to single-type features, multi-type electroencephalography (EEG) features provide a multi-level representation for analyzing multi-dimensional emotions. However, the high dimensionality of multi-type EEG features, combined with the relatively small number of high-quality EEG samples, poses challenges such as classifier overfitting and suboptimal real-time performance in the multi-dimensional emotion recognition task. As the number of EEG channels increases, the issue will become increasingly severe. Moreover, practical applications of affective brain-computer interface frequently encounters partial absence of multi-dimensional emotional label data due to diverse emotional self-assessment models, and ambiguity and variability in individual emotion perception. Approach To address these challenges, this study proposes a novel robust EEG feature selection method for incomplete multi-dimensional emotion recognition. The method leverages adaptive orthogonal latent semantic indexing to reconstruct the multi-dimensional emotional label space through second-order and higher-order relations, which could reduce the negative impact of missing values and outliers on label reconstruction. Simultaneously, it employs least squares regression with graph-based manifold learning regularization and global feature redundancy minimization regularization to enable EEG feature subset selection despite missing information, ultimately achieving robust and fast EEG-based multi-dimensional emotion recognition. Main results The proposed method was validated on three multi-dimensional emotional datasets with varying channel configurations, namely DREAMER, DEAP and HDED, under different label missing ratios. Experimental results show that the proposed method consistently outperforms thirteen state-of-the-art feature selection methods in terms of robustness for EEG emotional feature selection across various missing ratios. Significance The proposed method provides a robust and efficient solution for feature selection in multi-dimensional emotion recognition under incomplete EEG label scenarios, delivering reliable performance for practical affective brain-computer interface applications.

papers.title: FMRI-guided focal transcranial magnetic stimulation of anterior cingulate cortex reduces opioid seeking and restores connectivity.
papers.authors: Ma Z, Duan Y, Nguyen H, Lin S, Haque MM, Wang D, Hoffman S, Carney A, Scott T, Varlas E, Stein E, Xi ZX, Shaham Y, Lu H, Yang Y.
papers.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
papers.abstract: Relapse remains a major challenge in opioid addiction treatment. Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) has emerged as a potential therapeutic strategy for addiction, yet results had been mixed due to empirically selected stimulation targets and limited knowledge of neural circuit engagement. Here, we used a focal rat TMS platform to test whether high-density theta-burst stimulation (hdTBS) of the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), a corticostriatal node implicated in opioid relapse by prior causal and longitudinal functional MRI studies, decreases relapse-like oxycodone seeking and associated circuit dysfunction. Male rats self-administered oxycodone intravenously for 14 d and then underwent 13 d of electric barrier-induced abstinence, a procedure that suppresses drug taking while preserving drug availability and drug-associated context. During abstinence, the rats received seven daily sessions of sham stimulation or ACC-targeted hdTBS, with relapse tests and longitudinal functional MRI acquired during early and late abstinence to assess the behavioral and circuit-level effects of stimulation. Sham-treated rats showed a time-dependent increase (incubation) in oxycodone seeking and reduced ACC connectivity with dorsal and ventral striatum. In contrast, ACC-targeted hdTBS prevented incubation of oxycodone seeking and reversed abstinence-associated ACC-striatal connectivity reductions. Stimulation-sensitive functional circuits showed spatial correspondence with tracer-defined ACC projection patterns, suggesting that anatomical connectivity is critical to the circuit-level effects of focal stimulation. These findings support ACC-centered corticostriatal circuits as mechanistically informed targets for neuromodulation in opioid addiction and introduce a preclinical framework for linking stimulation, behavior, and longitudinal circuit remodeling.

papers.title: Beyond the Therapy Room: An Illustrative Example for Designing and Evaluating Technology-Delivered Memory Rehabilitation After Traumatic Brain Injury.
papers.authors: Morrow EL.
papers.abstract: Purpose Following conversations at the 2026 International Cognitive-Communication Disorders Conference, this viewpoint advocates for the principled development of technology-based memory rehabilitation after traumatic brain injury (TBI) and presents an illustrative example for maximizing resources in the development of new interventions. Method This viewpoint discusses how technology may address key unmet needs in TBI memory rehabilitation, the design fundamentals for this line of work, and an illustrative example of relevant guiding principles for technology-delivered intervention development. Results Technology holds considerable potential to extend memory care beyond the therapy room, implement findings from the cognitive neuroscience literature in the memory rehabilitation space, and broaden the real-world reach of memory assessments and interventions. However, it is critical that interventions are carefully designed and tailored to this clinical population and use case. Conclusions As rehabilitation models adjust to encompass TBI as a chronic condition, technology-delivered interventions that are developed in collaboration with end users will grow in importance. These tools are especially relevant to memory rehabilitation. To move the field forward, we must conduct intervention development work that is careful, iterative, and inclusive of multiple sources of data and end-user perspectives.

papers.title: Targeting central thalamus with transcranial ultrasound reduces arousal in healthy volunteers.
papers.authors: Hopkins AR, Cain JA, White EA, Abakians SM, Monti MM.
papers.abstract: Using low-intensity focused transcranial ultrasound stimulation, we test the causal roles of the central thalamus in arousal and the pulvinar in visuospatial attention in the healthy human brain. In a within-subjects, counterbalanced design, 27 healthy volunteers (two females) complete a vigilance task (Psychomotor Vigilance Task) and a visuospatial attention task (Egly-Driver Task) before and after sham, central thalamic, and pulvinar sonication. Targeting the central thalamus slows responses and increases lapses in attention during the vigilance task, indicating reduced arousal. Pulvinar sonication reduces (and slows) responses to visual stimuli presented contralaterally, suggesting a disruption of contralateral visuospatial attention. These results provide causal evidence linking the pulvinar to visuospatial attention and the central thalamus to arousal in the healthy human brain and demonstrate that ultrasound can elicit distinct behavioral changes in healthy volunteers when delivered to close but functionally distinct thalamic regions, underscoring its potential as a tool for noninvasive brain mapping.

papers.title: Neural limits of temporal feature binding in human visual cortex.
papers.authors: Schönemann N, Merkel C, Strumpf H, Felßberg AM, Bartsch MV, Schoenfeld MA, Hopf JM.
papers.abstract: Humans are able to track the change of color and orientation (CO) of an object at a stunning rate. However, spatially separating those features slows this rate by an order of magnitude - a temporal limit of feature binding that is little understood. Here, we investigate the underlying mechanisms using high-temporal resolution cortical source localization of the magnetic field response elicited by CO-pairs alternating at different frequencies in color and orientation. We show that (1) binding requires a rapid recurrent modulation (~120 ms) of activity in V1/V2, whose latency is independent of the alternation rate. (2) Performance drops to chance when the alternation rate becomes too high to accommodate the recurrent process within a single alternation. (3) CO binding itself is mediated by color-based attention, which gradually biases re-occurring CO combinations containing the attended color. These observations together demonstrate that CO-binding across space depends on rapid recurrent processing in early visual cortex, with its temporal limit being set by the time this process takes to be completed. Binding ultimately results from a slower and gradual attentional bias of the recurrent process instantiating a form of stroboscopic stationarity in the stream of alternations for unambiguous discrimination of the correct feature-combination.

papers.title: The intermediate hippocampus integrates shock-observation and spatial information during observational fear memory in male rats.
papers.authors: Michon Linde F, Gazzola V, Keysers C.
papers.abstract: Learning where danger lurks by observing others requires linking another individual's distress to one's own representation of space. How the hippocampus implements this mapping is unknown. We recorded Neuropixels activity across the dorsal, intermediate and ventral hippocampus of male rats during contextual fear learning by observation, subsequent rest and recall. Observers showed increased immobility in the context where they had witnessed a conspecific receive footshocks, with substantial inter-individual variability. Pyramidal neurons were recruited by shock observation, with enriched shock-excited cells in the intermediate hippocampus. In the dorsal and intermediate hippocampus, shock-observation responses scaled with baseline place-field firing, revealing a gain-like conjunctive code between observed distress and observer's position. Following learning, shock-context spatial representations were selectively stabilized in the intermediate hippocampus, and post-learning sharp-wave ripples preferentially reactivated shock-context ensembles, especially in animals expressing contextual freezing. These findings identify candidate hippocampal mechanisms by which socially acquired threat information are mapped onto the observer's spatial representation and consolidated into memory.

papers.title: Cephalopod-inspired embodied camouflage system for simultaneous evasion of artificial and human visual perception.
papers.authors: Zhu X, Zhang J, Wang L, Liang X, Zhu J, Hu X.
papers.abstract: Differences in visual perception mechanisms between biological and artificial intelligence make it difficult to design camouflage that is both visually natural and effective against modern detectors. Existing adversarial approaches often create conspicuous patterns and are typically static, limiting their use in dynamic real-world scenarios. Here we present CephCam, an embodied closed-loop camouflage system that integrates environment-aware color extraction, optimization-based texture generation that jointly balances visual naturalness and detector evasion, and angle-aware display compensation for physical deployment. This system involves an eye-brain-skin framework of sensing, computation, and display, motivated by the naturally evolved cephalopod camouflage, but implemented with specialized cameras, computing modules, and OLED screens on a model vehicle. CephCam targets simultaneous evasion of both human observers and modern object detectors across diverse digital and physical environments, significantly outperforming strong baselines targeting either alone. These findings underscore shared vulnerabilities in human and artificial visual processing systems, showcasing CephCam's potential for robust, adaptive, and embodied camouflage applications.

papers.title: Paracrine TMSB4X signaling from oligodendrocytes promotes diffuse glioma dissemination.
papers.authors: Chai KM, Tsai CH, Lin MY, Teng TC, Chen YS, Liu SJ, Chang CR, Wang CY.
papers.abstract: White matter invasion underlies the lethality of diffuse glioblastoma (GBM), yet its microenvironmental drivers remain poorly defined. Here, we demonstrate that tumor-oligodendrocyte (OL) crosstalk actively promote white matter-associated glioma expansion. In the primary GBM or white matter-invasive glioma, OL lineage cells accumulate at tumor borders and enhance glioma proliferation and migration via secreted factors. Proteomic analysis combined with RNA sequencing identifies OL-derived TMSB4X (thymosin β-4) activates AKT signaling to sustain tumor expansion and invasion. Furthermore, glioma-derived TGF-β stimulates OL differentiation and TMSB4X production, establishing a feed-forward circuit that reinforces tumor progression. Critically, genetic or pharmacological blockade in tumor-OL interaction attenuates glioma outspreading along the white matter in vivo. These findings redefine the OLs as pro-invasive modulators and suggest OL-glioma crosstalk as a therapeutic target in diffuse GBM. Glioblastoma spreads through the brain's white matter while hijacking nearby oligodendrocytes. These cells release TMSB4X, which activates AKT signaling in tumor cells and promotes growth and invasion. In turn, tumors secrete TGF-β, which stimulates oligodendrocytes to produce more TMSB4X. This feed-forward loop may offer a new therapeutic target to prevent glioma from invading the white matter after surgical resection.

papers.title: "What a beautiful gift, life": Dignity therapy and the making of a legacy in a patient with grade 4 glioblastoma.
papers.authors: Sireci F, Rossi J, Pisanello A, Coluccio G, Montepietra S.
papers.abstract: Objectives Grade 4 glioblastoma (GBM) carries a median survival of 12-15 months and confronts patients with rapid functional decline, identity disruption, and existential distress. Dignity therapy (DT) is a brief, empirically supported psychotherapeutic intervention that reinforces meaning, generativity, and personal dignity in life-limiting illness. Its application in primary brain tumors, where neurological impairment may threaten the cognitive capacities DT relies on, has rarely been described. Methods We describe the psycho-oncological trajectory of a man in his mid-40s with GBM of the corpus callosum. Psychological assessment began at diagnosis, with parallel support pathways for the patient and his caregiver. DT was delivered during the window of maximal cognitive competence, following Chochinov's standard protocol within a Cognitive-Interactionist framework. The resulting generative document was printed as a book and distributed by the patient to several hundred members of his community, a spontaneous amplification of DT's generative function not previously documented. As callosal disconnection syndrome advanced, therapy adapted through embodied, musical, and relational modalities, maintaining psychological contact through the terminal phase. Results This case demonstrates the feasibility and clinical relevance of DT in neuro-oncology when delivered early and flexibly adapted to cognitive decline.
